papers.title: Key attributes for industry 4.0–enabled occupational safety and health management in modern methods of construction: a Delphi–VAHP approach
papers.abstract: The adoption of Industry 4.0 technologies presents significant opportunities to enhance occupational safety and health (OSH) management within modern methods of construction (MMC). However, organisations often lack clarity on which factors are crucial for the adoption of Industry 4.0 technologies for OSH improvement in MMC. Existing studies have mainly investigated individual technologies, adoption barriers, or organisational capability factors, without systematically identifying and prioritising the comprehensive set of people, organisational, technological, and infrastructure attributes that enable effective Industry 4.0-enabled OSH management in MMC. This study addresses this gap by identifying, validating, and prioritising the key attributes for effective Industry 4.0-enabled OSH management in MMC using a four-stage methodological approach comprising SLR, expert verification, Delphi method, and voting analytic hierarchy process (VAHP). Through a combination of systematic literature review (SLR) and expert verification, 21 attributes were identified and grouped into four clusters: people, organisation, technology, and infrastructure. The 21 identified and validated attributes were then ranked by a group of experts through a two-round Delphi survey. Following this, the weights and importance of attributes were determined using the voting analytical hierarchy process (VAHP). The results indicate that organisation and people clusters achieved the highest relative priorities; Management support, workforce competence, and technology acceptance were identified as the highest-priority attributes. These findings reveal a sociotechnical hierarchy in which organisational and human capabilities are prioritised above technological and infrastructural capabilities, suggesting successful Industry 4.0-enabled transformation for OSH improvement depends more on social-subsystem capability than on technology deployment alone.

papers.title: Sharps injuries among healthcare waste workers: Implications for biosafety and occupational vaccination – A systematic review with meta-analysis
papers.abstract: This systematic review and meta -analysis estimated the prevalence of sharps injuries among healthcare waste workers (HWW) and evaluated hepatitis B virus (HBV) vaccination coverage and HBV and hepatitis C virus (HCV) infections. PubMed, Scopus, Embase, LILACS, SciELO, the Virtual Health Library, the CAPES Periodicals Portal, and Google Scholar were searched through 19 May 2026. Twenty-two studies involving approximately 9,000 HWW and 1,722 sharps injuries were included. Random-effects meta -analyses used logit transformation and restricted maximum likelihood estimation. The pooled prevalence of sharps injuries was 34.1% (95% CI, 22.8–47.5%), with substantial heterogeneity (I 2 = 98.9%). HBV vaccination coverage was 31.1% (95% CI, 8.2–68.3%) and was not associated with sharps injury prevalence (β = 0.338; p = 0.544). Pooled HBV and HCV prevalence estimates were 2.3% (95% CI, 0.3–15.4%) and 3.36% (95% CI, 1.17–9.23%), respectively. No HCV seroconversion was reported in follow-up studies. Approximately one-third of HWW experienced sharps injuries, highlighting the need to strengthen waste segregation, personal protective equipment use, biosafety training, HBV vaccination, and occupational surveillance to improve worker safety and reduce preventable blood-borne infections.

papers.title: Cultivating high-reliable organizing: A holistic perspective
papers.abstract: High-reliable organizing (HRO) has long been associated with how organizations sustain reliable performance under conditions of complexity, uncertainty, and change. While Mindful Organizing (MO), and Resilience Engineering (RE) have generated important theoretical insights, guidance on how organizations can cultivate HRO in everyday organizing remains fragmented. This conceptual essay develops a holistic perspective that positions HRO as an ongoing accomplishment rather than a fixed organizational capability or the outcome of implementing isolated concepts. Through a systematic comparison of the five established MO processes and the four resilience potentials, we show how the two perspectives can be related while preserving their distinct analytical orientations. MO focuses on the collective organizing through which people notice, interpret, coordinate, and respond to emerging situations, while RE emphasizes organizational potentials to monitor, respond, anticipate, and learn under changing conditions. Building on this synthesis, we develop the holistic framework of HRO, identify two additional organizing processes— preoccupation with things that go right and self-awareness —and develop an approach to cultivating and operationalizing HRO through collaborative inquiry, driving forces, and situated practices. Rather than prescribing predefined practices, we argue that organizations can cultivate mindsets and directions of attention that guide how established concepts are translated to context-sensitive action while remaining grounded in the scientific foundations of HRO, MO, and RE. The essay contributes a theoretically grounded perspective for understanding and cultivating high-reliable organizing as an ongoing accomplishment in complex sociotechnical systems.

papers.title: Identifying a dynamic information trading zone framework via insights from full-scale emergency exercises
papers.abstract: The article examines how the co-creation of a Common Operational Picture (COP) in multi-actor crisis response operations can be understood through the concept of Information Trading Zones (ITZ). The analysis is grounded in the theory of Situation Awareness (SA), including Endsley’s conceptualisation of individual, Team SA and Shared SA, and draws on Galison’s notion of trading zones as intercalation, the insertion of an intermediate concept or mechanism to bridge existing explanatory levels. In this study, ITZ is introduced as an intercalating construct linking information exchange, sensemaking, and coordinated action. Drawing on extensive qualitative analyses of five full-scale crisis exercises, the study traces the evolution of an operational framework that conceptualises ITZ as both a precondition for and an integral component of the co-creation of a COP. Within this framework, ITZ are positioned as socio-technical spaces where information is negotiated, interpreted, and stabilised across organisational boundaries, enabling the development of Shared and Team SA in the face of uncertainty. The article offers concrete recommendations for both researchers and practice, outlining how the interplay among ITZ, COP, and SA can inform the design of information systems that more effectively support coordination, sense-making, and decision-making in Emergency Management contexts.

papers.title: How homophily and sociality propensity influence stakeholder diversity in wildfire risk management networks: an ERGM analysis
papers.abstract: Recent wildfire management strategies emphasize stakeholder engagement in risk management and prevention as a means of enhancing systemic safety and operational reliability. Despite its growing importance, guidance on how to effectively implement such engagement remains limited. This study addresses this gap by combining Social Network Analysis (SNA) and Exponential Random Graph Models (ERGMs) to examine a sample of 256 stakeholders across seven wildfire management networks in different European countries. The objective is to identify the propensity of stakeholders to form ties, network diversity and structural dependency within wildfire risk management networks. The results make two key contributions to risk and resilience in crisis and emergency management body of knowledge. First, we show that sociality – the propensity of stakeholders to establish connections – is shaped by stakeholder profiles. Second, we find that homophily – the propensity of stakeholders to connect with similar others – emerges across multiple categories alongside structural network effects. We discuss the dual role of these mechanisms that facilitate engagement while simultaneously constraining the diversity of stakeholder types. The findings invite policymakers promoting stakeholder engagement and stakeholder diversity as strategies in risk management and crisis response to critically reflect about the mechanisms through which such engagement can be effectively fostered.

papers.title: Beyond static hazard labels: a two-layer temporal object-attribute model of construction accident escalation
papers.abstract: Construction safety research often categorises hazards as fixed labels, such as falls, electrocution, or struck-by. This supports reporting but explains little about what makes a condition hazardous and how the condition evolves over time. Accident prevention requires an understanding of how a hazard becomes critical and when worker exposure becomes harmful. This paper develops and demonstrates a two-layer temporal object-attribute model that explains accident escalation as the coupling of worker-independent hazard growth and worker-specific exposure evolution. A hazard is redefined as a worker-independent temporal state of objects, hazardous attributes, relations, controls, and an impact zone. Worker exposure is modelled separately, as the worker’s relation to that state and its impact zone. An accident occurs when a critical hazard state and a harmful exposure state align under actuation conditions. The model is applied through backward reconstruction of 1065 OSHA construction accident reports across six categories: fall, heavy equipment, confined space, electrocution, struck-by falling object, and fire-related explosion. The analysis reconstructs precursor hazard states, exposure configurations, transition mechanisms, and terminal hazard, exposure, and accident states. Escalation was driven mainly by relation change rather than new energy, and the pathway differed by category. Falls and confined spaces escalated through exposure around an already hazardous condition, whereas electrocution, struck-by, and heavy-equipment cases required an explicit change in the hazard state. The paper contributes a temporal object-attribute definition of construction hazards, a two-layer account of escalation through hazard-exposure coupling, and an empirical demonstration of accidents as coupled trajectories.

papers.title: How media narratives shape public sentiment toward electric micromobility: Stronger effects for e-scooters than e-bikes
papers.abstract: Public sentiment toward electric micromobility, particularly e-scooters and e-bikes, is increasingly shaping safety debates and regulatory responses; yet, these attitudes and perceptions have not been systematically evaluated within a unified framework, nor is it clear to what extent they reflect stable judgments versus sensitivity to external narratives. This study addresses these gaps by quantifying public sentiment toward e-bikes and e-scooters and evaluating their responsiveness to controlled negative media narrative exposure. A unified survey framework was developed to enable consistent evaluation, combining statement-based measures with image-based scenario assessments. Two complementary studies were conducted with Australian participants. Study 1 (N = 1027) established baseline sentiment in the absence of media exposure, and Study 2 (N = 1025) examined how responses shift following controlled exposure to negative news headlines. The results showed that public sentiment is multi-dimensional and mixed. While both modes received moderate recognition in terms of sustainability and legitimacy, practical acceptance remained lower, particularly for e-scooters. Exposure to negative media narratives produced broader and more consistent shifts toward less favorable sentiments for e-scooters, especially in perceptions of rider behavior and public-space interaction, whereas e-bike responses remained comparatively stable and more robust to media narrative exposure. In contrast, evaluations of concrete negative situations showed no systematic change following exposure, indicating that these evaluations are grounded in situational interpretation rather than external framing. The findings suggest that public sentiment should be used cautiously to inform policy development. While consistent concerns linked to observable safety issues justify targeted interventions, broader sentiment shifts may reflect narrative influence rather than actual conditions. Effective policy should therefore be informed not only by public sentiment but also by objective evidence on behavior, exposure, and risk.

papers.title: A longitudinal comparison of shared and private e-scooter crashes, near-miss rates, attributions and characteristics
papers.abstract: As e-scooters have become increasingly common in urban areas, safety concerns have grown. However, most safety research does not distinguish between shared and private e-scooter use. Moreover, no studies have examined within-person changes in safety outcomes over time. This study followed Australian e-scooter riders (n = 285) across two survey waves conducted 12 months apart (follow-up and final) and comprised two analyses. First, we compared riders’ most recent near misses and crashes on shared and private e-scooters in terms of their characteristics and riders’ attributions. At follow-up, 32.7% of participants were private-only riders, 51.2% shared-only, and 16.1% mixed-use. Most near misses involved another road user (78.1% at follow-up, 70.1% at final), while a substantial share of crashes did not (55.6%, 59.1%). Private e-scooters accounted for the majority of near misses involving another road user at both waves (64.0%, 76.6%). Near misses occurring on shared e-scooters were consistently attributed to riders’ own lack of experience. Second, we modelled within-person changes in near-miss rates. A Poisson generalised linear mixed model, with a random intercept for participant and riding exposure as an offset, tested whether near-miss rate changed between waves, adjusting for sociodemographic characteristics. Near-miss rate did not differ significantly between waves. Riders outside Queensland and Victoria had a lower rate than Queensland riders (IRR = 0.27). Riders with primary/secondary or bachelor’s degree education were associated with lower rates than those with post-school qualifications. Riders’ attribution of shared e-scooter incidents to inexperience suggests onboarding and practical training warrant further evaluation.

papers.title: Contextual and temporal determinants of injury severity in electric micromobility: a comparative analysis of E-bikes and E-scooters
papers.abstract: The rapid adoption of electric micromobility has reshaped urban transport while introducing significant and evolving safety challenges. Despite a growing volume of injury data, existing research has largely examined e-scooters and e-bikes in isolation, and conventional analytical approaches have routinely failed to account for the spatial and temporal structure of injury events. This study provides a comparative analysis of injury patterns and severity determinants among e-scooter and e-bike users in the United States, using 2,413 emergency department cases from the National Electronic Injury Surveillance System for 2021 and 2022. Cases were identified through product-code screening and reproducible narrative-based classification. Injury patterns were examined descriptively, followed by binomial logistic regression incorporating demographic, clinical, behavioral, temporal, and location-context characteristics. Cluster-robust standard errors accounted for dependence within NEISS location groups, while interaction terms examined whether the association between motor-vehicle involvement and severe outcomes varied across injury environments. E-bike users had a higher crude severe-outcome rate than e-scooter users (15.0% vs. 11.2%), although vehicle type was not independently associated with severe outcome after adjustment (OR = 1.071, 95% CI: 0.834–1.374, p = 0.591). Age, diagnosis, body region, drug involvement, and location context were significantly associated with severe outcomes. A significant interaction between location context and motor-vehicle involvement was observed (OR = 2.456, 95% CI: 1.070–5.639, p = 0.034), indicating that the association between motor-vehicle involvement and severe outcome varied across recorded injury environments. Drawing on a Safe Systems perspective, the study argues that effective policy must address the interaction between users, vehicles, and the built environment, prioritizing dedicated infrastructure and conflict reduction with motorized traffic over device-level regulation alone.

papers.title: A systems analysis of fatal railway level crossing crashes
papers.abstract: Fatal railway level crossing crashes represent a public safety challenge. Existing data on these crashes is limited, mostly focusing on frequencies rather than providing an in-depth understanding of the underlying causes. This study aimed to demonstrate the utility of using coronial findings, supplemented with reports from investigation agencies, to understand the system-wide factors contributing to railway crossing crashes and to explore the proposed recommendations. A systems thinking accident analysis approach, the AcciMap technique, underpinned the analysis. Over a 20-year period, 151 cases were identified, involving a range of road user types. Of these cases, 135 included sufficient detail to extract contributory factors and recommendations. A total of 483 contributory factors were extracted and used to develop an aggregate AcciMap. Most factors were associated with road user behaviour and/or individual characteristics, as opposed to systemic issues. Unique contributory factors were identified for crashes occurring at active crossings (those with dynamic warnings present) versus passive crossings (those with signage only). A total of 184 recommendations were extracted and mapped using the AcciMap framework. Recommendations tended to take a system-wide view of preventing future occurrences, acknowledging the complexity of managing risk at the interface of two transport modes. The analysis provided important information to support crash prevention efforts, including a set of common systemic recommendations identified from the data that require collaborative efforts across road and rail stakeholders. Mechanisms for supporting this collaboration should be further explored. The study also provided learnings regarding the nature of coronial investigations and areas for potential improvement.

papers.title: Safety in military organizations –A scoping review
papers.abstract: Safety culture, safety climate, and safety behavior have all been examined in military settings, but the research remains fragmented. Many studies focus mainly on climate measures or isolated subdomains, which can overlook broader structural and cultural influences. A more integrated understanding is needed of how these concepts relate and support effective safety in military organizations. Of 31 eligible studies identified, with three set aside after quality appraisal, this scoping review brings together findings from 28 empirical studies to explore how safety is practiced and maintained at individual, group, and organizational levels. The review identifies several recurring factors linked to effective safety behavior, including targeted training, adaptive leadership, open communication, and psychologically safe environments for learning. Although safety climate assessments are widely used to capture perceptions of safety, relying too heavily on them may hide important power relations, cultural norms, and system-level constraints shaping frontline behavior. A repeated issue in the literature is the gap between formal safety policies and the adaptive practices needed in real operations, especially in combat or other high-risk situations. Since most available evidence comes from peacetime and training settings, caution is needed when extending these findings to operational environments. The review proposes a tentative conceptual framework in which leadership style, operational realism, and learning systems interact to influence safety-oriented behavior. Rather than making firm causal claims, it suggests that more flexible, learning-oriented models may explain observed safety dynamics better than strictly compliance-based approaches. Future research should address gaps in gender, team processes, measurement validity, and longitudinal change.

papers.title: Organizational safety and adaptive work practices in aquaculture
papers.abstract: The aquaculture industry is marked by considerable operational variability stemming from shifting environmental conditions, biological processes, and complex work activities. While prior research has focused primarily on technical safety, fish welfare, and formal safety management, less attention has been paid to how workers manage variability in everyday practice. This qualitative single-case study examines organizational variability in a Norwegian salmon-farming company by addressing two research questions: (1) How do aquaculture workers manage variability in their daily safety practices? and (2) How do local work practices influence organizational safety? The empirical material comprises documents and nine semi-structured interviews with operational and managerial personnel. The analysis draws on both safety theories and organizational learning perspectives. The findings show that workers manage variability through adaptive work practices grounded in practical experience, teamwork, and continuous adjustment to changing environmental and operational conditions, rather than through strict adherence to formal procedures. Local work practices influence organizational safety by creating and sustaining safety knowledge within stable communities of practice, where newcomers gradually develop the competence and judgment needed to work safely. Although formal safety management systems provide an important framework, their effectiveness depends on how well they are integrated with everyday operational practice. Rapid organizational growth challenges existing learning processes by making practical safety knowledge harder to transfer and sustain. The findings demonstrate that organizational safety is achieved not only through formal safety management systems but also through adaptive work practices and the social processes that enable workers to manage operational variability.

papers.title: Transitioning from traditional hospital design to activity-based care: A longitudinal case study of differential occupational health and safety consequences across clinical settings and professional roles
papers.abstract: The activity-based care (ABC) model, adapted from activity-based offices, has emerged as a new approach to healthcare facility design. Evidence on its consequences for occupational health and safety-relevant outcomes remains limited. The study examines how transitioning from a traditional hospital design to the ABC model is associated with changes in employee experiences of task–environment alignment and psychosocial work environment, self-reported health, sick leave and turnover over time, and differences in changes across professional roles and clinic types. A repeated-measures survey was conducted in an outpatient hospital unit across 10 specialised clinics. Data were collected 3 months before relocation and at 6 and 18 months post-relocation. Generalised least-squares models examined change over time and tested interactions with professional role and clinic type. Sick leave and turnover were analysed over approximately 1 year before and after relocation using segmented interrupted time-series regression. Ratings of task–environment alignment varied across clinic types and professional roles. Consultation-based clinics and physicians and administrative employees showed persistent declines over time, while surgical/radiology clinics and nursing roles remained stable or improved. Stress and recovery indicators worsened similarly across all groups. Psychosocial conditions were stable, though job satisfaction, perceived quality of work and referral intentions declined. Turnover remained unchanged, while sick leave varied across contexts and roles. The consequences of ABC implementation are not uniform but depend on the alignment of the redesigned workspace and the task demands of different clinical settings and professional groups, a contingency that cannot be easily detected with single time-point post-occupancy evaluation.

papers.title: Healthy crew, healthy life: The captain’s role in commercial fishing crew health
papers.abstract: Objectives Commercial fishermen engage in one of the most dangerous professions in the United States. This qualitative study explored how the internal priorities of commercial fishermen captains influence the health and well-being of their crew members. Methods Data were collected via semi-structured qualitative interviews conducted under the 2025 Southeast and Gulf Coast Fishing First Aid and Safety Training program. Commercial fishermen and individuals working adjacent to the industry (n = 10) were recruited using purposive sampling. Using a priori qualitative coding, two coders performed a thematic analysis using ATLAS.ti. Results Overall, participants reported that crew health and wellness were affected by the captain’s attitudes. Participants (40%) explored crew preparedness as a central theme in captains’ approaches to crew well-being, with the captain’s knowledge of pre-existing conditions allowing for a proactive approach to medication management and injury/illness reduction (30%). Some (20%) highlighted a conflict of priorities between crew productivity and well-being or observed that captains’ attitudes towards zero-tolerance policy against substance use would influence substance use onboard the vessel (20%). Conclusion Preparing captains and crew members with safety knowledge and skills can mitigate predictable hazards. These findings highlight the importance of continued research and programming surrounding proactive health management among commercial fishermen captains.

papers.title: Are airbag vests effective in reducing thoracoabdominal injuries in motorcycle crashes? An epidemiological perspective
papers.abstract: Background Powered two-wheeler riders are disproportionately exposed to serious and fatal injuries in road crashes, trunk trauma representing a major contributor to this burden. Wearable airbags have been developed to mitigate impact forces on the trunk. We aimed to assess the effectiveness of inflated airbag vests in reducing the risk of trunk injuries among motorcyclists involved in real-world crashes. Methods We conducted a retrospective observational study combining two datasets of crash-involved motorcyclists: the EDAIR survey, targeting airbag users, with self-reported crash circumstances and injuries; and the SECU2RM survey, with self-reported crash circumstances and injuries extracted from linked trauma registry. EDAIR riders equipped with an inflated airbag vest during the crash were compared to riders without or with non-inflated airbag from EDAIR ( internal analysis) and SECU2RM ( external analysis). Health outcomes included thoracoabdominal injuries (TAI) and serious TAI. Risk ratios were estimated using log-binomial regression with propensity score weighting. Results Inflated airbag vest was associated with a 50% lower risk of TAI in the internal analysis (N = 764, RR = 0.50, 95%CI: 0.35–0.68) and a 37% lower risk in the external analysis (N = 853, RR = 0.63, 95%CI: 0.43–0.93). Associations with serious TAI were inconclusive. Conclusion This study provides the first real-world evaluation of airbag vest effectiveness. Despite distinct study populations and sources of bias, both analyses exhibited protective associations between inflated airbag and thoracoabdominal injury risk, consistent with biomechanical evidence. These findings support potential public health value of airbag vests. Larger-scale studies with improved crash kinetics and rider’s characterization are warranted to confirm these findings.

papers.title: Rural occupational health in Colombia: policy–practice gaps among agricultural workers in Bolívar, Valle del Cauca
papers.abstract: This study examines policy–practice gaps in occupational safety and health (OSH) protection among agricultural workers in Bolívar, Valle del Cauca, Colombia. A multi-method design combined 14 semi-structured interviews and two focus groups with an adapted ILO Vision Zero Fund survey administered to 200 agricultural workers. Survey data were analyzed descriptively and through exploratory Multiple Correspondence Analysis (MCA), and qualitative and quantitative findings were integrated during interpretation. Findings showed multidimensional patterns involving occupational protection, working conditions, health-service availability, agricultural practices, and productive autonomy. These patterns coexisted with informal, seasonal, short-term, day-labor, and subsistence work, limited occupational risk coverage, discontinuous prevention and training, and fragmented institutional coordination. Qualitative findings further highlighted women’s combined productive and care roles, local and traditional knowledge, community participation, and heterogeneity across territorial settings and agricultural practices as relevant to prevention and decision-making. Conventional social protection and occupational risk arrangements centered on formal, contributory employment may not fully respond to dispersed and unstable rural work. Strengthening rural OSH requires integrated, territorially adapted, gender-sensitive strategies linking prevention, social protection, sustained training, institutional coordination, community participation, and productive autonomy. The findings support assessing differentiated and progressive protection pathways, including the feasibility of subsidized occupational risk coverage for more vulnerable workers and small productive units, combined with contributory mechanisms where work arrangements are more stable. By linking worker-level realities with institutional and policy-implementation gaps, this study provides evidence to inform more equitable rural OSH policies responsive to diverse territorial realities in Colombia.

papers.title: Safety concepts through a memetic lens
papers.abstract: Within safety practice and science there are countless ideas, approaches and concepts to manage safety. Some of these safety concepts are picked up, discussed widely and spread, while others do not. Little is known about this subject. This paper provides a unique perspective on the development and adoption of safety concepts by using an evolutionary framework to explore reasons why. As a case, this paper traces the historic development of one of safety’s most influential and iconic safety concepts, the accident triangle, over nearly a century through successive cycles of replication, variation, and selection. Knowledge of factors that influence the adoption of safety concepts can contribute to the design of more effective concepts that attract attention and of social and organisational environments that are receptive of these concepts. In the end, provided the concepts in question are useful, this can contribute to enhancing safety and reducing harm. In addition, the insights gained in this paper can help safety professionals and academics to critically reflect on the development of safety concepts, to help them better understand how safety concepts evolve and can change meaning leading to various interpretations and reflect on what this means for their own adoption of concepts and eventually their practice.

papers.title: Unsupervised health index estimation in rotating machinery via domain-constrained autoencoders with residual-based loss adaptation
papers.abstract: Within Prognostics and Health Management (PHM), data-driven approaches are widely used to assess the condition of rotating machinery. However, constructing a reliable Health Index (HI) remains challenging particularly in unsupervised settings where explicit degradation labels are unavailable. Autoencoder-based methods can extract degradation-sensitive representations, but they often fail to produce HIs that are simultaneously monotonic, bounded, and physically consistent. Existing constrained approaches typically rely on manually tuned loss functions or optimizer-level modifications, which may lead to optimization conflicts and limited robustness. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a domain-constrained convolutional autoencoder for unsupervised HI estimation. The framework embeds trendability, monotonicity, and boundary constraints directly into the loss function and adaptively regulates their influence through a residual-based weighting mechanism. Unlike static penalty selection, the proposed strategy updates each constraint multiplier according to its observed violation during training, reducing the need for manual loss-weight calibration. A curriculum-guided initialization is further introduced to progressively enforce local constraints after the model has learned degradation-sensitive representations. The framework is validated on the PRONOSTIA and XJTU-SY datasets against a constrained autoencoder benchmark, demonstrating improved HI consistency and generalization. Although validated only on bearing datasets, the proposed weighting strategy is independent of the underlying architecture and may be extended to other PHM applications involving the joint optimization of multiple degradation-informed objectives.

papers.title: Data-augmented maritime accident severity prediction: A port state control records-based fusion approach
papers.abstract: Data-driven maritime accident analysis based on mainstream accident databases is approaching a high performance ceiling, calling for further breakthroughs from both data quality and modelling perspectives. Port State Control (PSC) inspection records provide additional pre-accident vessel safety information, offering a valuable opportunity to improve accident severity prediction. This study therefore proposes a PSC-assisted accident severity prediction framework that provides a basis for pre-accident assessment. First, a multi-source prediction database is constructed by integrating Paris MoU PSC inspection records with accident information from the Global Integrated Shipping Information System. To address the limited matched samples and high-dimensional categorical features, a two-stage augmentation strategy is developed. Finally, tree-model-based feature selection is applied, and predictive performance is evaluated. The results show that incorporating PSC data reduces the average Mean Squared Error (MSE) by 1.15%. Cross-validation further shows that the complete framework achieves an additional 1.99% reduction in average MSE compared with the PSC–accident fusion-only setting. In particular, the best-performing LightGBM model achieves an MSE reduction of 11.22% relative to the original accident-data-only baseline. This study demonstrates that PSC inspection records are a valuable supplementary data source for maritime accident severity prediction and highlights their significant role in enhancing vessel accident prediction models.

papers.title: Cybersecurity risk assessment in autonomous transport systems: A semi-quantitative framework incorporating logistics disruption propagation
papers.abstract: The increasing reliance of autonomous transport systems on vehicle-to-infrastructure communication, fleet-management platforms, positioning services, and warehouse coordination creates cybersecurity risks that may extend beyond an individual vehicle and affect logistics continuity. This study develops a scenario-based, semi-quantitative framework for the comparative assessment of cybersecurity risks in an SAE Level 4 autonomous freight corridor. The framework adapts the threat-analysis logic of ISO/SAE 21434 and combines attack feasibility with four consequence dimensions: safety impact, financial impact, operational disruption, and disruption propagation. Seven standardised cyber threat scenarios were evaluated using author-assigned ratings based on an operational five-point scoring rubric. Criterion weights were specified as structured case-study assumptions through a pairwise-comparison procedure, and the resulting risk scores were examined using five alternative weighting configurations, ablation of the disruption-propagation criterion, one-at-a-time input perturbations, Spearman rank correlations, and sensitivity analysis of the risk-classification thresholds. Under the baseline assumptions, V2I/ETA falsification obtained the highest risk score (R=16.80) and was classified as Critical, while denial-of-service affecting telematics and fleet-management systems ranked second (R=15.20) and was classified as High. These two scenarios retained their positions under all weighting configurations. Removing the disruption-propagation criterion did not change the ordinal ranking of the seven scenarios, but it changed the magnitude of the risk scores, particularly for scenarios affecting shared communication and coordination processes. The framework is designed as an exploratory semi-quantitative prioritisation tool. Dynamic network propagation, node-to-node transition probabilities, time-dependent cascade trajectories, and recovery processes fall outside the analytical scope of the study. The framework instead supports transparent comparison of cyber threat scenarios and links baseline risk, propagation-related consequences, proposed controls, and illustrative residual risk under explicitly stated case-study assumptions.

papers.title: Availability-based service-contract risk under true-demand failure and spurious shutdown: Dynamic and dependent tree theory quantification and finite-horizon propagation
papers.abstract: This paper studies provider-side risk screening for availability-based service contracts when downtime arises from failure after genuine demand or service loss following a spurious changeover. A self-contained two-fault-tree Dynamic and Dependent Tree Theory (D2T2) benchmark represents a modified pressure-vessel cooling system. The primary pump module is evaluated at equilibrium; the backup module includes startup failure and transient operation. The contract layer combines immediate failure with a mutually exclusive first-passage contribution after successful transfer. Direct generator-flux and Boolean checks correct a duplicated conditional weighting in the primary trigger intensity. Evaluations from 0 to 500 h are alternative restoration or reset scenarios. For the illustrative one-year contract with both durations set to 500 h, mean downtime is 35.322/382.293 h and breach probability is 0.5634/0.7992 under repair-enabled/mission-end recovery. The corresponding 95% Expected Shortfalls are EUR 46,344/EUR 420,888. These are two specified recovery scenarios, not identification bounds or uncertainty intervals with statistical coverage. Including the spurious branch raises mean downtime by 3.8%/3.8%. A stationary-marginal independent-pump approximation gives lower exposure, but changes mission dynamics as well as dependence. The contribution is the causal integration of disjoint regimes, immediate entry and first passage into contractual loss. Absolute pricing and acceptance require operational recovery data; the benchmark is not empirically calibrated.

papers.title: How anger, anxiety, and sleepiness shape everyday driving behaviour: A repeated-measures diary study with actigraphy
papers.abstract: Introduction: Driver behavior is a leading contributor to road crashes. Emotions such as anger and anxiety, along with fatigue, are well-established risk factors for unsafe driving. However, most research examines these influences at a single time point and overlooks how traits and situational context may interact to shape behavior. Method: This study used a seven-day diary design with 35 licensed drivers (Mage = 44.25; SD = 15.11; 54 % women) to investigate how anger, anxiety, and fatigue relate to aberrant and positive driving behaviors across everyday trips. A secondary aim was to explore whether trait propensities for anger and anxiety interact with situational context to shape behavior. A total of 346 trips were recorded, capturing trip characteristics, emotional states, sleepiness (Karolinska Sleepiness Scale), and self-reported behaviors (Driver Behaviour Questionnaire). Sleep was measured via wrist-worn actigraphy. Results: Anger and anxiety were low but common, reported on 31 % and 48 % of trips, respectively. Generalized estimating equations showed that trait anxiety was associated with increased odds of experiencing both anxiety and anger. Passenger presence and congestion were also associated with experiencing anxiety, and anger-prone drivers were more likely to experience anxiety under high congestion. Higher congestion was associated with fewer aberrant behaviors, consistent with drivers adjusting to increased demand. However, this pattern was weaker among drivers with higher trait anxiety, who reported more violations, errors, and lapses, specifically under high congestion. A similar interaction emerged for trait anger and violations. Aggressive violations were associated with anger, and this association varied by level of sleepiness; with sleepiness weakening the anger-aggression relationship while strengthening the anxiety-aggression relationship. Positive behaviors were associated with longer preceding-night sleep and driving without passengers. Conclusions: These exploratory findings suggest that driving behavior may be conditional on the combination of who the driver is and the context in which they drive.

papers.title: Beyond risk factors: Spiritual fitness and existential well-being as protective resources in the impulsivity–unsafe driving link
papers.abstract: Introduction: Unsafe driving contributes substantially to road traffic crashes, and impulsivity is a consistent behavioral risk factor; however, the mechanisms translating impulsivity into unsafe driving remain unclear, limiting targeted intervention. Method: Across two studies, we tested whether two modifiable psychological resources—spiritual fitness (SF; a secular construct reflecting value-based decision-making and moral conduct in traffic) and existential well-being (EWB)—mediate the link between trait impulsivity and aggressive/hostile driving behaviors (AHB) and anxiety-based performance deficits (APD). Study 1 used hierarchical and logistic regressions controlling for sex, driving experience, and crash involvement. Study 2 re-tested the model longitudinally over six months using bias-corrected bootstrapping (5,000 resamples), controlling for baseline mediator and outcome levels. Results: In Study 1, adding SF and EWB reduced impulsivity’s effects on AHB (β = 0.287 to 0.095) and APD (β = 0.292 to 0.092), with incremental ΔR2 of 0.132 and 0.152, respectively. Lifetime crash involvement was independently associated with lower EWB (OR = 0.69 per SD, 95% CI [0.49, 0.97]); drivers in the lower half of EWB showed roughly double the crash-involvement rate. In Study 2, total indirect effects were significant for AHB (ab = 0.037, 95% CI [.004, 0.078]) and APD (ab = 0.050, 95% CI [.010, 0.097]); EWB was the only significant longitudinal mediator of APD. An exposure-adjusted Poisson model corroborated these findings: each SD of EWB predicted a 34% lower crash rate per year licensed (IRR = 0.66), whereas impulsivity predicted an elevated rate (IRR = 1.51). Conclusions: Impulsivity affects unsafe driving indirectly through SF and EWB, with full mediation for APD (via EWB) and indirect-only mediation for AHB. Practical Applications: Brief EWB screening may aid fitness-for-duty assessment and post-license rehabilitation; a 4–6 session CBT-based module targeting rumination, intrusive thoughts, and attentional control is proposed as a testable intervention hypothesis pending controlled evaluation.

papers.title: Rider knowledge and self-reported compliance with e-scooter speed limits
papers.abstract: Introduction: E-scooter use and injuries have risen, prompting governments to tighten regulations. Knowledge of, and compliance with, the relevant regulations are poor in many jurisdictions. This study includes private and shared riders and measures both perceived compliance (respondents’ own beliefs about speed limits) and reported compliance (after respondents were told the legal limits), allowing a more careful examination of how knowledge may relate to compliance. Method: Riders were surveyed on their knowledge of speed limits and self-reported compliance in Queensland, Australia, in April and December 2024, and in April 2025, following a reduction in the footpath speed limit from 25 km/h to 12 km/h in November 2022. Using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM), we estimated two knowledge models (Model 1: 2024; Model 2: 2025) and two compliance models: perceived compliance (Model 3: 2024, based on respondents’ self-reported speed limits) and reported compliance (Model 4: 2025, after respondents were told the legal limits). Results: Knowledge of speed limits was low and fell further in 2025. Models 1 and 2 showed that rider type (shared, private or mixed use) and riding frequency predicted correct knowledge. Older and female respondents reported greater compliance, while more frequent riders reported lower compliance. Self-reported speed limits for other (non-footpath) locations were consistently negatively associated with perceived and reported compliance. By contrast, self-reported speed limits on footpath had no significant association with perceived compliance, and showed only a weak, borderline-significant association with reported compliance (Model 4). Effect sizes were modest throughout. Conclusions: Knowledge of e-scooter speed limits was poor, but riders more commonly underestimated than overestimated speed limits, particularly on non-footpaths. Over-estimation of the speed limit was associated with lower perceived and reported compliance (in non-footpath locations), though the evidence for this pattern was based on modest path coefficients. Practical Applications: Recommendations for improvement made.

papers.title: Subjective risk from the side? Investigating cyclists’ perceptions during overtaking maneuvers in a bicycle simulator
papers.abstract: Introduction: For cyclists in urban traffic, being overtaken by motorized vehicles is a daily occurrence. This situation can be objectively and subjectively safety–critical, particularly when drivers maintain an insufficient passing distance. It remains unclear which factors in these situations particularly affect cyclists’ perception of safety. This experiment therefore examines how different overtaking distances, vehicle types, overtaking speeds, and cycling infrastructures influence cyclists’ subjective safety in a bicycle simulator. Method: Twenty-eight participants experienced 36 overtaking scenarios in a controlled, simulated environment. They were asked to rate their subjective safety immediately after each overtaking maneuver, while lateral position was continuously recorded. Results: The results showed that passing distance and vehicle type had the largest effects on subjective safety, with small distances and large vans leading to the lowest safety ratings. Overtaking speed and cycling infrastructure also significantly affected subjective safety, but with smaller effect sizes. There were no interactions between the manipulated factors, indicating that they acted additively on cyclists’ safety perception within the tested conditions. Additionally, cyclists showed slight adjustments in their lateral position in response to the overtaking maneuver, moving closer to the curb. Conclusions: Overall, cyclists’ safety perception during overtaking was influenced by multiple additive factors, including vehicle and infrastructure characteristics. The study also showed that cyclists’ perception during overtaking situations could be investigated in a controlled simulator environment. Practical Applications: The findings highlight the importance of legal regulations on passing distances, vehicle types, speed limits, and cycling infrastructures. Targeting even individual factors may already enhance perceived safety. Additionally, simulator-based approaches allow the investigation of other (overtaking) situations that would be too risky or impractical in real traffic.

papers.title: Retrospective analysis of risk factors associated with road ambulance crashes and injuries in Victoria, Australia
papers.abstract: Introduction: Paramedics in developed countries are more likely to be killed while driving for work compared to the national average for all occupations. Most previous research has examined risk factors associated with road ambulance crashes in the United States where the types of emergency vehicles, medical personnel, and operating conditions may not be generalizable to other countries. Methods: This study examined risk factors associated with road ambulance crashes and injuries occurring between May 2017 and December 2023 using data from a single state-wide ambulance service in Victoria, Australia. Results: Factors associated with crash and injury crash risk were examined using multivariable logistic regression analyses. Of the 2,524 crashes with a reported outcome, two resulted in serious injuries, 2.6% resulted in personal injury, 2.7% required a vehicle to be towed, and 94.6% resulted in vehicle/property damage. The most common crash type across all levels of severity involved a collision with another vehicle. Metropolitan location, intersections, inexperienced paramedics and first responders (ambulance community officers) were associated with increased odds of a crash. Responding with warning lights and sirens, and traveling with a patient on board were both associated with reduced odds of a crash. Factors associated with increased odds of injury crash included traveling on public streets or roads, traveling on freeways or highways, involvement of at least one other vehicle, intersections, and single responder ambulances. Future research should aim to reduce missing data to improve the validity and generalizability of these findings. Conclusions: This is the first study to examine crash and injury crash risk factors associated with road ambulance crashes in Australian paramedics. Practical applications: The findings identify environment, trip, paramedic and vehicle related factors associated with ambulance crashes and injuries that can be used to support interventions for the areas and individuals at greatest risk.

papers.title: Odds of sickness absence and disability pension after bicycle injuries: A Norwegian nationwide register study
papers.abstract: Introduction: Increased bicycling is a key strategy for health and environmental goals, yet it may increase the number of cycling injuries, which is a risk factor for subsequent work disability. Low socioeconomic status (SES) is a known risk factor for both general traffic injuries and work disability, but less is known about social inequalities in long-term work disability following bicycle-specific accidents. This study assessed the risk of work disability among injured bicyclists and investigated associations with SES and injury severity. Method: We conducted a nationwide population-based case-control study, linking Norwegian Trauma Registry data (2015–2018) with administrative registries on welfare benefits and SES. The sample included 975 injured bicyclists (cases) aged 18–58 and 4,875 matched controls. Work disability, operationalized as receipt of sickness benefits, work assessment allowance, and disability pension, was assessed for four years post-injury. Injury severity was classified using the New Injury Severity Score (NISS). Results: Cases had significantly higher rates of work disability than controls. Four years post-accident, the odds of being on work assessment allowance or disability pension were more than doubled for cases (OR 2.44, 95% CI: 1.82–3.27). The odds increased markedly with injury severity (OR 7.40 for NISS ≥ 16). Bicycle injuries were more common among higher-income individuals (52% in the highest income quartile), in contrast to patterns observed for other road user groups. The relative increase in work disability associated with injury was stronger among high-income individuals (OR 3.32) than among low-income individuals (OR 1.26). Conclusions: Bicycle injuries substantially increased the odds of long-term work disability. Injured cyclists had a high socioeconomic profile, but injury severity was the strongest predictor of long-term work disability. Practical Applications: These findings indicate that assessment of the burden of cycling injuries should incorporate long-term functional and socioeconomic consequences.

papers.title: The dooring risk in Europe: Cycling infrastructure guidelines often underestimate the car door zone
papers.abstract: Background: Although collisions between cyclists and the opening doors of parked vehicles (dooring) are not among the most frequent types of accidents, their consequences are often serious. In this study, we focused on this type of accident, specifically in the common setting of parallel on-street parking. Methods: Door zones of the 50 best-selling passenger cars on the European market were manually measured. Cycling-infrastructure design recommendations were compiled for 24 EU Member States and the United Kingdom.Results: Recommended cyclist clearance from parked vehicles is often shorter than the reach of fully opened car doors, creating a clear collision risk. We assessed 1,250 combinations of door widths and buffer sizes (83 unique); the door zone extended into the cycle lane in 92.5% of combinations, and protruded by more than 50 cm in 10%. In addition, we found that the average width of passenger cars sold in Europe has increased by 9 cm over the last 20 years, further exacerbating the mismatch between vehicle dimensions and current cycling-infrastructure guidelines. Conclusions: To our knowledge, this is the first study to empirically evaluate the relationship between actual car–door reach and official design guidelines. Our findings demonstrate a systematic mismatch between current recommendations and vehicle dimensions, highlighting a persistent safety risk for cyclists. These results provide a strong evidence base for revising design standards. Where a cycle lane is placed beside parallel parking, the findings indicate that designers should provide on the order of 2.0 m of usable cycling space to enable safe maneuvering when doors are opened unexpectedly. Practical Applications: Urban planners and policymakers should update cycling–infrastructure guidelines to account for wider vehicles and prevent dooring collisions. In addition, broader strategies such as restricting oversized vehicles in urban cores or redesigning street layouts to eliminate conflicts between cyclists and parked cars should be considered.

papers.title: Head and thorax impact conditions in bicycle and e-scooter collisions with cars: Insights from an extensive multibody simulation dataset
papers.abstract: Introduction :The rapid growth of bicycle and e-scooter use has led to an increase in related injuries, with the most severe affecting the head and, less often, the thorax during collisions with cars. Although both groups use the same helmets, impact conditions remain insufficiently documented to evaluate current protections or determine whether their requirements should differ. To address this gap, this work aims to characterize head and thorax impacts during bicycle– and e-scooter–car collisions. Method: A full-factorial accident-reconstruction study using multibody simulations was conducted to assess the effects of crash configuration (crash scenarios, vehicle types, speeds, etc.) on impact chronology, impact velocity, impacted body regions, and injury metrics (peak accelerations, HIC 15 , thoracic Con3ms) of the head and thorax for impacts with both the car and the ground. Results: Across 2,475 simulations, e-scooter riders showed higher normal head impact velocities than cyclists (median 4.2 vs 3.2 m/s for car impacts and 3.3 vs 3.1 m/s for ground impacts), while cyclists exhibited higher tangential velocities. Similar trends were found for the thorax. These differences led to greater injury severity for e-scooter riders, who reached a median HIC 15 of 1,810 compared with 1,347 for cyclists, with the highest values most often occurring during ground impacts. Higher vehicle speed, e-scooter use, SUV involvement, and “head-on” or “side-on-head” scenarios were associated with increased normal head and thorax impact velocities, as well as higher HIC. Conclusions and Practical Applications: These findings are highly valuable for the design and evaluation of targeted protective technologies for bicyclists and e-scooter users.

papers.title: Exploring the role of exposure and design characteristics in the safety of bicycle streets in the Netherlands
papers.abstract: Introduction : The ‘bicycle street’ is a street design choice used to prioritize cycling on low-speed urban roads. Similar concepts exist across many countries and have increased in popularity over the last two decades. However, empirical evidence on the objective safety of this type of infrastructure has remained limited. This study aims to fill this gap by exploring the relationship between bicycle street design and injury crashes in the Netherlands, while controlling for exposure. Method: For a sample of 87 bicycle streets – split into 140 unique design segments – data were collected on design characteristics, bicycle and motor vehicle counts, and police-recorded injury crashes from 2018 to 2023. Negative binomial regression models were estimated for six crash groups, distinguishing between road sections and intersections, and between total injury crashes and cyclist involvement. Results: As expected, traffic exposure was strongly related to crash frequency, with bicycle volume primarily associated with road-section crashes and motor-vehicle volume with intersection crashes. Several predictors appear related to increased crash counts: a higher intersection density, the presence of roadside parking, wider edge strips, centerline marking and a shopping/entertainment environment. Brick pavement, a wider center strip and a wider usable riding lane were associated with fewer crashes. Conclusions: The results largely support insights from earlier literature: intersections and parking maneuvers are known risk factors, brick pavement is related to lower speeds, and a retail environment often involves more interactions and thus more potential conflicts. The findings also indicate that scross-sectional design is relevant for safety. Practical applications: Road authorities should carefully consider the available road space, surrounding environment, traffic mix and the street’s function in the (bicycle and motor-vehicle) network before deciding if a street is suitable to become a bicycle street. Designs should maintain sufficient usable lane width for cyclists, minimize parking and consider brick pavement.

papers.title: Understanding public perceptions about contemporary speed enforcement methods: The pros and cons of mobile average speed cameras
papers.abstract: Introduction: Speeding continues to be the largest contributor to road fatalities, with speed enforcement the primary countermeasure in place to prevent this behavior. Mobile average speed cameras have the potential to further prevent speeding behavior, as they are more unpredictable and can capture speeding along wider lengths of road. However, little is known about how drivers perceive these cameras, including deterrence related perceptions and perceptions of procedural justice. As such, this study aimed to examine the perceptions, attitudes, and concerns about mobile average speed camera enforcement methods, compared to other traditional methods (e.g., fixed spot speed cameras, mobile spot speed cameras, vehicle mounted mobile radar, and fixed average speed cameras). Method: A total of 887 respondents ( M age = 42.8 years, SD = 17.7 years), completed a cross-sectional survey. Results: It was identified that mobile average speed enforcement occupied a middle ground in terms of deterrence perceptions compared to the other enforcement methods, yet they were viewed less favorably than fixed enforcement methods in terms of fairness, respect, and trustworthiness. Correlations, a linear regression and ANOVAs revealed the large role dysfunctional attitudes plays in intention to speed when there is mobile average speed enforcement. It was also found that respondents expressed reduced confidence in mobile average speed camera effectiveness across complex road environments, particularly among those holding stronger dysfunctional, pro-speeding attitudes. Conclusions: The results highlight that, in addition to deterrence capacity, perceived legitimacy and attitudes towards speeding can influence the effectiveness of mobile average speed enforcement. Practical Applications: The findings therefore suggest that transparent implementation, community engagement, and complementary behavioral interventions should also be considered to maximize road safety outcomes.

papers.title: Uncovering hidden factors in traffic crashes through text mining of Ohio police narratives
papers.abstract: Introduction: Road traffic crashes pose a significant public health challenge, with traditional crash data often relying on broad classifications that obscure critical details. This study addresses the knowledge gap created by ambiguous categories, “Other Improper Action” and “Not Discernible,” within the Ohio crash dataset. Method: Employing a multi-faceted analytical framework that combines descriptive statistics, N-gram analysis, and Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) topic modeling on over 67,000 free-text crash narratives from 2020 to 2024, the study uncovers the latent contributing circumstances previously masked by these labels. Results: The analysis reveals that “Other Improper Action” incidents are disproportionately linked to adverse environmental conditions and a lack of formal traffic control. Text mining further extracted hidden behavioral and environmental factors, predominantly severe spatial awareness deficits, striking legally parked vehicles in urban environments and environmentally induced loss of vehicle control resulting in infrastructure strikes. In contrast, “Not Discernible” crashes are more prevalent in daylight and at signalized intersections. Rather than a lack of physical information, the NLP models revealed that investigative ambiguity primarily stems from conflicting driver accounts, specifically mutual lane change encroachment and right-of-way disputes. Conclusions: These findings not only validate the presence of recognized crash mechanisms, but transform vague data classifications into actionable intelligence. Practical Applications: This methodology provides transportation safety professionals with the granular evidence needed to refine statewide data collection protocols and develop targeted, engineering-backed safety interventions.

papers.title: Driving safety in dementia: An updated systematic review of crash risk and driving impairment
papers.abstract: Introduction: Dementia is a progressive neurodegenerative condition associated with declines in cognitive functions essential for safe driving. While on-road and simulator studies consistently demonstrate impaired driving performance, evidence regarding motor vehicle crash (MVC) risk remains mixed. This review synthesised contemporary evidence on the impact of dementia on real-world driving behaviour and crash involvement. Methods: A systematic search of CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, Transport, PsycINFO, and Scopus was conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. Quantitative studies published from January 2015 were included if they examined licensed adult drivers with clinically diagnosed dementia and reported outcomes related to MVC involvement, driving performance, or unsafe behaviour compared with cognitively healthy drivers. Methodological quality was assessed using the Joanna Briggs Institute tools. The review was registered with PROSPERO (CRD420251107288). Results: Thirteen studies met the inclusion criteria, including cross-sectional, cohort, and case–control designs. Findings for MVC involvement were heterogeneous: population-based studies generally reported no increased crash risk, whereas studies of medically referred drivers indicated elevated risk in selected subgroups. In contrast, studies examining driving errors and unsafe behaviours consistently demonstrated poorer performance among drivers with dementia, particularly in cognitively demanding situations such as hazard response and intersection negotiation. Naturalistic studies further identified persistent unsafe events during everyday driving, even among individuals adopting compensatory strategies in early disease. Conclusions: Dementia is associated with clinically meaningful impairments in driving behaviour and performance, evident even in the early stages of the disease. Differences in exposure, self-regulation, and regulatory processes largely explain variability in MVC findings. A multidimensional approach integrating MVC, performance-based, and naturalistic data is required to inform fitness-to-drive decisions. Practical applications: MVC involvement alone is an insensitive safety indicator. Performance-based and naturalistic measures provide more sensitive markers of impairment, supporting earlier risk identification, targeted intervention, and the development of in-vehicle monitoring and assistive technologies to enhance safety and prolong safe mobility.

papers.title: Quantifying distance to crossings in pedestrian railroad trespassing crashes using aerial imagery with exploratory semi-supervised learning
papers.abstract: Introduction: Railroad trespassing is entering or occupying a railroad right-of-way or property without authorization. Despite being illegal, it is one of the major causes of rail-related fatalities in the United States. Previous studies have identified shortcuts as the primary motivation for pedestrian railroad trespassing; however, no studies have specifically investigated the relationship between pedestrian trespassing crashes and their distances from the nearest crossings. Method: This study bridges this gap by utilizing the crash latitude-longitude data from the Federal Railroad Administration (FRA) dataset to access historical aerial images of the crash sites in Google Earth. The distances between crash locations and the nearest crossings were estimated from these images. Additionally, the potential of semi-supervised learning (SSL) to estimate these crash distances was explored. Three common SSL models, including self-learning, label spreading, and label propagation, were trained using the FRA dataset. The self-learning model performed best, using only 25% of the labeled data. The performance metrics of the SSL models indicated that they can potentially estimate crash distances with acceptable accuracy if more distance-related variables are included in model training. Results: Results from exploratory analysis and statistical tests revealed that most non-crossing crashes occur within 500 to 600 feet of a crossing. Adolescent pedestrians were more often involved in crashes farther from crossings. The pedestrians’ location on the right-of-way, the pre-crash events, and the railroad tools involved had significant relationships with crash distances. Practical Applications: These findings can be utilized to develop policies and deploy safety countermeasures and detection systems.

papers.title: Insights into vulnerable road user injury trends in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic: Canadian city trends 2012–2022
authors: Linda Rothman, Andrew Howard, Meghan Winters, Natasha Saunders, Alison Macpherson, Brent E. Hagel, Colin Macarthur, Tate HubkaRao, Ian Pike, Saroar Zubair
Marie Soleil Cloutier, M. Anne Harris, Tim Chevrier, Moreno Zanotto, Pamela Fuselli, Brice Batomen
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Over the last decade, there have been major changes in travel modes and the implementation of road safety interventions in Canadian cities. The COVID-19 pandemic acted as a catalyst for many of these rapid changes. It is, therefore, important to examine trends in vulnerable road user injuries (VRU), specifically among pedestrians and cyclists, that have occurred alongside these developments.The objectives of this study were to: (a) compare data availability and comprehensiveness of VRU injuries across cities and databases and (b)assess the short-term impact of the COVID-19 pandemicby describing the temporal trends in VRU injuries in the different databases across fourCanadian cities from 2012 to 2022. METHODS: We used four data sources from Montréal (Quebec), Toronto (Ontario), Calgary (Alberta), and Vancouver (British Columbia): police-reported, insurance-reported, hospital emergency department (ED) visits and hospitalizations. Descriptive analyses and comparisons of quarterly counts of VRU injuries from 2012 to 2022 were conducted by data source and by city. Injury trends were examined using an interrupted time series study design with March 11, 2020 (the World Health Organization declaration of the COVID-19 pandemic), as the interruption point. RESULTS: The VRU injury burden estimates differed by data source with police-reported injuries generally lower than ED visits and hospitalizations except for Calgary pedestrian hospitalizations. Across all cities, fewer pedestrian injuries than expected were observed after 2020 relative to pre-pandemic trends. Generally, there were more cyclist non-motor vehicle injuries after the start of the pandemic. CONCLUSIONS: VRU injury burden differs by database, as data are collected for different purposesusingdifferent injury definitions. Cities and provinces had different policy responses to the pandemic emphasizing that local context is important when examining VRU injury trends. PRACTICAL APPLICATIONS: Linked, comprehensive, standardized, and timely VRU data across Canada are needed to accurately assess injury burden andfacilitate safe sustainable transportation.

papers.title: Injury rates tell an incomplete story, but a more complete measurement narrative may be possible
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Despite years of research challenging their validity, injury rate metrics continue to significantly influence decision-making in many organizations. In this paper, we argue that both the source of this problem and a solution rest in understanding the narrative power of these metrics. We explore this idea by developing and applying a set of alternative injury measurement tools specifically designed to provide more comprehensive and compelling narratives of injury performance. Comparing alternative measures with traditional stand-alone injury rates demonstrates how the overall narrative of injury performance changes through metric design. Our overall goal is not to fix the statistical validity of the metrics, but to improve safety decision-making through more complex discourse. METHOD: The analysis in this paper rests on three large organization case studies. In each case, study data from the organization was presented back to senior executives using: the injury rate alone; the average injury severity; and a weighted combination of rate and severity known as SAIF. The resultant conversations were then analyzed, supplemented by individual interviews with conversation participants. RESULTS: This research highlights the importance of presenting injury rate and severity measures together and demonstrating their interplay, rather than as stand-alone metrics. Four guidelines are proposed for improving narratives and conversations based on injury metrics. The four guidelines are: pairing measures, continuous variability, a simple communication mechanism, and highlighting differences. CONCLUSIONS AND PRACTICAL APPLICATIONS: Together, these guidelines enable users of injury measures to generate more dynamic discussions from their metrics.

papers.title: Evaluating subjective cycling safety via 360°Images and HMDs: A comparative study
papers.abstract: Introduction: Subjective safety is a key determinant of cycling behavior and traffic risk perception, yet it is rarely assessed systematically in infrastructure evaluation. Because perceived safety does not necessarily correspond to objective indicators such as crash statistics or design standards, reliable methods are needed to capture experiential safety dimensions relevant to research and practice. Immersive technologies such as head-mounted displays (HMDs) may provide a controlled, scalable, effort- and resource-efficient addition or even alternative to rarely conducted on-site assessments. Method : This study investigated whether static stereoscopic 360° images presented via an HMD can approximate real-world evaluations of subjective cycling safety. Following two preparatory studies on representativeness ( N 1 = 92) and usability ( N 2 = 20), a comparative study was conducted with two independent cohorts ( N 3 = 129). One group assessed a bicycle street in real traffic conditions ( n = 64), while the other evaluated the same locations using twelve 360° panoramas in an HMD ( n = 65). Subjective safety was measured using five items adapted from a national cycling safety survey. Bayesian independent-samples t tests were conducted to examine convergence or divergence between assessment modes. Results : Findings indicated convergence for overall subjective safety ( BF 10 = 0.67) and perceived conflicts with motor vehicles ( BF 10 = 0.81), suggesting that HMD-based assessments can reproduce general safety impressions. However, participants in the HMD condition reported higher perceived conflict frequency with pedestrians ( BF 10 = 735.95), more obstacles ( BF 10 = 7.14), and lower perceived suitability for children and older adults ( BF 10 = 2.83). Usability ratings were highly positive. Conclusion and Practical Applications : Static HMD-based assessments seem to validly capture key aspects of perceived cycling safety while offering a resource-efficient and controlled alternative to field surveys. The approach enables systematic integration of user perception into infrastructure planning and supports the development of safer cycling environments.

papers.title: Investigating the role of Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) in reducing sideswipe collisions in rural Ohio
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Rural roadways continue to experience disproportionately high fatality rates per vehicle-mile traveled compared with urban facilities, underscoring persistent safety challenges that demand targeted interventions. Among the most prevalent crash types on rural roads are sideswipe collisions, frequently attributed to driver error, limited roadway delineation, and reduced situational awareness. Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS), including Blind Spot Warning (BSW), Lane Departure Warning (LDW), and Lane Keeping Assistance (LKA), offer potential countermeasures by enhancing driver perception and lateral control; however, existing effectiveness evidence is predominantly frequency-focused and urban-aggregate, and the severity-conditional performance of these systems in rural sideswipe crashes remains unquantified. METHOD: This study evaluates the influence of ADAS on the severity of rural sideswipe crashes using data from 49 rural Ohio counties for 2017-2023. A 50-foot spatial buffer approach matched each ADAS-equipped crash with nearby conventional-vehicle crashes to control for roadway and environmental context, and a Bayesian Network was applied to model the dependencies among driver, vehicle, roadway, and environmental factors. Model credibility was assessed through repeated cross-validation, hold-out discrimination testing, and bootstrap analyses of structural stability and conditional probabilities. RESULTS: The results reveal a clear hierarchy of evidence: driving under the influence and higher speed environments were the structurally robust determinants of severe outcomes, whereas ADAS-severity associations were small and condition-dependent, protective when systems were operating and under adverse weather, but unfavorable in dark conditions consistent with degraded camera-based sensing on unlit, poorly marked rural roads. CONCLUSIONS AND PRACTICAL APPLICATIONS: The findings indicate that ADAS benefits in rural settings are contingent on system operation and sensing conditions, supporting safety strategies that pair ADAS adoption with pavement-marking maintenance, roadway lighting, driver education on system limitations, and sustained enforcement of impaired-driving and speed laws.

papers.title: Configuring hidden and visible camera enforcement for risky driving deterrence
papers.abstract: Road rule violations such as speeding and mobile phone use while driving remain major contributors to road crashes worldwide. Camera-based enforcement is widely implemented to address these behaviours, yet the relative and combined effects of overt and covert enforcement remain insufficiently understood. This investigation develops and tests a deterrence-based framework for identifying the perceived effectiveness of hidden and visible camera enforcement, focusing on key mechanisms including perceived certainty of apprehension and punishment avoidance. A cross-sectional, scenario-based survey was conducted with 1,167 licensed drivers in Australia. Participants evaluated four enforcement configurations (no enforcement, covert cameras, overt cameras, and combined covert and overt cameras). Outcomes included deterrence perceptions, willingness to engage in offending behaviours, and attitudes towards enforcement. Ordinal random forest models were used for variable selection, followed by cumulative link mixed-effects models to estimate effects while accounting for repeated measures. Covert enforcement was associated with higher perceived certainty of apprehension, whereas overt enforcement reduced punishment avoidance and willingness to offend. Punishment avoidance emerged as a central behavioural mechanism, showing stronger associations with willingness than perceived certainty. Combined enforcement aligned these mechanisms, increasing perceived certainty while reducing opportunities for undetected violations. Visible enforcement was also associated with more positive attitudes, indicating a complementary role in supporting legitimacy. The findings demonstrate that deterrence is not a property of individual enforcement mechanisms, but an emergent outcome of how enforcement is configured. Effective strategies should therefore balance uncertainty, visibility, and communication across the road network. These results extend deterrence theory by showing that key mechanisms are co-produced through enforcement configurations and provide practical guidance for designing more effective and publicly acceptable enforcement systems.
