papers.title: Odds of culpability associated with the presence of drugs in injured drivers
papers.abstract: Responsibility analysis was conducted on almost 10,000 drivers injured over a 10-year period in Victoria, Australia as a result of a vehicular collision and in whom comprehensive toxicology testing in blood was conducted. Multivariable logistic regression models were fitted to compute unadjusted (OR) and adjusted odds ratios (aOR). In the multivariable model, adjustments were made for gender, age group, vehicle type, and whether the crash occurred in metropolitan or rural areas. The psychoactive drug-free driver was the control group. Drivers with ethanol (alcohol) present at any concentration (>0.01 % BAC) confirmed the well-known large increases in OR that occur with rising blood ethanol concentration, with an aOR of 16.4 (95 %CI 11.1–24.2). Drivers positive to methamphetamine and no other psychoactive drug also showed a large increase in the odds of culpability (aOR 17.2, 95 %CI 10.2–29.2). Drivers with Δ 9 -tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) in blood showed a modest increase in odds when all concentrations (> 1 ng/mL) were assessed (aOR 1.5, 95 %CI 1.1–2.0) that trended to a possible increased aOR 2.1 (95 %CI 0.9–4.9) when concentrations were 10 ng/mL or higher. Benzodiazepines in drivers also showed a significant increase in odds (aOR1.8, 95 %CI 1.2–2.8), as well as antidepressants (aOR 1.3, 95 %CI 1.0–1.6). Opioids such as codeine and oxycodone showed no measurable increase in the odds of culpability, whereas combinations of ethanol with methamphetamine or THC gave aOR of 22.6 (95 %CI 3.0–168) and 20.0 (95 %CI 7.3–54.5), respectively, as well as drivers positive to both THC and methamphetamine (aOR 14.6, 95 % CI 5.9–36.4). Drivers positive to one or more illicit drug, or a larger selection of psychoactive drugs in the absence of ethanol both gave similarly large increase in odds (aOR 4.0, 95 %CI 3.3–5.0). This study contributes to a better understanding of risks associated with driving in the presence of common psychoactive drugs.

papers.title: How do automated vehicle Penetration, Vehicle-Size Composition, and desired headway shape urban traffic conflict Patterns? An analysis using a calibrated microsimulation model
papers.abstract: Automated vehicles (AVs) may improve urban road safety, yet aggressive calibration and mixed-traffic interactions may produce nonlinear patterns in TTC-defined surrogate events. This study examines how AV penetration, vehicle-size composition, and desired headway calibration shape simulated TTC-defined surrogate outcomes. Using SUMO microsimulation for Charlottenburg, Berlin, with TTC-based analysis, LightGBM modeling, and spatial hotspot mapping, we evaluate 12 scenarios varying AV penetration (0-100%) and the composition of small AV12 and larger AV46. Both AV classes share the same driving parameters and differ primarily in physical dimensions. The scenario matrix is evaluated at AV desired headways of τ = 0.6, 0.8, and 1.0 s, yielding 36 nominal scenario-headway combinations and 34 effective configurations; human-driven vehicle (HDV) headway remains fixed at 1.0 s. Under 0.6 s calibration, total TTC-defined conflict frequency declines with increasing AV penetration, reaching reductions of approximately 45% under full automation. However, mixed-traffic configurations at the 0.6 s headway produce a larger proportion of selected short-TTC events (TTC < 0.5 s). Sensitivity analysis using minTTC thresholds of 0.3, 0.5, and 0.75 s shows that the 0.6 s setting consistently produces the greatest concentration of short temporal margins, whereas 0.8 s represents an intermediate profile. Spatially, conflicts shift from network-wide dispersion under HDV-dominant conditions to localized concentration at critical junctions under AV-dominant traffic. Differences between AV12- and AV46-dominant configurations are comparatively small and vary across headway and TTC-threshold settings. LightGBM identifies relative speed and desired headway as the strongest predictive associations. The findings highlight the context- and calibration-dependent nature of simulated AV surrogate-safety outcomes, particularly the roles of market penetration, desired headway, and vehicle-size composition.

papers.title: Age 70 as a threshold for vulnerable road user case fatality: A population-based study of older drivers in Taiwan
papers.abstract: Age-based licensing renewal policies are implemented in aging societies to protect vulnerable road users (VRUs), yet the rationale for selecting age thresholds remains uncertain. This study examined whether age 70 represents a threshold for VRU case fatality among crash-involved older drivers and whether license status modifies this association. This population-based cross-sectional study analyzed Taiwanese police-reported crash data from 2011 to 2024 involving nonprofessional car drivers aged ≥ 50 years and VRUs. Driver age was modeled categorically and continuously using restricted cubic splines (RCSs). License status was examined as an exploratory effect modifier. A prespecified primary linear-spline analysis directly tested for a change in slope at age 70, while supporting RCS analyses evaluated overall nonlinearity. Multivariable logistic regression with cluster-robust standard errors estimated adjusted odds ratios (AORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Among 602,782 crash-involved VRUs, 2,789 sustained fatal injuries (0.46%). The prespecified analysis did not detect a change in slope at age 70 (change-in-slope AOR per year, 1.001; 95% CI, 0.977-1.025; P = 0.95), and the selected 3-knot RCS specification provided no evidence of overall nonlinearity (P = 0.24). Compared with drivers aged 50-64 years, odds of VRU case fatality were higher among drivers aged 65-69 years (AOR 1.15; 95% CI, 1.03-1.28) and ≥ 70 years (AOR 1.14; 95% CI, 1.01-1.29). However, among drivers aged 65-99 years, age ≥ 70 years was not independently associated with VRU case fatality (AOR 1.08; 95% CI, 0.93-1.25; P = 0.32). Unlicensed driving was associated with higher odds of VRU case fatality (AOR, 1.92; 95% CI, 1.62-2.28). Overall, the prespecified analysis did not detect a change in slope at age 70, while the association with unlicensed driving highlights a potentially important correlate of VRU case fatality among crash-involved older drivers.

papers.title: Dynamic estimation of airport taxiway hotspots using spatio-temporal traffic and kinematic risk modeling
papers.abstract: At busy airports, airfield operations are among the most safety-critical phases of flight because aircraft move through complex taxiway and runway-crossing networks. Despite ground-surveillance advances, taxiway conflicts remain a concern. We develop a traffic-based method for dynamic taxiway hotspot estimation that identifies conflict-prone locations without incident or accident histories. Unlike static FAA-defined hotspots, the method represents airfield infrastructure as a directed graph and uses agglomerative clustering to identify critical intersections. Hotspot scores combine spatial utilization probabilities from Runway-Gate routes with a KDE-based temporal overlap estimated from intersection arrival times. The trajectory-level score incorporates aircraft kinematics, including relative speed and convergence geometry. We validated the model using one full day of surface-surveillance data from Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (1 July 2019) and cross-validated it on an independent post-pandemic day (10 September 2024). The model identified clusters corresponding to all three 2019 FAA-designated hotspots within the northern study area, ranking two of them among its top five (Recall@5 =0.67 vs. 0.33 for an aircraft-count baseline). Cross-year validation also identified both 2024 FAA hotspots as stable or rising high-risk clusters, and the method flagged conflict-prone locations not shown in FAA airport diagrams. Arrival and departure operations yielded distinct hotspot patterns: arrival risks clustered at runway exits, while departure risks clustered at runway-entry merge points. Sliding windows capture temporal changes, enabling dynamic estimation. By combining traffic-based hotspot detection, kinematic risk integration, operation-specific analysis, and a trajectory-level collision-risk score, the method bridges offline analysis and real-time conflict-risk monitoring.

papers.title: Practical validation of synthetic pre-crash scenarios
papers.abstract: The representativeness of synthetic pre-crash scenarios is crucial for assessing the safety impact of Driving Automation Systems through virtual simulations. However, a gap remains in the robust evaluation of synthetic pre-crash scenarios' practical equivalence to their real-world counterparts; that is, whether they are similar enough for the intended assessment purpose. Conventional significance testing is inadequate, as it focuses on detecting differences rather than establishing practical equivalence. This study addresses the research gap by extending our previous work on a Bayesian Region of Practical Equivalence (ROPE)-based equivalence testing framework by introducing a binning-based approach to define appropriate statistics and equivalence criteria. Two novel binning-based statistics are proposed to quantify localized and aggregate distributional discrepancies between synthetic and reference datasets. The statistics incorporate bin weights derived from system re-simulation outcomes, enabling discrepancies in regions with greater influence on safety-impact estimates to be emphasized. The proposed approach further provides diagnostic insight into the distributional regions driving non-equivalence, facilitating targeted dataset generation and improvements. The framework's applicability is demonstrated through a case study, which tests the practical equivalence of two synthetic rear-end pre-crash datasets with a previously developed reference dataset for the safety impact assessment of an Automatic Emergency Braking system. The results show that the framework provides informative assessments of practical equivalence and diagnostic insights into the divergence of datasets. Although the demonstration focuses on rear-end pre-crash scenarios, the framework is generic and extensible to broader validation contexts, providing an interpretable and principled basis for practical equivalence assessment across diverse synthetic data applications.

papers.title: What creates safe and efficient pedestrian–vehicle interactions? a naturalistic study to design human-like behaviour for automated vehicles
papers.abstract: Safe and efficient interaction with pedestrians is critical for the successful deployment of autonomous vehicles (AVs). While vehicle speed and acceleration are vital communication signals for this interaction, the ways in which human drivers use these kinematic communication signals remain under-explored. To design motion-based communication for AVs, this study aims to explore how drivers control their speed as a function of initial interaction conditions, and how this translates into more or less successful interaction outcomes. We analysed naturalistic trajectory data of vehicles and pedestrians from two zebra crossings in Leeds, UK, comprising 981 interactions. Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) was applied to quantify the mediating effect of vehicle kinematics on the relationship between initial time gap and interaction outcomes (crossing order, efficiency, and safety). Based on these models, vehicle speed profiles associated with optimal and worst outcomes were identified and compared using Generalized Estimating Equations (GEE). PLS-SEM results confirmed that vehicle kinematics significantly mediate interaction outcomes, exerting a strong influence on efficiency and safety, and a weaker influence on crossing order. Minimum vehicle speed in particular exerted a strong influence on crossing order and safety, suggesting that the speed to which the driver drops is a key communication signal to pedestrians. The mediation results and trajectory analysis revealed that drivers used different strategies to achieve balance between their efficiency and interaction safety: in yielding scenarios (time gap > 3 s), they decelerated early and softly to maintain a low non-zero speed (∼1 m/s) at a far distance (>10 m) to ensure safety while conserving momentum to ensure efficiency; in ambiguous non-yielding scenarios (time gaps ∼ 1 - 3 s), they employed a two-stage strategy: a proactive initial deceleration to prepare for potential danger and reduce uncertainty, followed by an assertive acceleration for efficiency; in unambiguous non-yielding scenarios with a narrow time gap (< 1 s), they sacrificed a small amount of efficiency and adopted proactive deceleration before pedestrians displayed a clear crossing intention to ensure safety. This study expands the understanding of interaction beyond binary yielding choices, offering new insights into the proactive strategies human drivers use to negotiate right-of-way safely and efficiently. Emulating these kinematic strategies can support better integration of AVs into human traffic.

papers.title: Similar predicted fatal-crash risk, different contribution architectures: A temporally validated analysis of vehicle–pedestrian crashes in Japan
papers.abstract: Vehicle-pedestrian crashes with similar predicted fatal-crash risk may arise from different combinations of contributing conditions, while the distinction between risk magnitude and risk composition has received limited attention. This study investigated whether reproducible multivariable contribution architectures exist among vehicle-pedestrian crashes with comparable model-predicted fatal-crash risk. Nationwide police-reported crash data from Japan were analyzed using temporally separated 2023 and 2024 cohorts, comprising 74,002 vehicle-pedestrian crashes, including 1,838 fatal crashes. Four classification models were evaluated using the 2023 cohort, with the 2024 cohort reserved for independent temporal validation. XGBoost was selected as the nonlinear base model and achieved a PR-AUC of 0.203 and ROC-AUC of 0.877 in the 2024 test cohort. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) were then used to decompose model predictions, and signed SHAP contributions were conditioned on overall predicted risk, aggregated across seven domains, normalized, and clustered. Two contribution profiles were identified. One showed relatively greater contributions from road-user characteristics, whereas the other showed greater contributions from environmental conditions, roadway geometry, and traffic control and speed regulation. The profiles were highly reproducible in 2024, with high centroid cosine similarities and an adjusted Rand index of 0.975 relative to an independently fitted 2024 solution. Both profiles occurred across the full predicted-risk distribution and were not well reproduced by simple partitions based on predicted risk, pedestrian age, or day/night conditions. Profile-specific SHAP interaction analysis further revealed systematic differences in nonlinear predictor combinations, particularly the interaction between pedestrian age and day/night conditions. These findings demonstrate that similar predicted fatal-crash risk can arise through distinct and temporally reproducible contribution architectures, suggesting that predicted risk magnitude alone does not fully characterize the multivariable circumstances underlying fatal vehicle-pedestrian crashes.

papers.title: Validating crash surrogates: a causal graphical framework and a SHRP2 case study of hard braking
papers.abstract: Although there has been a variety of crash surrogates have been applied in traffic safety areas, formal discussions on how to validate crash surrogates for practical use remain limited. To fill this gap, this study seeks to propose a validation procedure suitable for traffic safety applications. To first establish key assumptions required for valid crash surrogates, this study reviews discussions on surrogate outcome from causal mediation, medical research, epidemiology clinical trials, and economics perspectives. A causally valid surrogate, whether full or partial, is a special type of mediator that lies on the causal pathway from the primary explanatory variable for a given research question (i.e., the "treatment") to the final crash outcome. Moreover, it captures an identifiable portion of the treatment's effect on the outcome, thereby enabling causal inference on the final crash outcome through the surrogate. To determine whether a candidate surrogate satisfies the above properties, the proposed validation procedure consists of three main components: (1) verifying the assumptions required for identifying the causal relationship between the candidate crash surrogate and the crash outcome; (2) quantifying the extent of surrogacy; and (3) evaluating the absence of a surrogate paradox and the comparability of the surrogate. A case study using SHRP2 Naturalistic Driving Study data is then presented to demonstrate the proposed procedure. Specifically, the case study examines whether hard braking is a causally valid surrogate for rear-end crash occurrence.

papers.title: Microplastic removal under different salinity levels using kaolin-assisted coagulation with modified Caryocar brasiliense coagulants
papers.abstract: The increasing occurrence of microplastics in aquatic systems has intensified the search for efficient removal strategies, particularly for low-density polymers such as polyethylene (PE), whose limited settling capacity hinders separation from water. This study developed and compared two coagulants derived from pequi tree bark extract ( Caryocar brasiliense) for PE removal under different salinity conditions: a magnetic iron oxide nanoparticle-functionalized coagulant (E-PTB@NPsFe) and a Mannich-modified cationic coagulant (E-PTB/MR). Kaolin was used as a mineral ballasting agent to promote floc formation and sedimentation. The process was optimized by response surface methodology using a central composite rotatable design, considering coagulant dosage, ballast concentration, and salinity as independent variables. Under optimized conditions, E-PTB@NPsFe achieved predicted removals of 96.1% for turbidity, 90.9% for gravimetric PE removal, and 80.0% for microplastic removal, using 76 mg L⁻¹ coagulant, 0.19 g L⁻¹ kaolin, and 9 g L⁻¹ salinity. E-PTB/MR achieved 90.0%, 90.1%, and 72.1% removals, respectively, but required higher coagulant dosage and salinity; moreover, its application in real coastal waters was limited by decreased pH and increased organic load. Mechanistic analyses indicated that E-PTB@NPsFe formed larger, more heterogeneous flocs consistent with sweep flocculation and particle entrapment, whereas E-PTB/MR produced compact polymer-mediated aggregates. In a real saline coastal water matrix, E-PTB@NPsFe maintained effective removal with limited physicochemical disturbance and no increase in residual iron. The magnetic system also retained relevant PE removal capacity over successive reuse cycles. Model validation showed satisfactory agreement between predicted and observed values across evaluated responses, supporting the predictive adequacy of the models under the tested conditions. These results demonstrate that combining natural polyphenol-based coagulants, magnetic functionality, and mineral nucleation is a promising strategy for removing low-density microplastics from saline water matrices under controlled treatment conditions.

papers.title: Diesel exhaust particles from underground coal mining: Breathing-zone-to-lung transport, regional dosimetry, and deposition hotspots
papers.abstract: Diesel exhaust particles (DEPs) pose a major inhalation hazard in underground coal mines, but their transport and regional deposition in the respiratory tract remain poorly resolved. Using an anatomically detailed respiratory tract coupled with breathing zone model (CM1) as the comparative baseline, we combined three respiratory models of varying anatomical completeness with three particle release strategies to define six Eulerian–Lagrangian tracking scenarios (M1–M6). Particles from 1 nm to 10 μm were simulated at inspiratory flow rates of 15–90 L/min. DEPs of 500 nm showed the greatest distal penetration, reaching 62.7% at 30 L/min. Lower respiratory tract (LRT) deposition decreased for 10 nm DEPs from 43.84% to 32.70% but increased for 1 μm DEPs from 27.59% to 45.49% as flow increased. Model completeness and release strategy strongly influenced deposition estimates. The LRT only configuration (M6) underestimated 1 nm DEP deposition by 88.36% and overestimated deposition of submicron DEPs by up to 59.15%. A new strategy (M7) reproduced total and regional deposition within 8% and 15% of CM1, respectively, while reducing tracking time by more than 20-fold. These findings provide an efficient framework for DEPs exposure assessment and underscore the need to represent the breathing zone and upstream airways.

papers.title: What is the plume parameter Γi for a pool fire?
papers.abstract: The purpose of this note is to determine the plume parameter, 𝛤 𝑖 , for a canonical fire configuration, namely a pool fire. The evaluation of this parameter, which characterizes the plume nature (forced or lazy), requires knowledge of the vertical velocity and temperature of the gases in the near-field region above the fire source. Order-of-magnitude estimates of these two quantities are obtained by combining two formulations of the convective heat release rate. A numerical application presented for a heptane pool fire indicates a plume parameter greater than unity, which thus suggests a lazy plume behavior. This is a result that is likely to be of interest to researchers who use surrogate buoyant plumes in their laboratory experiments for smoke propagation and control issues.

papers.title: Smouldering suppression in corn pith–alginate insulation via a combined bio-based phosphorus and boron flame-retardant system
papers.abstract: Bio-based thermal insulation must resist fire without losing its insulating function. Corn pith and alginate panels were engineered with a phytate-derived phosphorus compound (PA-THAM) and disodium octaborate tetrahydrate (DOT), and retained low thermal conductivity (approximately 0.035 W m -1 K -1 ) and low density (59 kg m -3 ). Thermogravimetric analysis showed the peak mass-loss rate falling by approximately 65 % and the maximum degradation temperature rising from 280 °C to 310 °C. Smouldering was strongly suppressed: 8 wt% PA-THAM alone reduced the propagation speed by nearly an order of magnitude and induced self-extinction at an onset temperature of 310 °C, while the combined PA-THAM/DOT system raised the smouldering ignition threshold by 70 °C and 90 °C depending on loading, with no propagation to burn-out. Under flaming conditions the same formulations behaved very differently: cone calorimetry gave a moderate reduction in peak heat release rate, of up to 20 %, and a longer flaming period, but no resolvable change in total heat release, effective heat of combustion or smoke production. This identifies a predominantly condensed-phase barrier, formed by phosphorus-induced dehydration and carbonisation and possibly reinforced by boron-mediated crosslinking, and shows that smouldering performance cannot be inferred from bench-scale flaming tests.

papers.title: Detection and measurement framework for surface cracks on charred layer of wood based on deep learning and image processing techniques
papers.abstract: Pyrolysis occurs after wood being exposed to elevated temperatures and leads to formation of cracks. Cracks serve as pathways for additional heat and mass flux and will affect internal temperature profile. Crack dimensional data is therefore important for analyzing the behavior of wood under fire. However, most of the existing studies measure cracks after specimens cooled to room temperature. Crack size data during high temperature exposure is limited. This study proposes a vision-based framework for crack detection and measurement under high temperature exposure. The framework identifies crack regions using a deep learning model trained on charred crack images of GLT larch samples. Total crack area, total crack length, and crack width distribution were extracted from the detected crack regions by image processing techniques. Validation was conducted at normal temperature by comparing results of proposed vision-based measurement and independent reference measurement. The relative error is mostly below 10%, showing reasonable agreement. The proposed method was applied to video data from an ISO834 test of a GLT cedar specimen. Results show that crack occupied approximately 16% of the heated surface, after 19 minutes of exposure. The results suggest the potential applicability of the proposed method for crack measurement at high temperatures.

papers.title: Fracture mechanisms of tempered glass at elevated temperatures: competition between mechanical degradation and crack healing
papers.abstract: Tempered glazing is widely used in modern curtain wall systems, but it may break and fall out under fire-induced thermal shock, potentially exacerbating fire spread in high-rise buildings. Flexural strength is a key mechanical parameter for predicting thermal breakage of glass. However, its evolution and the associated fracture mechanisms at elevated temperatures remain insufficiently understood. Steady-state three-point bending tests were conducted from ambient temperature to 500 °C. The mean flexural strength decreased from 217 ± 8 MPa at ambient temperature to 192 ± 14 MPa at 250 °C, showed a slight recovery at 300 °C with a value of 213 ± 15 MPa, and then dropped to 136 ± 15 MPa at 400 °C. These results indicate that the evolution of the high-temperature bending performance of tempered glass is not governed solely by elastic modulus degradation. To further investigate the underlying mechanisms, a sequentially coupled thermo-mechanical finite element model was developed to reproduce the experimentally measured flexural response and dominant fracture behavior. The model incorporates temperature-dependent elastic modulus and accounts for the residual prestress state following high-temperature stress relaxation. Numerical results show that the adverse impact of prestress relaxation on flexural strength becomes significant only above approximately 350 °C. In contrast, high-temperature in situ scanning electron microscopy revealed crack-tip blunting and localized crack closure, providing direct evidence of crack-healing processes at elevated temperatures. These processes alleviate crack-tip stress concentration and contribute to strength retention. By integrating experiments, numerical simulations, and microscopic observations, the high-temperature fracture behavior of tempered glass was shown to be governed by the competition between thermally induced mechanical degradation and crack healing. Up to approximately 300 °C, crack healing partially offset the adverse effect of modulus degradation on strength. At higher temperatures, prestress relaxation and modulus degradation became dominant, leading to rapid strength loss.

papers.title: Burning ceilings: heat feedback and the thermal environment
papers.abstract: The heat flux and flame length originating from a simulated burning ceiling were investigated using an inverted propane burner surrounded by an inert ceiling. Temperature profiles within the gas phase were measured both radially and as a function of distance from the ceiling – with the maximum temperatures measured at 10 mm offset for most cases. A correlation was found linking the normalised flame length to the normalised fire size to the 2/5 power in the range 5 kW-20 kW. The peak gas temperature, and incident heat flux to the ceiling were correlated based on their radius relative to the flame length and compared against data from previous work. The findings and power relationships of this study aligned well with findings from other authors. This study extended the range over which these relationships were found to hold to smaller dimensionless fire sizes.

papers.title: Development and testing of the collaborative wildfire evacuation platform WUISHOW
papers.abstract: This paper presents the development and testing of WUISHOW, a digital collaborative graphic evacuation decision-making tool designed to support wildland-urban interface (WUI) fire stakeholders in emergency planning and response. The tool is a Graphical User Interface based on the WUI-NITY wildfire evacuation simulation platform and has been developed with a dual purpose: (1) to assess end-user needs and (2) to visualise wildfire evacuation simulation results through procedural generation. WUISHOW is implemented using a virtual-reality game engine and serves as an interface for collaborative decision-making, enabling multiple interaction modalities and hardware deployments. The WUISHOW includes both a desktop version and a multi-touch table version, and presents interactive wildfire evacuation modelling. User testing was performed through semi-structured interviews with stakeholders and potential end-users in Australia, New Zealand, North America, and Europe, followed by an online survey to quantify the interview findings. Most but not all interviewees found simulation and visualisation tools such as WUISHOW to be useful, but identified significant barriers to adoption, such as trust in and access to accurate and valid input data. End-users saw value in the WUISHOW particularly for preparedness, training, community engagement, and inter-agency communication, but questioned whether it would be suitable for fast-paced, real-time emergency operations.

papers.title: Integrity and fire performance of intumescent coating protection of steel elements subjected to tensile deformations
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Steel elements may be subjected to large deformations in case of fire or as a consequence of previous accidental events that triggered the fire, such as an earthquake or explosion. In such cases, fire protective intumescent coatings (ICs) applied on the steel elements can crack or detach and expose the steel to higher thermal effects than assumed in design. However, there is at present little knowledge on the entity of deformations that are tolerated by the IC and to what extent cracks in the IC may cause reduced fire protection performance. This project was aimed at advancing such knowledge by means of an experimental campaign, where four different types of ICs (one water-based, one solvent-based, and two epoxy-based) were evaluated. Tensile tests of free film coating specimens were performed to assess the stress-strain relationship of the coatings. Then, ICs were applied on 39 steel plate specimens, which were first subjected to different tensile strains and then tested in an electric furnace under constant heating rate. The damage of the IC after the tensile test was evaluated and graded and the performance of the strained specimens during fire exposure was assessed against the performance of unstrained reference specimens. The results show that, while the two water- and solvent-based ICs could tolerate tensile pre-strains levels up to 16% without significant visible damage at 20°C nor reduction of the insulating performance during fire, the two epoxy-based ICs showed large cracks and detachments when subjected to tensile pre-strain larger than 5-8% and were not able to provide the required fire protection.

papers.title: Statistical modeling of geometry and dispersion range of firebrands generated from real structural fires
papers.abstract: : Spot fires caused by firebrands generated from structural fires are a primary factor driving large-scale fire spread in urban areas and the Wildland-Urban Interface (WUI). To quantitatively assess the risk of such fire spread, mathematical models predicting the geometry and dispersion range of firebrands based on fire scales and meteorological conditions are essential. In this study, we modified an existing scaling law by incorporating the stack effect specific to structural fires, and inductively modeled the actual geometry and dispersion range of firebrands observed in past fire incidents and a full-scale experiment. By introducing a hierarchical Bayesian model into the analysis, we were able to comprehensively evaluate and synthesize data across multiple fire incidents with differing physical scales and observation methods. The results demonstrated that the dimensionless projected area of firebrands ( ) increases as the dimensionless heat release rate (HRR, ) increases and as the dimensionless downwind distance ( ) decreases. Regarding the dispersion range, the downwind distance ( ) was shown to increase with larger and dimensionless wind speed ( ). Furthermore, the variance in the dimensionless crosswind distance ( ) becomes broader as and increase. The findings of this study can be utilized to quantitatively assess spot fire risks under potential future fire scenarios and to formulate effective fire protection measures.

papers.title: Quantifying the Financial Consequences of Building Fire Incidents: A Unified Assessment Framework
papers.abstract: : Building fire incidents cause financial consequences worldwide, such as US $13.2 billion for property damage and US $1.9 billion for business losses in the USA in 2014. Current estimates vary across countries and predominantly focus on property damage without addressing indirect and fire protection costs. This paper develops and applies a unified cost assessment framework for building fires that enables cross-country comparisons and integrates direct, indirect and fire protection costs for residential and non-residential buildings. Cost methodologies are identified and documented for the developed workflow in the framework for selecting and adopting cost equations and adjusting inputs using severity factors, Purchasing Power Parity and the Consumer Price Index. The framework is calibrated by comparing with available estimates for England in 2019/20 and applied to the USA in 2014. Case studies are developed using the framework for England in 2024/25, the USA in 2024 and Taiwan in 2023, and demonstrate uncollected cost components, such as household costs for residential buildings of £15.2 million for England, US $405 million for the USA and NTD $53.45 million for Taiwan. The research findings provide a comprehensive tool for quantifying the cost of fire in buildings, supporting and strengthening decision-making on fire protection application and resilience planning.

papers.title: Numerical investigation of obstacle porosity and spatial arrangement in vented dust explosions: Comparison of distributed-porosity rack and pallet configurations
papers.journal_name: Journal of Loss Prevention in the Process Industries
papers.abstract: Internal congestion can substantially affect vented dust-explosion loads, yet aggregate porosity does not describe how obstructed regions are spatially distributed. This study investigates the numerical sensitivity of explosion overpressure to obstacle porosity and spatial arrangement using a FLACS-CFD DustEx framework previously calibrated against an unobstructed experimental reference. Fifteen simulations were conducted for a centrally ignited maize-starch cloud in a vented enclosure, comparing an unobstructed configuration with two continuous rack-like and twelve discrete palletized regions of equal gross obstacle volume. Prescribed porosity ranged from 0 to 0.9; at each matched porosity, both layouts had identical fluid-accessible volume and initial dust mass. The unobstructed case produced a maximum monitored overpressure of 0.341 bar(g). At porosities of 0.4–0.9, maximum overpressures ranged from 0.325 to 0.493 bar(g) for racks and from 0.451 to 0.586 bar(g) for pallets, with pallet values 18.9–38.8% higher at equal porosity. In contrast, for fully impermeable regions, the rack and pallet predictions were 0.383 and 0.252 bar(g), respectively. The rack–pallet ordering was consistent across maximum overpressure and maximum positive pressure-rise rate but reversed between impermeable and partially porous cases. Published experimental benchmarks support the FLACS/PDR methodology for selected obstructed gas-explosion conditions, while dust-explosion studies provide complementary evidence for the combustion modelling framework. The present application, based on idealized rack and pallet volumes with prescribed equal area and volume porosities, is methodologically supported but has not been directly validated against corresponding physical storage configurations. Accordingly, the calculated pressure differences represent internally consistent, model-dependent trends rather than experimentally confirmed severity rankings.

papers.title: Comparative assessment of consequence modelling tools for compressed hydrogen releases using experimental data
papers.journal_name: Journal of Loss Prevention in the Process Industries
papers.abstract: : Quantitative risk assessment of accidental hydrogen releases requires reliable prediction of the physical effects associated with loss-of-containment scenarios. This work compares the predictive performance of PHAST v9.0, HyRAM+ v5.1.1, and EFFECTS v13 against three experimental benchmarks for compressed hydrogen dispersion, jet fire flame length, and radiation. Model predictions were compared with measurements using parity plots and statistical performance metrics. For dispersion, all three tools satisfied the established acceptability criteria for pointwise comparisons in simple geometry, including mean relative bias within ±0.4, mean relative square error below 2.3, and at least 50% of predictions within a factor of two of the measurements. PHAST showed the lowest mean relative square error (0.097), and EFFECTS the highest fraction of predictions within a factor of two (0.95). For jet fire flame length, the three tools showed comparable performance and generally overpredicted the experimental values, particularly for larger nozzle diameters. PHAST and HyRAM+ predicted all flame lengths within a factor of two of the measurements, while EFFECTS had only one value outside this range. For jet fire radiation, only PHAST and HyRAM+ could be compared quantitatively. Both remained within a factor of two of the measurements for all points, but PHAST reproduced the experimental values more closely overall, with a total mean relative square error of 0.021. Overall, all three tools showed satisfactory performance, although accuracy depended on the phenomenon considered and the underlying modelling assumptions. PHAST provided the most consistent performance across the three benchmarks, while EFFECTS performed particularly well for hydrogen dispersion.

papers.title: Structural response to hydrogen gas explosions: Surface mapping resolution dependency in one-way coupled numerical simulations
papers.journal_name: Journal of Loss Prevention in the Process Industries
papers.abstract: The hydrogen economy is growing and as such also the quantities of hydrogen gas produced, transported and stored. The increased quantities make large accident scenarios in hydrogen infrastructure possible, e.g. hydrogen gas explosions. A key question is to what extent the surrounding built environment can withstand this. Blast wall design is part of answering that question. Large scale numerical simulations can be used to design blast walls, but it can require utilisation of coupled CFD (Computational Fluid Dynamics) and FEA (Finite Element Analysis) to obtain an optimised design. In utilisation of one-way coupling methodologies, it is found in the literature that the mapping resolution is seldomly reported to be systematically analysed. Adequate mapping resolution when using a one-way coupling methodology for hydrogen gas detonation blast effects has therefore been investigated in this study. A mapping resolution of 0.25 m was sufficient to accurately capture the initial peak deflection of the blast wall of the replicated experiment. The results were also validated against an experiment and benchmarked against other studies that have used the same experiment for validation. Results showed that a one-way coupling method with a systematically chosen mapping resolution gave better or similar results than previous studies in terms of shockwave arrival time and peak deflections at the blast wall. The results demonstrate that a systematically selected mapping resolution enables accurate one-way CFD–FEA predictions of hydrogen detonation blast effects, supporting blast wall design without the need for more computationally demanding two-way coupling approaches.

papers.title: Bridging tacit knowledge loss and data scarcity of coke drum integrity management using a multi-stage hybrid decision-analytic framework
papers.journal_name: Journal of Loss Prevention in the Process Industries
papers.abstract: Maintaining the structural integrity of coke drums in delayed coking units remains a critical challenge for refineries due to severe cyclic thermal and mechanical loading that promotes complex damage mechanisms, including thermomechanical fatigue, shell bulging, and weld cracking. Effective integrity management is further complicated by limited inspection data, fragmented historical records, high uncertainty, and the gradual loss of experienced subject-matter expertise. Conventional data-driven artificial intelligence approaches often require extensive datasets and are therefore unsuitable for such data-constrained environments. To address these challenges, the research was structured in two complementary parts: Part I focused on the development of a novel Integrity Management with Validation and Verification (IMV 2 ) methodology, while Part II concentrates on its application, validation, and verification through an industrial coke drum case study. This study presents and validates an integrated Integrity Management with Validation and Verification (IMV 2 ) framework designed to support integrity management decision-making under conditions of data scarcity. The framework combines the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP), Fuzzy AHP (FAHP), Decision-Making Trial and Evaluation Laboratory (DEMATEL), Bayesian Networks (BNs), ranked-node probability modelling, and the Technique for Order Preference by Similarity to Ideal Solution (TOPSIS) within a unified decision-support architecture. The methodology systematically captures tacit expert knowledge, quantifies causal relationships among degradation drivers, transforms qualitative judgments into probabilistic representations, and ranks integrity management strategies through a transparent and auditable process. The proposed framework was validated through a real refinery coke drum case study, demonstrating its capability to integrate sparse inspection information with expert judgment while effectively handling uncertainty and missing data. Results show that the model successfully captures the complex interdependencies among failure modes and produces strategy rankings consistent with established engineering practice. Sensitivity, robustness, and statistical analyses confirm the stability of BN-based outputs despite significant data limitations. Furthermore, convergence between probabilistic assessment, sensitivity analysis, and Minkowski-based mathematical verification demonstrates the framework’s global robustness. Observed rank variations were limited to alternatives that were mathematically and statistically indistinguishable, indicating that such variations arise from the underlying data structure rather than methodological deficiencies. Overall, the IMV 2 framework provides a reliable, interpretable, and defensible approach for high-risk refinery asset management. By enabling dynamic updates, preserving organisational knowledge, and establishing a rigorous audit trail for decision-making, it offers a practical blueprint for integrity management in environments characterised by uncertainty, limited data availability, and complex failure mechanisms.

papers.title: Performance evaluation of quantitative optical gas imaging (QOGI) technique for fugitive methane emission quantification
papers.journal_name: Journal of Loss Prevention in the Process Industries
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT: Quantitative Optical Gas Imaging (QOGI) is increasingly adopted to support Leak Detection And Repair (LDAR) programs and process safety monitoring; however, its quantitative performance strongly depends on operating and environmental conditions. This study presents a controlled laboratory assessment of the performance of a QOGI system, with particular focus on methane emission rates close to the declared Minimum Leak Detection Rate (MDLR) of the instrument. Fourteen experimental configurations are investigated by systematically varying key parameters, including measurement distance, wind conditions, thermal contrast between the gas plume and the background, framing, and viewing angle. The results show that, under favorable operating conditions, QOGI provides a stable and highly consistent response, with good linearity between measured and actual emission rates. From a statistical perspective, the median is identified as the most robust central tendency index when a limited number of acquisitions is available, making it particularly suitable for practical field applications. Measurement distance is identified as the primary driver of performance, while correct wind configuration is essential to avoid systematic bias. Thermal contrast further enhances stability, whereas observation geometry has a marginal influence when the plume is fully captured. Overall, the study identifies favorable operating conditions within the investigated experimental domain in which QOGI delivers reliable and decision-useful quantitative information, providing practical guidance for its effective deployment in process safety, LDAR applications, and regulatory contexts.

papers.title: Ontology-driven representation and reasoning for hazard and operability studies
papers.journal_name: Journal of Loss Prevention in the Process Industries
papers.abstract: Within Process Safety Management, Process Hazard Analysis methods such as Hazard and Operability (HAZOP) studies provide a structured basis for identifying credible deviation scenarios and demonstrating that risks are understood and managed. In practice, however, HAZOP outputs are typically recorded as heterogeneous tables or narrative text, making reuse difficult and complicating systematic checks for missing causes, consequences, or safeguards. This paper presents an ontology-driven, reproducible pipeline that converts published chemical process HAZOP studies into a machine-readable knowledge graph, enabling structured analysis and completeness checking, while also creating a foundation for applying expert domain knowledge in retrieval-augmented generation and for future automation of HAZOP studies. An ontology in the Web Ontology Language (OWL-DL) was designed to capture core concepts from International Electrotechnical Commission standard IEC 61882:2016 for HAZOP studies, including node, guideword, deviation, cause, consequence, safeguard, and recommendation. The ontology was populated from a unified spreadsheet compiled from twelve published HAZOP studies using Protégé, an ontology editor, and its Cellfie plugin for spreadsheet-to-ontology transformation, while graph-based exploration was supported via Neo4j, a graph database platform. Logical consistency was verified using HermiT, an OWL reasoner, constituting the genuine description-logic reasoning step in this study, while a separate, non-inferential completeness audit – a property-presence check implemented in Python with Owlready2 – was used to evaluate whether each deviation instance was linked to the required core relationships. The ontology remained logically consistent, and the audit demonstrated that ontology-based completeness checking can reveal missing safety-relevant relationships in HAZOP records, supporting more systematic, traceable quality assurance and providing a practical step toward digitalised process safety workflows.

papers.title: Non-engineered housing construction and earthquakes: A global review of structural performance and vulnerability drivers
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction
papers.abstract: Non-engineered housing accounts for a disproportionate share of earthquake-related casualties worldwide, yet remains under-served by integrated research that bridges its structural, social, and regulatory dimensions. Through a systematic review of more than 200 studies, we synthesise the global literature on the seismic performance of non-engineered construction, the factors driving its vulnerability, and the ways in which housing safety has been conceptualised in this sector. Across the principal typologies — unreinforced load-bearing wall structures, confined masonry, reinforced concrete with masonry infill, timber and wood construction, and hybrid mixed systems — seismic behaviour is shown to depend less on the strength of individual elements than on the integration of those elements into a coherent structural system, a framing that accounts for both the persistent vulnerability of the most prevalent typologies and the unexpected resilience of certain vernacular hybrid systems. The physical vulnerabilities documented across the literature are themselves the surface expression of deeper socio-economic constraints — most notably economic limitation and limited technical capacity within the informal construction workforce — operating within a governance environment whose institutional absences from regulation, oversight, technical guidance, and capacity-building constitute the enabling conditions for vulnerability to emerge and persist. We propose a coordinated research and policy agenda spanning uncertainty-aware risk assessment, context-specific structural modelling, locally grounded design criteria and guidelines, and post-earthquake recovery pathways, framing non-engineered housing as a substantive research domain requiring integrated technical, socio-economic, and governance attention.

papers.title: The days are long but the years are short: Temporal mismatches in wildfire governance and the multiple temporalities of wildfire recovery
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction
papers.abstract: Social science on wildfire has garnered increased attention with scholarship particularly focused on pre-fire and near-term impacts. However, the long-term impacts of wildfire and long-term recovery are less well understood and less represented in scholarship. This article takes up the questions of long-term wildfire recovery with special attention to time. We examine existing scholarship on disaster recovery models as well as empirical literature on disaster recovery to show how phase-based disaster models, which dominate disaster recovery practice, are guided by implicit assumptions about temporality that need re-working in light of the ways that ecosystems, communities, and individuals experience wildfire. Specifically, we look at cascading impacts, uneven recovery timelines and trauma as three generators of what we call temporal mismatches between dominant phase-based models and lived experience. We argue that dominant phase-based models operate as mechanisms of temporal governance, which encompass certain lived realities of time in wildfire recovery to the exclusion of other less linear experiences of time. We conclude considering the implications of a conceptual reorientation to time in wildfire recovery models and practice, shedding light on an under-examined dimension of recovery.

papers.title: Recovery without recovery: Adaptation and unresolved loss following the Jagersfontein mine tailings disaster
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction
papers.abstract: Rebuilding homes and paying compensation do not establish that disaster-affected people are recovering their lives. More than two years after the September 2022 Jagersfontein mine tailings disaster in South Africa, we conducted two rounds of semi-structured interviews with affected people and observed their living conditions. People reported defective housing, inadequate compensation, the non-replacement of income-producing assets and continuing social and emotional harm. Most interviewees had limited means to replace what they had lost. They described drawing on pension income, relying on family for support, postponing purchases of basic household items and reducing their expectations of fair compensation. Repeated negotiations with the mine operator added distress and indignity. Some stopped pursuing compensation because they regarded the process as exhausting or futile, not because their issues had been resolved. We distinguish between recovery as an administrative phase, the interventions undertaken in its name, and recovery as lived experience. The Jagersfontein case demonstrates that recovery interventions can coexist with continuing deprivation and generate additional harm.

papers.title: Probabilistic modeling of wind-borne debris interactions for pre-disaster hurricane damage prediction in coastal communities
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction
papers.abstract: Hurricane damage prediction models typically evaluate residential buildings in isolation, neglecting the wind-borne debris that couples the fate of neighboring structures. This study proposes a probabilistic framework for pre-disaster damage prediction that explicitly represents debris-induced interdependencies at the community scale. The framework comprises three components: a debris generation model linking predicted roof damage to debris quantity and size; a probabilistic trajectory model that jointly characterizes debris direction and travel distance while accounting for community layout and density through angular exposure and plan area ratio; and an integrated damage prediction model that propagates direct wind damage and secondary debris impacts across a building inventory. The framework is implemented and validated using the Lake Charles testbed, focusing on residential buildings in Lake Charles, Louisiana, during Hurricane Laura. It reproduces observed spatial damage patterns and overall damage severity, achieving a 17.0% improvement in exact match accuracy compared with a FEMA HAZUS-based baseline. Because the framework explicitly represents debris generation, transport, inter-building interaction, and debris-induced damage, it identifies the structures and components that can be strengthened in advance of landfall, supporting proactive preparedness, emergency resource allocation, and early-stage planning for coastal community resilience.

papers.title: Supporting and constraining processes of risk recognition and preparedness in disaster education practice: A case study in Memuro Town, Hokkaido, Japan
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction
papers.abstract: : Previous studies on evacuation behavior have examined cognitive and psychological factors, while recent research suggests that preparedness and behavior may vary with residents’ everyday conditions and disaster education. However, the processes through which risk recognition and evacuation preparedness are formed and reconsidered remain insufficiently understood. This study examined disaster education practices in Memuro Town, Hokkaido, Japan. Data from 105 participants across four events were analyzed using the Modified Grounded Theory Approach, with contextual qualitative data used for concept generation and supplementary information informing derived analytical perspectives. The analysis constructed an explanatory process comprising four core categories: Preconditions, Attitudes, Recognition, and Preparedness. Relational conditions, mobility options, and information access rooted in everyday life shaped participants’ attitudes and conditioned how risks were recognized and preparedness was considered. Flood-risk explanations and scenario visualizations were associated with reconsideration of static and dynamic risk recognition, while discussions and workshop activities were associated with reconsideration of information-gathering strategies, evacuation criteria, routes, and support arrangements. Because educational components were combined and varied across events, component-specific effects could not be established. Some preconditions and attitudes appeared not to be readily altered through disaster education alone. In particular, feasible responses to mobility constraints often depended on family, community, or external assistance, while resignation associated with limited mobility could constrain both recognition and preparedness. These findings suggest that risk recognition and preparedness formed or reconsidered through disaster education may differ according to participants’ preconditions and attitudes, highlighting the need for differentiated educational approaches and links with support systems and planning.

papers.title: Wet-year precipitation anomalies and geohazard economic losses in China: A province-year sensitivity and climate-exposure assessment
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction
papers.abstract: : Wet years can become economically costly when hydroclimatic anomalies coincide with geohazard-prone terrain and exposed socioeconomic systems. However, national-scale evidence on how interannual precipitation variability is associated with geohazard-related economic damage remains limited. Using a province-year panel for mainland China from 2003 to 2022, this study estimates precipitation-damage sensitivity within an administrative annual framework that links province-level wet-year anomalies to reported economic losses. We then combine precipitation detrending scenarios, CMIP6 multi-model precipitation pathways, and SSP-consistent provincial GDP pathways to quantify a model-based historical trend-associated damage component and to conduct GDP-adjusted consequence stress tests under alternative hydroclimatic and socioeconomic pathways. Under the main log1p GDP-normalized outcome specification, a one-standard-deviation increase in annual precipitation anomaly was associated with a 0.758-unit increase in the transformed loss index (province-clustered 95% CI 0.585–0.932). The estimate remains positive under alternative outcome definitions, extended socioeconomic controls, daily precipitation exposure metrics, and alternative inference procedures. Under the linear ten-bin detrending specification referenced to 1982, the model-implied trend-associated damage component for 2003–2022 was 42.7 billion CNY at 2020 prices, with a conditional 2.5th–97.5th percentile range of 14.9–59.3 billion CNY from paired trend–response draws. Under SSP5-8.5, median cumulative consequences for 2025–2099 were 2.15 trillion CNY at 2020 prices (conditional model–parameter 2.5th–97.5th percentile range 1.23–4.52 trillion CNY), the highest median among the four scenarios. Overall, the study provides province-year evidence on precipitation-related geohazard loss sensitivity and a bounded stress-test framework for screening GDP-adjusted consequence burdens under coupled hydroclimatic and socioeconomic change.

papers.title: A hierarchical knowledge- and data-learning Bayesian network model – Application of dynamic risk assessment for oil and gas pipelines subjected to cascading disaster chains
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction
papers.abstract: This study explored a knowledge- and data-driven dynamic risk assessment method for oil and gas pipelines subjected to cascading disaster chains. Firstly, a hierarchical disaster causation model (HDCM) was constructed to describe causal disaster relationships and cascading transmission paths of oil and gas pipeline disasters within a unified framework. This mainly comprised the following basic elements: disaster-causing factors, disaster-pregnant environments and disaster-bearing bodies, as well as a full disaster scenario of ‘gestation–propagation–evolution–disaster–catastrophe’. This framework can provide a foundation of causal knowledge. Further, an innovative hierarchical knowledge- and data-learning Bayesian network (HKDLBN) was constructed based on the HDCM to reveal the mechanisms of risk state transmission and accumulation across different disaster layers for oil and gas pipelines. This mainly comprised network model construction, knowledge and data learning, and causal logical reasoning. This model dealt with modelling uncertainties by systematically integrating domain knowledge and observational data. Finally, a dynamic risk assessment of cascading disaster chains was completed for oil and gas pipelines using Bayesian reasoning. It clearly showed the risk level of each node within the full-disaster scenario. This method could be used to develop safety barrier-intervention measures and achieve disaster chain-reduction effects. Using the major accident of the ‘11·22’ Donghuang oil pipeline leakage and explosion as a case study, the results showed that the HKDLBN proposed in this paper could more reasonably and effectively assess the oil pipeline risk than the traditional FBN and DBN models.

papers.title: Assessing flood economic loss magnitude through explainable machine learning: Evidence from Spain
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Floods are among the most destructive disasters in Spain, causing significant human, infrastructural, and economic impacts while diminishing overall resilience. Estimating economic losses is essential for developing disaster management strategies to attenuate flood impacts. However, predicting large-scale events remains challenging, particularly due to the limited integration of resilience aspects. Previous studies have predominantly focused on disaster-specific attributes, often overlooking resilience features that offer a deeper contextual understanding of the factors stakeholders can actively act on. Machine Learning (ML) models are frequently used to evaluate losses. However, end-users often perceive them as a black box, lacking the technical expertise to interpret the results. This study develops an ML framework to predict the magnitude of economic losses from floods by jointly incorporating disaster and resilience indicators. To enhance its interpretability, the SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) technique was applied to quantify the influence of each feature on the predicted loss magnitude level, thereby improving transparency in the model’s decision-making process. A dataset of 2,867 flood events described by 54 variables spanning disaster magnitude, meteorological, and resilience features was compiled and analyzed, with 36 features retained after integration and selection. Among the evaluated ML models, the Gradient Boosting Classifier (GBC) demonstrated the best predictive performance. Integration of GBC outputs with SHAP analysis confirmed that, as expected, meteorological variables contribute to the magnitude of economic loss, while features related to regional resilience emerged as comparably influential predictors. Notably, resilience factors significantly influenced flood loss magnitude, demonstrating their importance in determining flood outcomes. This study represents the first application of explainable AI to estimate flood economic losses in Spain. The results demonstrate the value of using interpretable ML in identifying actionable resilience factors that can inform evidence-based strategies for disaster risk reduction and management.

papers.title: Revealing disparities in human tolerance to infrastructure disruptions: Empirical evidence from Typhoon Yagi in China
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction
papers.abstract: Extreme hazards can severely disrupt infrastructure systems and significantly reduce the well-being of society. To understand the well-being impacts of infrastructure disruptions, existing studies have conducted empirical analyses of household tolerance levels based on post-disaster surveys in developed countries. However, the empirical understanding of households’ tolerance and susceptibility to infrastructure disruptions remains limited in the Chinese context, as well as across residents’ different functioning activities. This study conducted a post-disaster survey following Typhoon Yagi in 2024, China, to systematically examine disparities in tolerance level across social subgroups under disruptions of power, transportation, water, and communication. Interval-censored Accelerated Failure Time (AFT) models are employed to identify key determinants of tolerance level. Based on the estimated AFT models, household susceptibility curves are constructed at both the infrastructure service level and the activity level. The results reveal pronounced disparities in the tolerance level across different social groups. Specifically, households with women, activity limitations, higher service needs, and lower satisfaction levels with government generally exhibit shorter tolerance. The key influencing factors of tolerance mainly include income, home ownership, vehicle ownership, previous experience, disruption duration, service needs, and satisfaction levels. Moreover, this study finds that households are most susceptible to water disruptions, followed by communication, power, and transportation. Activity-level susceptibility curves further uncover internal differences in households’ priority for needs. Compared with empirical studies from other countries, the tolerance level in China exhibits distinctive patterns shaped by local socioeconomic structures, culture, and policy. These findings facilitate developing human-centered infrastructure resilience analysis tailored to China’s context.

papers.title: Child-centred disaster preparedness: a three-step framework informed by embodiment and experiential learning
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction
papers.abstract: Current disaster education initiatives for children often rely on repetitive messaging such as evacuation drills and emergency kit preparation. While these approaches provide essential information, they are largely information-based, lack interactivity, and often fail to engage children in meaningful ways. As a result, children’s existing knowledge, creativity, and capacity for decision-making are underestimated, leaving a gap between awareness and actual preparedness. This research addresses this gap by proposing a three-step child-centred framework for Child-Centred Disaster Risk Reduction (CC-DRR). The framework was developed through a Research through Design approach, using a designed intervention that draws on embodiment aspects (real-world/real-time action, cognitive offloading, and collaboration) and experiential learning theory. The interventions were tested with 60 children aged 6–11 years in Southeast Queensland, Australia. The intervention functioned as a structured activity designed both to engage participants and to generate research insights. Data were collected through qualitative methods (observations of children interacting with the intervention and semi-structured interviews) and quantitative measures (a Likert-scale questionnaire). The resulting three-step framework: Presentation, Activity, and Reflection , is informed by experiential learning theory and supported by embodiment aspects. It provides practical scaffolding for developing effective CC-DRR activities and for enhancing children’s risk perception. Findings from qualitative and quantitative analysis highlight the value of embodiment in engaging children with perceived preparedness and self-efficacy, particularly through dialogue and interaction with physical tangibles. Quantitative results indicate an increase in children’s self-efficacy in preparedness behaviour, associated with their engagement with elements of the designed activity.

papers.title: Adapting a large-scale disaster recovery program to different community contexts: An evaluation of the Australian Red Cross 2019-2020 Black Summer Bushfire Recovery Program
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction
papers.abstract: It is well established that psychosocial disaster recovery programs should be adaptable to different community contexts, yet there is limited research into how this process of adaptation plays out in different communities within the same country. This paper presents an evaluation of the Australian Red Cross Bushfire Recovery Program (‘the Program’), which was delivered in communities nationally for three years following the 2019-20 bushfires in Australia. This paper presents a focused analysis of how this multi-jurisdictional psychosocial recovery program was adapted to different community contexts across Australia, with attention to changing needs over time. Semi-structured interviews and focus groups were conducted with 71 individuals including community members, service providers and Red Cross staff in four case study communities across Australia, with annual data collection for three years (2021-23). The Program’s outputs encompassed a variety of activities and events centred on psychosocial support and literacy. Participants across all locations and years of the evaluation perceived its flexible, community-based approach as a key strength, however most community members and service providers felt that the Program ended too soon. This paper presents examples of Program adaptation to provide long-term psychosocial support during disaster recovery. These findings highlight key considerations for emergency management organisations, funders, and researchers including exit planning, consideration of existing gaps in social services and psychosocial support in communities, and supporting communities when additional crises occur in addition to the disaster that the program was designed to support.

papers.title: Heat stress and urban economic growth in China: Dynamic effects, channels, and evidence from functional data analysis
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction
papers.abstract: Against the background of global climate warming, the impact of high-temperature variation on urban economic growth has become an increasingly important issue in climate economics and urban sustainability research. Using daily maximum-temperature observations and city-level economic data for 247 prefecture-level and higher-level cities in China from 1992 to 2023, this study constructs a long-term functional representation of daily temperature for each city. Annual economic outcomes are linked to the corresponding calendar-year segments of the long-term temperature trajectory through a functional regression framework, allowing the estimated temperature coefficient to vary continuously over the complete 1992–2023 time domain. The results show that, first, changes in daily maximum temperature exert pronounced nonlinear, stage-specific, and cyclical effects on urban economic growth, with both the direction and magnitude of the effects adjusting dynamically over time. Second, the impact of high temperature exhibits clear urban heterogeneity: cities with higher heat exposure and higher levels of economic development are more sensitive to temperature changes and show larger fluctuations in the coefficient curves. Third, consumption, investment, and foreign trade constitute important channels through which high temperature affects urban economic growth. This study reveals the complex dynamic relationship between long-term daily temperature variation and urban economic growth, providing empirical evidence for cities to address climate risks, optimize economic structures, and enhance economic resilience.

papers.title: Assessing the value of impact-based forecasting and early action for floods
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction
papers.abstract: This paper assesses the effectiveness of Impact-based Flood forecasts (IbF) in reducing flood impacts. The new system is developed in the Geographical, Environmental, and Behavioural (GEB-IbF) model framework, where it is applied to the April–May 2024 flood in the Sinos River catchment, southern Brazil. The system correctly issued evacuation warnings to 88,883 households (76.1% of all flooded households) and recommended protective measures that reduced estimated flood damages by $4–5 million. Comparing conventional meteorological warnings (MW; rainfall severity) and general flood warnings (FW; flooded area) with impact-based warnings (IbW; expected number of buildings hit and damaged) demonstrates that IbW provide timely, useful, and actionable information. IbW enhances a flood early warning system in four main ways: (I) IbW reach a larger number of administrative units (593-708 for IbW vs. 580-682 for FW), especially upstream and rural areas; (II) IbW reduce falsely warned households by 19.9% (in medium flood scenarios) and 33.5% (in severe flood scenarios) compared to FW; (III) IbW prompt more affected households to act, with 4–11% more households correctly evacuating and implementing protective actions; and (IV) IbW achieve greater damage reduction (25.2-30.6% of total damage) than FW (21.9-21.6%), under the medium and severe flood scenarios, respectively. These results highlight the need for investment in operational flood forecasting and continuous gathering of impact-related data. Besides, this study shows that improved human response to warnings can double avoided damage and evacuations, emphasizing the urgency for continuous training and awareness raising among the local population and local authorities.

papers.title: The 2021 western North America heat wave: Analysis of overlapping social vulnerability and heat in nine US cities
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction
papers.abstract: Previous research has shown that low income and otherwise vulnerable populations experience a disproportionate burden of heat-related illness. A heat wave event of unprecedented magnitude occurred in the summer of 2021 in western North America. In some locations, temperatures peaked 10°-20°C above maximum summer temperatures of the previous decade. We obtained gridded temperature estimates for Boise, Las Vegas, Los Angeles, Oakland, Portland, Sacramento, Salt Lake City, San Francisco, and Seattle. We aggregated average minimum and maximum heat wave temperatures and linked to social vulnerability index (SVI) scores, which are based on American Community Survey data. Within each location, we examined if census tract level vulnerability was associated with higher heat wave temperatures. Spearmans’ rank correlation coefficients showed a significant positive association between overall SVI and minimum and/or maximum temperature in all locations except Oakland and San Francisco. Of significant positive results, coefficients ranged from 0.09 to 0.61. Associations between temperature and individual SVI themes (socio-economic status, household characteristics, racial & ethnic minority status, and housing type and transportation) generally mirrored results for the overall SVI. We also evaluated local indicators of spatial association to identify spatial clustering of census tracts experiencing both high SVI and high temperatures. Significant global spatial autocorrelation was identified in all locations except Oakland and San Francisco. Our analysis found that census tracts with higher social vulnerability experienced the hottest temperatures during one of the most intense North American heat waves in recent history, further exacerbating their already elevated risk of heat-related morbidity and mortality.

papers.title: A novel nexus of international migration, land use change, and disaster vulnerability: A structural equation modeling (SEM) analysis for Kerala, India
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction
papers.abstract: This study empirically examines how migration-induced development indirectly intensifies disaster vulnerability through land-use pathways in the State of Kerala, India. GIS mapping and Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) are applied to analyze micro- and meso-level data from 968 Local Self-Government Units (LSGUs) across all 14 districts of the State to evaluate causal relationships linking migration and remittances to paddy land conversion and house damage during the catastrophic floods in 2018–2019. The model demonstrates that international migration strongly predicts paddy land conversion (β = 0.606, p < 0.001), which in turn increases flood damage (β = 0.128, p < 0.001), even after controlling for climate vulnerability factors. The migration-disaster relationship is fully mediated (99.7%) by land-use change rather than by alternative socio-economic and direct climate vulnerability parameters. The findings of the study put forward an integrated policy approach connecting migration, agricultural land use, and disaster risk reduction. The study advances literature by developing a novel integrated framework linking migration, paddy land conversion and disaster vulnerability, and validating this relationship through quantitative evidence.
