papers.title: The 2015/16 El Niño drought impacts on household food security, adaptation expenditure and coping strategies: A gender-based perspective
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction
papers.abstract: The 2015/16 El Niño-driven drought is the most severe South Africa has experienced in decades, causing widespread nationwide welfare losses. While drought affects all households, understanding how its impacts manifest across male- and female-headed households (MHHs and FHHs) is critical, as heterogeneity in household composition could shape the magnitude and distribution of the welfare losses. Using a household panel data (2010–2017) combined with gridded drought data, the study first examines food security and adaptation expenditure gaps between MHHs and FHHs, and the extent to which the drought influence these gaps. The study then uses a fixed-effects estimator to investigate how drought relates to household food security and adaptation expenditure over time and across MHHs and FHHs, as well as how households used available resources to cope during the drought episode. The decomposition results show that, while there is no adaptation expenditure gap between the two household types, MHHs spend 24% more on food per capita than FHHs, and drought does not influence this food expenditure gap. The food security gap is entirely due to differences in household and headship characteristics, including education, age, employment and household income. Further, the results reveal that average households and MHHs experienced reductions in food security of 11.9 and 15.1 percentage points, respectively, in 2015/16, compared to FHHs, while adaptation expenditure showed no significant response to the drought. However, as the drought extended into 2017, FHHs experienced a greater reduction in food security (11.8 percentage points). MHHs and FHHs also coped differently with the drought: MHHs relied more on government transfers, while FHHs and households overall relied more on wealth. Beyond food security, the drought had adverse effects on health outcomes, with younger children in MHHs experiencing greater impacts.

papers.title: A framework for climate resilient retrofits in a multi-hazard environment
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction
papers.abstract: The frequency and severity of climate hazards across Canada is increasing, with communities facing several hazards concurrently or consecutively. This has led all levels of government to consider ways to improve the resilience of their communities. While established retrofit guidance documents provide key information for singular climate hazards, there is a critical gap when navigating a multi-hazard reality. This paper presents a structured framework and resulting database of 186 climate-resilient retrofit measures for residential buildings, synthesized from 274 sources across five climate hazards (wildfire, extreme heat, flooding, extreme wind, and ice and snow). A novel interrelationship framework is developed that classifies each retrofit as conflicting, complementary, or coordinating with respect to other measures and hazards — enabling prioritization of retrofits that protect against multiple hazards simultaneously, avoid maladaptation, and that can be sequenced efficiently. Each measure is also characterized by generalized estimates of cost, effort, expertise, invasiveness, and emissions impact to support prioritization under real-world constraints. This information, along with the guidance from each source, was synthesized into a publicly accessible database which has been integrated into national and municipal level tools such as Climate Insight's Solution Finder and Clean Foundation's Flood Resilient Residential Retrofits Handbook. Two case studies, examining retrofit planning for a flood-extreme heat scenario and wildfire-extreme heat scenario demonstrate how the developed framework aids in selecting appropriate adaptation strategies for multi-hazard retrofit planning. While developed for the Canadian residential context, the underlying adaptation objectives and hazard science are broadly applicable to similar climates and building types globally.

papers.title: How urban flooding impacts healthcare accessibility and spatial inequalities?
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction
papers.abstract: Urban flooding is increasingly shaping the ways in which people access healthcare, with uneven consequences across places and population groups. Focusing on Shanghai, one of China's most densely populated and economically developed cities, this study examines how flooding disrupts residents' healthcare accessibility and intensifies its inequalities by integrating flood records, dynamic population data, road networks, and hospital service capacities. Healthcare accessibility was assessed based on healthcare travel time and a Gaussian two-step floating catchment area method, while inequality was measured using the Gini coefficient. Results showed that as general hospital level increased (primary, secondary, and tertiary general hospitals), travel time rose from 15.02% to 18.23%, while specialized hospitals experienced a 17.64% increase. The proportion of residents experiencing reduced accessibility increased from 45.82% to 57.35% across general hospital levels, with specialized hospitals at 55.19%, indicating higher sensitivity of higher-level services. Flooding amplified existing center-periphery disparities, disproportionately reducing accessibility in peripheral areas. Temporal variations are also evident, with more pronounced disruptions occurring at night and on weekends, highlighting the interaction between flooding and human mobility patterns. Children and older adults exhibited more spatially uneven accessibility changes and pronounced localized disadvantages. Across all hospital types, flooding led to more substantial increases in accessibility inequality for higher-level hospitals. These findings highlight how environmental hazards intersect with spatial structures and social vulnerability to shape healthcare access. The study underscores the importance of place-based health planning and adaptive resource allocation to reduce inequalities and enhance urban resilience in flood-prone cities.

papers.title: Beyond exposure: institutional response, resilience, and mental health after the 2024 Spanish floods
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction
papers.abstract: In October 2024, a record-breaking flood struck Spain, causing extensive damage, loss of life, and widespread public criticism of institutional preparedness and response. Despite the magnitude of this event, its psychological impact on both affected residents and volunteers, as well as the factors shaping this impact, remain largely unexplored. This study examines post-disaster mental health consequences and their associations with risk exposure severity, emotional experiences, psychological resilience, and perceived institutional and community support. Data were collected using a cross-sectional design with quantitative and qualitative data involving 71 flood victims and 69 volunteers. Results revealed an exceptionally high psychological burden in both groups (81.7% of victims and 68.1% of volunteers)scoring above the established screening cut-off for post-traumatic stress symptoms. Poorer mental health was associated with exposure and negative emotional experiences (e.g., feeling helpless) while psychological resilience was a protective factor in both groups. Dissatisfaction with institutional support and response speed was linked to worse mental health among victims. Qualitatively, two themes emerged: the profound emotional impact of the disaster (outlining exposure factors and mental health consequences, such as sensory memories, anger, exhaustion, etc.), and deep dissatisfaction with institutional management, characterized by widespread feelings of abandonment, disorganization, and loss of trust in authorities. Overall, findings indicate that psychological impacts following floods are shaped not only by hazard exposure but also by preparedness, response quality, and institutional trust. Strengthening a timely response, and psychosocial preparedness should be central components of disaster risk reduction strategies to mitigate long-term mental health consequences.

papers.title: Scale, threshold and the recoverable social gradient of projected heat exposure: a paired census-tract analysis of European outermost and metropolitan territories
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction
papers.abstract: European adaptation policy assumes that projected heat exposure follows comparable social gradients in outermost-region archipelagos and in continental metropolitan areas. Using a single climate product (ADAPTECCA-CMIP6 ESD-RegBA, 2.5 km insular and 5 km continental, reference 1971–2000), four identically defined exposure indices and identical 2022 census-tract socioeconomic data, we compare the Canary Islands (1,387 tracts) with the Madrid metropolitan area (2,756 tracts) as a static-population counterfactual. On one dataset the standardised deprivation–warming coefficient ranges from −0.001 to +0.618 according to the analytical unit, aggregation level and conditioning set alone. It is recovered where the unit contains both social and climatic heterogeneity — Gran Canaria +0.618, Tenerife +0.493, central Madrid +0.396, with intervals clustered on the climate grid cell — and not in four smaller islands or in the metropolitan corona, a condition that cuts across the insular–continental distinction. It survives a change of climate product that alters projected magnitudes twofold, but not the construction of the exposure index: locally normalised percentile thresholds attenuate it by 30–56% in the archipelago and eliminate it in the metropolitan case, returning coefficients indistinguishable from zero on the same tracts that return +0.396 on an absolute-threshold index. Approximately 816,000 residents of 2022 live in tracts combining high projected end-century warming with high deprivation, dispersed mainly across two islands in one case and concentrated in the other at 92% in a single municipality that holds 72% of the estimation-sample population. What fails to transfer between territories is not the social mechanism but the scale at which it can be measured: among tract pairs under 10 km apart, projected change differs by 21.4 days on average in the archipelago and 1.4 in the metropolitan area. Vulnerability assessments should report the effective resolution of the hazard field and the spatial variance of the exposure index before estimating social gradients.

papers.title: Protecting cities from wildfires using water distribution systems via pre-wetting: a preliminary hydraulic screening framework
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction
papers.abstract: Wildfires are increasing in frequency and severity. They are reaching major cities, such as Los Angeles, CA and causing billions of dollars in destruction, pollution, and loss of lives. This study investigates using the existing water distribution system (WDS) to fight, not only single-structure fires, but warding off a wildfire approaching the entire city. A strategy entitled the “Immediate Access Strategy” or IAS is introduced in which sufficient water to simultaneously open all hydrants for a specified time at the wildfire front is maintained in the storage tank(s) and large pipes go from the tank(s) to the hydrants on the wildfire front. Numerous simulations of the network solver EPANET, which calculates the flow and pressures throughout the system at all times, were performed for analysis. Different protection levels were defined to give options as the robustness of the wildfire fighting effort. Scenarios were outlined for various flowrates at the hydrants, depending on the firefighting needs. It is envisioned that the structures be pre-wetted prior to the fire, which would require less water than extinguishing the fire. Costs to upgrade the system normalized by the current value of the WDS assets were calculated. It was found that protecting the entire city at a high flowrate level would cost up to seven times the value of the current system assets, but to pre-wet the structures on the fire front could cost as little as 1.2 times the current value. The system could be improved incrementally, as funds became available. Technical details were explored here, but policy and planning practicalities are also important.

papers.title: Effects of post-disaster subsidies on business recovery in Japan: A doubly robust estimation
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction
papers.abstract: This study examines the effects of approval for a post-disaster business recovery subsidy on sales recovery among MSMEs following the July 2020 flash flood in Kyushu, Japan. Using subsidy approval as the treatment, it investigates how effectiveness differs across disruption conditions. To address non-random program participation, we employ a doubly robust (DR) estimation framework combining propensity score weighting and outcome regression. On average, approval was associated with a 14.97-percentage-point increase in sales recovery, measured on an index where pre-flood sales equal 100. The estimated effect was largest (25.07 percentage points) for businesses experiencing capital-related disruptions, such as temporary closure, reduced operating capacity, or insufficient operating funds. The effect remained positive (19.85 percentage points) for businesses facing both capital-related disruptions and additional constraints, including labor shortages, rising material costs, and external shocks such as COVID-19. The results suggest that the subsidy supported sales recovery by helping restore production capacity, although its effects were partly offset by concurrent demand shocks, factor-related disruptions, and the timing of approval relative to outcome measurement. The findings also highlight the potential value of complementary instruments such as business interruption (BI) and contingent business interruption (CBI) insurance. Limitations include potential residual self-selection bias, reliance on a single post-disaster observation, the absence of information on interactions with other support measures, and the inability to distinguish approval effects from cash-disbursement effects. Future research should use longer-term panel and administrative data to examine how approval, disbursement, and other financial instruments jointly influence MSME recovery.

papers.title: Crisis translation: A student-led crowdsourcing initiative of a disaster relief term-base after 2023 Türkiye-Syria earthquakes
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction
papers.abstract: Large-scale disasters generate acute multilingual communication needs that often exceed the reliability and governance capacity of automated translation alone. The February 2023 Türkiye–Syria earthquakes exemplified this challenge: while international search-and-rescue teams arrived and volunteer language support surged, high-stakes crisis communication still required dependable, domain-specific terminology and carefully coordinated translation and interpreting. This paper studies a case-based response through TermQuake, a student-led crowdsourcing initiative establishing a disaster-relief term-base at Boğaziçi University in Türkiye. Drawing on crisis-translation scholarship, it reframes translation and interpreting as communicative mediation that supports disaster risk reduction by bridging expert-to-expert and expert-to-non-expert communication, where domain-specific terminology competence is decisive for preventing harmful misunderstandings. While machine translation and LLM-based systems can reduce latency, their limitations—restricted language and resource coverage, infrastructural constraints, and risks of context insensitivity—support a hybrid approach requiring human post-editing and terminology verification for accuracy, cultural appropriateness, and institutional trust. The paper documents TermQuake’s development from an initial terminology resource into a mature platform, including terminology creation and verification, community-building through crowdsourcing, mobile-app development, and ongoing project governance. The case demonstrates that—despite expanding AI-enabled capacity for fast content generation—crisis settings continue to require human expertise, offline-accessible infrastructure, and robust terminological foundations to ensure semantic accuracy and cultural appropriateness. The study also highlights interdisciplinary collaboration as a driver of effective crisis translation, advancing resilience-focused evidence for preparedness planning, capacity-building, and policy development.

papers.title: A multi-objective design procedure for the seismic retrofit of framed structures with fluid viscous dampers
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction
papers.abstract: The 2025 Global Assessment Report on Disaster Risk Reduction highlights the persistent societal and economic burden of disasters and warns that post-disaster reconstruction too often restores pre-existing conditions rather than systematically incorporating risk-reduction measures. This reinforces the need for preventive seismic upgrading, particularly in Europe, where much of the building stock was constructed before modern seismic design standards. The European challenge is twofold: dedicated provisions for buildings equipped with energy-dissipation systems were introduced only in the second generation of Eurocode 8, leaving their practical implementation dependent on engineering judgement and iterative design; meanwhile, several methodologies proposed in the literature typically address a single structural performance target at one seismic limit state. Yet earthquakes of different intensities can cause distinct structural and non-structural damage, with economic losses and functional disruption even when structural safety is preserved. This paper presents the first formulation and numerical validation of a multi-objective methodology for designing fluid viscous damper (FVD) systems in existing framed buildings. The procedure simultaneously considers displacement-based performance targets at different limit states, reflecting different performance requirements and supporting risk-informed retrofit decisions. These targets are used to determine the damper properties through constrained optimization and their subsequent distribution along the building height. In this formulation, FVDs are idealized as purely viscous dissipators, neglecting the elastic deformability of the damper–brace assembly. The proposed methodology thus represents a step toward integrating multi-level seismic performance requirements into practical retrofit design, supporting the development of more proactive strategies for reducing the vulnerability of existing buildings.

papers.title: A catastrophe modelling approach for rapid post-event flood loss estimation
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction
papers.abstract: Catastrophe models are central to quantifying flood risk and informing insurance, reinsurance, and disaster risk management decisions. As flood impacts intensify under climate change and rapid urban expansion, robust and transparent loss estimation is increasingly critical across diverse climatic and socio-economic settings. This need is particularly acute in data-scarce regions, including arid and semi-arid environments where short-duration, high-intensity rainfall generates destructive flash floods in sparsely monitored catchments. Despite advances in open geospatial data, catastrophe-scale flood loss estimation remains largely dominated by proprietary modelling platforms, and there is limited evidence that fully open, auditable workflows can reconstruct hazard and quantify economic losses for recent extreme events. Here we show that a fully open-data catastrophe modelling framework can reproduce the April 2024 Dubai flash floods and generate economically plausible loss estimates without reliance on proprietary tools. We integrate bias-corrected satellite precipitation (GPM-IMERG), a hydro-conditioned global bare-earth digital elevation model (FABDEM), 2D hydrodynamic modelling, open building exposure data, and calibrated global depth-damage functions within a transparent end-to-end workflow. The reconstructed flood footprint achieved a Critical Success Index of 0.65 against Sentinel-1 observations, while estimated ground-up losses were approximately AED 16 - 18 billion (USD 4 - 5 billion). Sensitivity analysis of urban Curve Number values showed that perturbations of ±5 and ± 10 produced relatively modest changes in aggregate losses, with the principal spatial patterns remaining broadly stable. These results demonstrate the potential for globally accessible datasets and open modelling tools to support rapid, transparent post-event flood-loss assessment in data-scarce environments, while highlighting the importance of accounting for uncertainties in rainfall forcing, urban drainage representation, exposure and vulnerability.

papers.title: From externally initiated participation to autonomous engagement: Motivational transformation in community-based disaster risk reduction
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction
papers.abstract: Sustaining community participation is an important challenge in community-based disaster risk reduction (DRR), particularly in contexts where local actors are increasingly constrained by demographic change. Although community-based initiatives are widely recognized as fundamentally important for DRR, participation is not always driven by individuals’ intrinsic motivation. Participation is often initiated through external factors such as assigned roles within local organizations. This study examines two community organizations engaged in the preservation of historical Sunadome (traditional sand-retaining weirs) in Fukuyama City, Hiroshima Prefecture, Japan. Those Sunadome serve both disaster mitigation and cultural heritage functions. Using a mixed-methods approach combining questionnaire surveys and semi-structured interviews, the study analyzes participants’ affiliation motives and the processes through which externally initiated participation evolves over time. The results identify two distinct pathways through which externally initiated participants transition toward more autonomous and sustained engagement: one pathway is mediated by socially oriented extrinsic motivation through interpersonal relationships; the other pathway involves direct internalization through alignment with the perceived purpose and value of the activity. These findings highlight the important roles of organizational structures and leadership practices in facilitating motivational transformation. By elucidating how externally initiated participation can be integrated into sustainable community-based DRR, this study contributes theoretical insights into volunteer motivation and presents practical guidance for the design of resilient community organizations under conditions of demographic decline.

papers.title: Trusted intermediaries: Fostering multicultural community leadership in disaster communication
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction
papers.abstract: Culturally and linguistically diverse (CALD) communities can experience disproportionate disaster risks due to barriers to timely, relevant and culturally appropriate communication. Yet less is known about how community leadership shapes access to disaster information, resources and support. Drawing on participatory action research with 33 participants from seven cultural groups in Cairns, North Queensland, this study examines CALD community leaders as trusted intermediaries within disaster communication ecologies. Findings show that community leadership encompasses cultural interpretation, network mobilisation, practical and emotional support, and connections with institutional systems. Leadership was grounded in trust, cultural knowledge, community embeddedness, established relationships and formal position. The CALD Disaster Leadership Communication-Ecology Framework conceptualises intermediary leadership across five interconnected systems: cultural and ethical, institutional, network, media and interpersonal. Communication ecology and relational leadership explain how culturally embedded leaders connect community relationships, communication resources and institutional systems, mobilising social capital through these connections. The findings also identify constraints, including limited institutional recognition and support, unpaid labour and emotional demands, alongside questions of representation, accountability and institutional dependence. Recognising and appropriately supporting CALD community leadership can strengthen culturally responsive disaster communication while maintaining institutional responsibility for disaster management. Developed from a single regional study, the framework requires further examination across cultural, geographic and disaster contexts.

papers.title: Debris-cast: A two-stage machine learning framework for hurricane debris prediction using multi-source geospatial data
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction
papers.abstract: Accurate hurricane debris estimation is important for contractor mobilization, temporary debris-management site planning, and resource allocation. Existing tools often rely on fixed empirical formulations and limited inputs, which can restrict their ability to represent nonlinear relationships among hazard intensity, the built environment, vegetation, terrain, and flood exposure. This study evaluates a two-stage machine-learning framework for hurricane debris estimation using multi-source geospatial data, observed and post-event hazard inputs, and operational debris-removal records. The framework first classifies whether debris removal was recorded within a spatial unit and then estimates debris volume for debris-present cells. Random Forest and XGBoost models were evaluated for construction and demolition, vegetative, and combined debris from Hurricanes Helene and Milton in Pinellas County, Florida, using H3 hexagonal and equivalent-area square grids at two spatial resolutions. Classification showed higher observed performance at finer resolutions, with the highest AUC of 93.9% for construction and demolition debris using Random Forest at H3 resolution 9. Regression results revealed a scale-dependent tradeoff. Coarser grids generally produced stronger model fit and lower area-normalized error, with R 2 reaching 0.869 for vegetative debris, whereas finer grids provided greater spatial detail and lower raw per-cell MAE. Hexagonal and square grids showed comparable observed performance. The study demonstrates retrospective and screening capability using historical data. Pre-landfall forecasting, transferability across regions and events, and operational deployment require further validation using independent datasets and true forecast inputs.

papers.title: Seismic social vulnerability assessment in cross-border regions: Application to Albania, Greece and North Macedonia
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction
papers.abstract: Assessing social vulnerability is essential to understanding how communities may experience and recover from disruptive events. Such an impact assumes specific features when the communities are located in cross-border-regions (CBRs). This study evaluates social vulnerability related to seismic hazard in the CBR shared by Albania, Greece, and North Macedonia, an area exposed to high seismic hazard due to its location along active tectonic structures of the Hellenic and Balkan regions. To do so, the Social Vulnerability Index ( SoVI ) framework is applied and adapted to the features of CBRs. The indicators selected for the SoVI assessment capture key dimensions of vulnerability, including demographic structure, socio-economic conditions, institutional performance, and service availability. To account for heterogeneity in the scale of data availability and differences in indicator importance, two scenarios are analysed using alternative weighting schemes for each indicator. The results reveal a strong influence of methodological choices on social vulnerability outcomes, as well as the need to address CBR social vulnerability in an integrated manner. The spatial variability of SoVI across and within national borders highlights key differences in how vulnerability manifests across distinct administrative and socio-economic contexts. In addition, integrating SoVI with seismic hazard using a simplified social risk matrix approach enables the identification of priority areas for targeted mitigation measures, emergency planning, and resilience-oriented policy interventions. Overall, the findings emphasise the importance of harmonised methodologies and integrated indicator systems in capturing the differentiated nature of social vulnerability in complex cross-border environments and its impact on the seismic social risk.

papers.title: Strategic implementation of green roofs for urban pluvial flood risk reduction: A case study of Milan, Italy
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction
papers.abstract: The rise in intensity and frequency of extreme precipitation events is increasing the concern regarding pluvial floods in European cities. Urbanisation exacerbates the impacts of pluvial floods by affecting the infiltration process. Nature-based solutions, particularly Green Roofs (GRs), are promoted to mitigate these risks, as GRs can be implemented on existing buildings without requiring additional ground space. This study presents a risk-based framework to evaluate the potential of GRs in reducing pluvial flood risk in Milan by examining three implementation strategies, namely Water Depth (WD), Area (Ar), and Random Iteration (ITE). The framework integrates a hybrid hazard model, combining the empirical Curve Number method with a Cellular Automata approach using a hydrograph. The proposed hybrid approach enables us to link land-use-driven changes in flood volume to flood propagation. Extreme rainfall events with durations of 1, 6, and 24 hours were derived from ERA5. Residential building exposure data were extracted from OpenStreetMap and municipal datasets. Vulnerability was integrated within the framework using the INSYDE model, complemented by four additional vulnerability functions for sensitivity analysis. Results indicate that GRs can effectively reduce pluvial flood-induced losses, with reductions of 16-69% across different rainfall durations. However, their effectiveness declines with longer rainfall periods and higher return periods. Among the allocation strategies, WD provided higher benefits for events with durations of 1 and 6 hours. Overall, GRs can substantially reduce flood risk. The study provides an integrated framework to support evidence-based decision-making for the strategic implementation of GRs for pluvial flood risk reduction.

papers.title: Basin water storage degree for risk-informed debris-flow warning support: A forward-looking proof of concept in a small mountain catchment
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction
papers.abstract: Small mountain catchments require hydrological indicators that characterize antecedent storage before rapid rainfall and channel responses develop. Application is difficult where monitoring records and debris-flow inventories are limited. This study develops Basin Water Storage Degree, termed BWSD, as a dimensionless forward-looking indicator of apparent storage for risk-informed debris-flow warning support. BWSD recursively reconstructs an apparent storage increment from rainfall, stage-derived channel drainage, and a monitored evaporation-based atmospheric water-loss proxy, then normalizes it using a critical-reference threshold constructed only from information confirmed before each decision. A purpose-built monitoring system was deployed in the 0.8461 km 2 Fengshuwan study subcatchment within the broader Fengshuwan basin, Zhejiang Province, China. The daily record covered 908 days from 12 October 2023 to 6 April 2026. No critical study-subcatchment-scale debris-flow response was confirmed. The apparent storage increment reproduced seasonal wetting, drainage, recession, and hydrological memory, reaching 473.1 mm on 26 June 2025. During the 543-day formal evaluation, maximum BWSD was 0.936 under standard daily information control and approximately 0.987 under episode-embargo analysis. The June 2025 process involved minor sediment-laden runoff and localized sediment and clast transport without coherent critical propagation. Several rainfall-memory indicators exceeded their forward-looking reference levels during this confirmed non-critical process. Short-lead persistence, XGBoost attribution, sensitivity analysis, and Monte Carlo propagation supported temporal coherence, hydrological interpretation, and uncertainty stability. The results establish proof-of-concept evidence for sequential apparent-storage assessment, reference-level stability, and high-storage non-critical discrimination within the monitored envelope. Documented events and independent catchments are required to quantify event-detection skill and operational warning performance.

papers.title: Making snow avalanche information actionable: How Alaska decision-makers perceive and use avalanche science
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction
papers.abstract: Snow avalanche-prone regions face complex and changing conditions that require informed decisions for safety and planning. Scientific information about past and future snow avalanches (hereafter called avalanche information) has much to contribute to this decision-making context. To examine how decision-makers currently use avalanche information and perceive the potential actionability of future avalanche model outputs presented through future avalanche hazard maps, we conducted 18 in-depth interviews with decision-makers and practitioners across multiple sectors (transportation, emergency management, utilities, recreation, homeowners, municipal government, ski area operations, commercial guiding, and avalanche engineering) in Alaska. The participants regularly interpret and apply avalanche information in both operational and planning contexts. Interviews explored how information is used, how future avalanche hazard maps are evaluated, and how uncertainty is understood and managed. Findings show that situational awareness for decision-making is built from the integration of diverse data sources. Participants viewed future avalanche hazard maps as potentially useful in long-term infrastructure and land-use planning but perceived them as having limited value in real-time operations. In practice, uncertainty is treated as inherent, and decisions are routinely made despite incomplete information. These findings highlight the need for future avalanche hazard maps that align with existing information practices, decision contexts, and approaches to managing uncertainty.

papers.title: Flood evacuation models: A simplified probabilistic approach with application to a case study in Rome
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction
papers.abstract: Flood events clearly induce significant impacts in urbanised regions. Over the last decades, advances in computational capacity, high-resolution digital elevation data, and open-access geospatial datasets have enabled the development of Evacuation Models (EM). However, many EMs are often not so suitable for operational use by civil protection authorities, due to their significant data requirements, high computational burden and complex parametrisation. In this context, this work aims to bridge this gap by proposing a screening-level, operational tool based on a simplified probabilistic methodology, that integrates pedestrian movement under uncertainty with a streamlined representation of flood arrival time, and then produces evacuation-time distributions and spatially explicit estimates of floodwater-pedestrian interaction probability. The approach is applied to a flood-prone urban area in Rome (Italy). Results highlight the role of network topology, route branching and behavioural variability in determining evacuation performance, revealing critical areas where existing Evacuation Plans (EPs) may require revision. Finally, we state the need for integrating simplified evacuation models into emergent decision-support frameworks, including Digital Twins for urban flood management.

papers.title: Public health emergencies in Jordan: appraising multi-agency preparedness
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction
papers.abstract: Jordan faces a complex landscape of public health threats arising from infectious disease outbreaks, environmental hazards, technological incidents, humanitarian crises, and regional instability. These risks place sustained pressure on national institutions responsible for preparedness, response, and resilience. While multiple governmental and non-governmental agencies contribute to public health emergency preparedness and response (PHEPR), coordination gaps, overlapping mandates, and fragmented governance structures continue to challenge the effectiveness of a unified national response. This study proposes a methodological framework to assess multi-agency preparedness for public health emergencies in Jordan. This research integrates document review, stakeholder analysis, and key informant interviews across Jordan’s principal PHEPR institutions. Network-informed mapping, visualized using the Kumu platform, were applied to map perceived inter-organizational connectedness, identify key coordinating nodes, and reveal structural gaps within the national PHEPR ecosystem. Findings highlight the central coordinating roles of the Ministry of Interior, the Ministry of Health, and the National Center for Security and Crisis Management, alongside a limited institutional integration of the Jordan Center for Disease Control. The results reveal persistent challenges in role clarity, information sharing, and operational coordination. The proposed approach is adaptable to other resource-constrained and crisis-prone settings seeking to reinforce multi-agency readiness for public health emergencies.

papers.title: Evacuation routing under radiological dispersion: Reducing cascading congestion risk in nuclear emergencies
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction
papers.abstract: Radiological emergencies may produce spatially heterogeneous exposure fields and simultaneously disrupt evacuation through traffic congestion. Reducing disaster risk in such events therefore requires evacuation strategies that consider both direct exposure and network-level functional degradation. This study develops a coupled radiological-dispersion, evacuation-routing, and cascading-congestion framework to evaluate evacuation risk under an I-131 release scenario. The atmospheric dispersion of I-131 is simulated using HYSPLIT and mapped onto a weighted road network to quantify route-level exposure. Four routing strategies are compared: the shortest-time path, the minimum-dose path, the low-betweenness path, and an integrated path. Performance is evaluated using dynamic dose equivalent, weighted betweenness centrality, network-efficiency retention ratio, capacity-redundancy sensitivity, and Pareto analysis. Localized congestion scenarios were imposed on road segments within contaminated areas. The results showed that the shortest-time and minimum-dose paths remained highly dependent on high-betweenness nodes. The low-betweenness path reduced structural bottleneck dependence. The integrated path maintained comparable radiation exposure and exhibited a relatively stable Pareto trade-off across four departure times. Prolonged congestion at high-betweenness nodes within radiation-affected road segments further increased radiation exposure along the selected path. The proposed framework supports risk-informed emergency routing and disaster risk reduction in hazardous environments.

papers.title: Identification of risk amplification effects in rainstorm disaster chains using coupled disaster system theory and Bayesian networks
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction
papers.abstract: : The risk amplification effects inherent to disaster chains are crucial for disaster prevention but have rarely been empirically substantiated because of the lack of suitable evaluation methods. Thus, this study proposes a coupled framework integrating disaster system theory and Bayesian networks ( CF-DST-BN ). By leveraging multivariate indicators spanning subhazards, bearing bodies, and damage, the framework captures three amplification effects from 359 rainstorm disaster chain events in the core area of the agricultural‒pastoral transition zone in northern China. (i) The cascading hazard transmission increases the expected secondary hazard-event count by 31.76%, primarily along 4 tertiary, 2 quaternary, and 1 quinary diffusion paths. (ii) The amplification effect of exposure manifests in two ways within three- to five-level chains: a superimposed effect resulting from multiple distinct secondary hazards acting upon the same type of exposed objects and a scope expansion effect occurring because multiple distinct secondary hazards affect different types of exposed objects, thereby expanding the overall scope of affected targets. (iii) Disaster damage is amplified via two mechanisms in higher-order chains: first, multiple secondary hazards produce compounded damage; second, a single secondary hazard expands the damage scope. Unexpectedly, the risk diffusion paths of rainstorm-induced disaster chains become irreversible as the number of layers increases, which is a process that is shaped primarily by the disaster-prone environment. This hybrid approach offers dual utility, as it captures both risk amplification effects and decodes the causal relationships that underlie risk propagation, thus providing practical guidance for policymakers and researchers involved in disaster prevention and mitigation.

papers.title: Risk perception, self-protective culture, and emergency preparedness: A case study at the University of Macerata (Italy)
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction
papers.abstract: Understanding how risk perception relates to self-protection is essential for improving emergency preparedness within higher education institutions. This study analyses these two dimensions among members of the University of Macerata (Italy) through a case study based on 174 questionnaires. Risk perception and self-protection were operationalised using multidimensional indicators and analysed through the Fuzzy Quadrant Mapper, which combines fuzzy logic, TOPSIS and profile classification to account for the uncertainty inherent in subjective assessments. The results show that previous emergency experience, emergency training and institutional trust are positively associated with higher levels of preparedness. However, the relationship between risk perception and self-protection is not linear. Nearly half of the participants (46.56%) were classified into profiles in which both dimensions were misaligned, demonstrating that a high perception of risk does not necessarily lead to greater preparedness. Emergency training emerged as the factor most consistently associated with higher scores in both dimensions, highlighting its role in transforming awareness into protective capacity. These findings suggest that risk perception and self-protection should be analysed as complementary but distinct constructs. Beyond the specific case of the University of Macerata, the proposed methodological framework offers a transferable approach for identifying preparedness profiles and supporting evidence-based risk communication, emergency education and disaster risk reduction strategies in university settings.

papers.title: Beyond volume proxies: An exposure-based scenario-screening framework for conditional potential loss of life in tailings storage facility portfolios
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction
papers.abstract: Tailings storage facilities (TSFs) are expanding, and occasional failures can cause severe downstream impacts. This study presents a screening-level framework for conditional Potential Loss of Life (PLL, given failure) using open datasets, Google Earth Engine (GEE), and an Excel release model. The workflow estimates dam geometry by DEM cut-and-fill, caps release at 0.90 of storage, routes a MERIT Hydro-guided corridor, applies exponential thickness decay with minimum-thickness trimming, and evaluates PLL on the WorldPop 100 m grid. Each site is evaluated using 144 equally weighted deterministic combinations and summarised with scenario-exceedance curves, scenario-set Value-at-Risk at 95% (VaR95) and scenario-set Expected Shortfall at 95% (ES95). Across 17 sites, upper-tail PLL spans nearly three orders of magnitude, with VaR95 from 0.1 to 148 and P99 from 0.15 to nearly 200. A high-consequence group emerges, while most remain low. Scenario-exceedance curves reveal varied distributions, including long-tail behaviour where typical outcomes are low but some combinations produce severe PLL. Partial rank analysis showed a stronger independent association of PLL with exposed population ( = 0.64) than with stored volume ( = 0.16), although the 17-site sample limits generalisation. The framework supports standardised ranking and prioritisation, complementing site-specific breach hydraulics and evacuation analyses. Results should be interpreted within assumptions on routing, release estimation, transferable depth-fatality curves, population uncertainty and equal design weighting. Estimates represent conditional consequences, not probabilistic annual risk. Future work should extend beyond PLL, which captures only fatality consequences and cannot substitute for assessing displacement, livelihoods, environmental harm or wider social consequences.

papers.title: Occupational Exposure in Metal Additive Manufacturing: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis of Airborne Nanoparticle Exposure, Stratified Synthesis of Metals, and Evidence-Gap Mapping of Physical and Process-Safety Hazards
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Metal additive manufacturing (metal AM) can expose workers to nanoparticles, metal-containing aerosols, dermal contamination, inert atmospheres, physical agents, and reactive powders, but exposure magnitude and comparability remain uncertain, and the depth of empirical workplace evidence differs markedly across these domains. Objectives To quantify occupational nanoparticle exposure, synthesise airborne-metal and dermal evidence, and map — rather than quantitatively pool — the physical and process-safety hazard domains for which comparable workplace evidence remains insufficient across the metal-AM workflow. Methods PRISMA 2020 review registered on Open Science Framework (OSF) searched four databases to 2 March 2026. Forty-eight unique studies were included after blinded dual screening. Quantitative data were re-extracted in long format at study and exposure-scenario level. Risk of bias used review-specific Office of Health Assessment and Translation (OHAT)/Navigation Guide-informed criteria; metrological quality was appraised separately using American Industrial Hygiene Association (AIHA)/Exposure Assessment Strategies Committee (EASC)-informed criteria. Nanoparticle concentrations were pooled using restricted maximum-likelihood (REML) random effects with Knapp-Hartung adjustment, with study-level aggregation to preserve independence. Metals were considered for formal pooling using explicit comparability criteria defined for the final quantitative synthesis Results Nine independent studies contributed to the primary nanoparticle meta-analysis: pooled geometric mean (GM) 10,225 particles/cm 3 (95% CI 6,034–17,326), I 2 =93.9%, and 95% prediction interval 2,111–49,526. Core, strict and leave-one-study-out sensitivities were similar; excluding Karlsson et al., whose inputs were reported as bounds, yielded GM 10,557 particles/cm 3 . Task-specific excursions often exceeded central exposure levels. No metal met criteria for formal pooling; only two independent studies per element provided directly comparable personal inhalable geometric means for Ni, Co, Cr, Fe, Mn, and Mo. Dermal evidence was sparse, and several physical/process-safety domains lacked comparable workplace measurements. Conclusions Metal-AM exposure is strongly task-, process-, material-, containment- and context-dependent. Nanoparticle exposure can be summarised quantitatively, but substantial heterogeneity and the wide prediction interval preclude treating one pooled value as representative of all workplaces. Metal evidence should remain stratified until more comparable personal measurements are available.

papers.title: Workload and Thermal Stress Constraints in a Combustible Dust Manufacturing Environment: A Mixed-Methods Study
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Tapioca starch production generates substantial combustible dust exposures governed by IEC 60079-10-2 zone classification. Maintenance lapses, inadequate housekeeping, and ignition-source mismanagement are the principal human contributors to dust explosion risk, yet the workload mechanisms that compromise these safety behaviors across structurally distinct occupational roles remain poorly characterized. Methods A sequential explanatory mixed-methods design was employed at a tapioca starch facility in northeastern Thailand. Multidimensional workload was quantified using the NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX) and thermal stress was measured with Wet Bulb Globe Temperature (WBGT) per ISO 7243:2017 across three occupational groups: Truck Drivers (TD), Mechanical Maintenance Workers (MMW), and Control Room Operators (CRO). Semi-structured interviews were analyzed by reflexive thematic analysis and integrated with quantitative findings via a joint display. Results Weighted Workload (WWL) differed significantly across groups (Welch's F(2, 23.71) = 259.80, p < 0.001, η 2 = 0.852, 95% CI [0.751, 0.893]). MMW recorded the highest WWL (91.93 ± 1.91) and the greatest thermal exceedance (+6.5°C above the ISO reference limit). CRO maintained elevated cognitive workload (WWL = 81.84 ± 6.16) under full thermal compliance. TD were defined by extreme temporal demand (93.00) under modest thermal exceedance (+1.0°C). Mixed-methods integration identified three occupation-specific constraint pathways logistic-thermal, physical-thermal, and cognitive-psychological loading formalized in a preliminary Constraint-Based Workload Framework (CBWF). Conclusions Workload composition, not thermal exposure, differentiated the three occupational groups. Constraint type rather than demand magnitude should guide role-specific ergonomic and process-safety intervention in combustible dust environments.

papers.title: Occupational Exposure to PFAS and Cardiovascular Risk: Why the 2026 ECHA Restriction Makes Worker Health Surveillance Urgent
papers.abstract: In March 2026 the European Chemicals Agency opened the final consultation on a universal restriction of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS). The debate has centred on environmental and consumer exposure. Workers carry the highest internal doses, and the regulatory process counts them as an exposure cohort without treating them as a population to be monitored. Italy holds Europe's most informative occupational evidence, generated by the Veneto contamination linked to the Miteni plant, and that evidence is discordant: worker biomarker studies link serum PFAS to cardiovascular risk markers and a community mortality analysis reports the first formal demonstration of an association with cardiovascular mortality, while the occupational cohort from the same plant shows no excess. Two Italian courts reached opposite conclusions on causation in 2025. We argue that the discordance itself makes structured health surveillance of PFAS-exposed workers urgent, and set out the rationale for the systematic review we have registered.

papers.title: Comprehensive evaluation of anti-vibration gloves by integrated indicators: hand-arm vibration transmissibility, forearm muscle activity, hand temperature and finger dexterity
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Anti-vibration gloves are widely used to mitigate hand-arm vibration exposure in industrial environments. While thicker vibration-dampening materials generally improve vibration reduction, they may negatively affect usability. However, existing evaluation methods often rely on single performance metrics and do not adequately capture the trade-offs between vibration attenuation and wearability-related indicators such as muscle activity, hand temperature, and finger dexterity. Methods This study proposes a comprehensive platform for evaluating anti-vibration gloves by integrating multiple performance indicators, including hand–arm vibration transmissibility, forearm muscle activity, hand temperature, and finger dexterity. Five glove specimens with varying thicknesses of rubber-based vibration-dampening materials were assessed. Hand–arm vibration transmissibility was measured following ISO 10819 (2013). Forearm muscle activity was evaluated using electromyography, hand temperature was monitored with a wearable sensor, and finger dexterity was assessed according to ASTM F2010/F2010M-18. A weighted scoring model was developed to quantify overall glove performance. Results Across Gloves A–C, greater damping-material thickness was generally associated with lower vibration transmissibility, while wearability-related indicators showed corresponding trade-offs. However, these trends were not monotonic across all five specimens, indicating that glove construction and material properties other than thickness also influenced performance. Among the five gloves, one specimen with flexible lining materials exhibited notably lower muscle activity despite its thickness. The weighted scoring model enabled balanced comparisons across all indicators. Conclusion The trade-offs between vibration attenuation and wearability-related indicators varied considerably depending on glove design and material properties. The proposed approach provides a laboratory-based framework for comparing anti-vibration gloves under controlled conditions, rather than a direct assessment of HAVS risk reduction in workplace exposure scenarios.

papers.title: The Job Demands-resources Model Explains How Workplace Conditions Shape Health, Motivation, and Performance
papers.abstract: : Background The Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) model links work conditions to employee health and performance. This study examined associations among leadership, psychosocial resources, sleep disturbance, fatigue-related functioning, health, and performance among US Navy surface-ship crews. Methods This cross-sectional study included 5,122 eligible survey records from 47 ships. Confirmatory factor analysis used 4,769 complete records, and adjusted latent-variable models used 4,673 cases. Analyses accounted for clustering within ships. Additional sensitivity analyses examined alternative model specifications, within-ship patterns, and results from ship-level bootstrap samples. Results Psychological safety and perceived crew resilience were positively associated with command-referent performance. Supervisor safety climate was associated with self- and department-referent performance, but its command-referent coefficient was uncertain. Job demands were associated with greater stress, sleep disturbance, and fatigue-related impairment. Fatigue-related impairment was associated with greater stress and poorer general health, while sleep disturbance was also associated with poorer health. Leadership assessment was associated with all four psychosocial resources, although its overlap with psychological safety limits interpretation. Conclusion Resource-performance associations varied by resource and performance referent, whereas sleep disturbance and fatigue-related impairment were more consistently related to health and strain. Strong performance ratings should not be taken as evidence that workload and recovery demands are sustainable. As the study was cross-sectional and self-reported, the findings represent associations rather than causal effects.

papers.title: Human Performance Limits as Safety Constraints in High-Risk Operations: A Documentary Analysis of Accident Investigation Reports
papers.abstract: Background Fatigue, stress, workload, time pressure, and uncertainty are frequently identified in accident investigations, but they are often retained as general contributing factors rather than translated into operational constraints on safe decision making. This study examined how public investigation reports can support that translation in high-risk work systems. Methods A structured documentary analysis examined 27 purposively selected investigation cases from five agencies and nine domains. Source-linked extractions were separated from normalized categories. Unsupported labels were removed; incomplete dimensions were retained. Distinct-case frequencies and co-occurrences were examined using historical evidence grades, domain exclusions, and a same-case sensitivity excluding additional analyst interpretations. Human coding reliability was not measured. Results The corrected analysis coded degraded situational awareness in 14 cases, diagnostic uncertainty in 12, workload overload in three, and fatigue or sleep debt in four. Excluding additional analyst interpretations reduced the first two counts to five each; fatigue and workload counts were unchanged. All seven uncertain-hazard/inventory cases were in process safety. Procedural controls occurred in 14 cases, but this was not a count of stopping rules alone. Twenty-five cases supported all four analytical dimensions. Conclusion The Safety-Critical Decision Constraint Matrix offers an episode-centered format for comparing documentary evidence and bounded control implications, rather than a new accident theory. Broad labels and recurrent combinations were interpretation-sensitive. The contribution is transparent documentary organization, not validated coding performance, causal inference, or demonstrated control effectiveness.

papers.title: Longitudinal Changes in Brain Age After Shift Work: Mini Literature Review and an MRI-based Case Report
papers.abstract: Background Shift work characterized by irregular working hours is increasingly prevalent in modern society and is associated with numerous adverse health outcomes. Previous research has focused primarily on metabolic, cardiovascular, and sleep-related effects, and little is known about how shift work specifically impacts brain aging. Methods This longitudinal case report investigated shift work’s impact on MRI-based predicted brain age using repeated magnetic resonance imaging measurements on two healthy physicians before and after shift work initiation. The validated models, brainageR, MIDIconsortium/BrainAge, and ENIGMA_brainage, were used to estimate magnetic resonance imaging-based brain age. Results Based on the three models, both participants showed higher predicted brain age estimates at follow-up after shift-work initiation; however, because the models were applied to the same MRI scans, this concordance should be interpreted descriptively. ENIGMAbrainage showed the greatest change magnitude. Conclusions These preliminary, hypothesis-generating observations show higher follow-up MRI-based predicted brain age estimates in two individuals after shift-work initiation, but do not establish an exposure-related biological effect. Larger longitudinal studies with control groups and longer follow-up are required to determine whether such changes reflect sustained biological aging, transient structural fluctuation, or measurement-related variation.

papers.title: Scale Development and Validation of the Japanese Employee Engagement Questionnaire
papers.abstract: Background This study aimed to develop the Japanese employee engagement questionnaire (EEQ) and to examine its reliability and validity among workers in Japan. Methods This study was a secondary analysis of de-identified survey data collected from full-time employees in Japan through an internet survey company. A 9-item EEQ was developed based on definitions of employee engagement drawn from both academic literature and statements by governments and organizations, to ensure applicability in research and practice. The short version of the New Brief Job Stress Questionnaire, one item from the WHO Health and Work Performance Questionnaire, and the Psychological Safety Scale were also administered. Reliability was assessed using internal consistency and test–retest reliability. Validity was evaluated by examining structural validity, known-groups validity, convergent validity, and discriminant validity. Results A total of 208 participants completed the initial survey, and 106 of them completed the two-week follow-up for assessing test-retest reliability. Exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses consistently supported a single-factor structure with good model fit. Additional discriminant validity analyses indicated that employee engagement and work engagement were related but empirically distinguishable constructs. Cronbach’s alpha for the EEQ was .926, and the intraclass correlation coefficient was .792. For known-groups validity, the EEQ differentiated between groups expected to differ in employee engagement (i.e., managers’ leadership, supervisor support, psychological safety at work, and work performance). The EEQ showed significant positive correlations with meaningfulness of work, work engagement, and other job resources and positive outcomes. Conclusion These findings provide initial evidence that the Japanese EEQ is a reliable and valid tool for measuring employee engagement among workers in Japan.

papers.title: A Realist Inquiry of Job Demands, Multi-level Resources, and Burnout among Early Childhood Education Professionals in Colorado: A Structural Equation Model
papers.abstract: Background Understanding burnout in the early childhood education (ECE) workforce is critical due to the mental and physical consequences on individuals and the young children in their care. This study examined 1)how job demands impact emotional exhaustion, depersonalization, and personal accomplishment outcomes and 2)if multilevel resources moderate the relationship between demands and outcomes. Methods This study administered an electronic 89-item survey via convenience sampling to ECE staff employed in five Head Start agencies in Colorado (n=359). A structural equation model (SEM) was developed to test the effects of a latent job demands factor on staff outcomes, and included multilevel workplace supports as moderators. SEM was chosen to account for measurement error and to model the relationships among latent constructs representing job demands, supports, and burnout dimensions simultaneously. Results Survey participants were majority female (94%), white (67%), Hispanic (53%), and half worked in classrooms (51%). A log-likelihood ratio test of the final model indicated good fit ( p <.05). Job demands led to increased emotional exhaustion (β=0.86, p <.001) and depersonalization (β=0.34, p <.001), and did not impact personal accomplishment (β=-0.06, p =0.27). Resources did not moderate the impact of demands on outcomes, but coworker support decreased depersonalization (β=-0.31, p <.001). Additionally, multilevel resources (supportive work culture, coworker support, and psychological capital) led to increased personal accomplishment (β=0.13, p =.01; β=0.20, p <.00; β=0.45, p <.001, respectively). Conclusion ECE organizations should reduce the burden of demands to decrease emotional exhaustion and depersonalization while fostering multilevel support to increase personal accomplishment. This would benefit the well-being of the ECE workforce and young children.

papers.title: Effect of National Cultural Dimensions on Lost Workdays Among Migrant Workers in the Korean Chemical Process Industry
papers.abstract: Background We aimed to examine the association between Hofstede’s national cultural dimensions in migrant workers’ countries of origin and workdays lost due to industrial accidents in process safety management (PSM) workplaces within the Korean chemical process industry. Methods Using industrial accident data collected between 2015 and 2024, we analyzed 382 migrant workers from 15 countries. Correlation and regression analyses were conducted using six cultural dimensions as independent variables: power distance index (PDI), individualism (IDV), masculinity (MAS), uncertainty avoidance index (UAI), long-term orientation (LTO), and indulgence (IND). Results Among the six dimensions, only IND demonstrated a statistically significant, albeit modest, negative association with lost workdays. The correlation remained significant after Bonferroni correction at both the individual and national levels, but the regression model explained little variance (R 2 = 0.025), indicating a statistically detectable signal rather than a practically strong predictor. Mean lost workdays among workers from low-IND countries were 2.3 times those among workers from high-IND countries, partly reflecting the concentration of all six fatalities in the low-IND group. Leave-one-out and country-threshold sensitivity analyses yielded consistent estimates. The absolute IND score of the country of origin was more closely associated with lost workdays than the cultural distance from South Korea, consistent with the possibility that restraint-oriented cultural values persist after migration. Conclusion These findings suggest that targeted health monitoring for migrant workers from low-IND countries, along with an organizational culture that promotes proactive hazard reporting, may help reduce lost workdays in the chemical process industry.

papers.title: Work Schedules, Sleep Health, Fatigue, and Occupational Safety Among Bus Drivers: A Systematic Review
papers.abstract: Background Bus driving is a safety-sensitive occupation, yet evidence on how duty timing, duration, and recovery structure jointly influence sleep health, fatigue, and occupational safety remains fragmented. This review synthesized bus driver-specific evidence and distinguished it from broader professional-driver context. Methods Using a Population-Exposure-Comparator-Outcome (PECO) framework, Scopus, PubMed, Web of Science, and Transport Research International Documentation were searched for English-language empirical studies published from 2017 to 2025, without geographic restriction. Study selection, design-specific Joanna Briggs Institute appraisal, and narrative synthesis followed PRISMA 2020 and PRISMA-S principles. Results Sixteen bus driver studies were included. Across countries and designs, long or irregular work, night and rotating duties, split shifts, early starts, and inadequate recovery were associated with poorer sleep, greater sleepiness or fatigue, circadian disruption, and safety-relevant impairment. Evidence converged on a review-derived pathway from schedule exposure through disrupted sleep and fatigue to reduced alertness and adverse safety outcomes. Compensation design, route pressure, supervisor support, reporting culture, and regulatory enforcement modified this pathway. Samples were predominantly male where sex was reported, and sex-disaggregated evidence was limited. Conclusions Bus driver fatigue is a systems-level occupational safety issue. Controls should combine biologically informed scheduling, protected recovery time, sleep-disorder screening, nonpunitive fatigue reporting, supervisor support, and compensation arrangements that do not reward fatigue-inducing work. Better longitudinal and intervention studies with objective sleep and verified safety outcomes are needed.

papers.title: Work-related Characteristics and Migration-based Disparities in Fatal Occupational Injuries in South Korean Fisheries
papers.abstract: Background The South Korean fishing industry has increasingly relied on migrant labor to address substantial shortages of fishers. However, empirical knowledge regarding occupational injuries among migrant fishers remains sparse, creating a knowledge gap that threatens both individual safety and the long-term sustainability of the industry. By comparing determinants of fatalities among compensated injury cases for migrant and non-migrant fishers, this study identifies underlying structural vulnerabilities and proposes evidence-based systemic reforms to promote safety equity in the fishing industry. Methods We analyzed nationwide fishery accident-compensation claims for South Korean coastal and offshore fishers from 2004-2014, using eXtreme Gradient Boosting-SHapley Additive exPlanations to capture non-linear interactions, which were then confirmed through Firth-penalized logistic regression with explicit interaction terms. Results While case fatality ratios were comparable, the characteristics and determinants of these fatalities varied significantly by migration status. This disparity was associated with the inferior working conditions faced by migrant fishers, such as concentration in offshore fisheries, exposure to nighttime operations, and engagement in high-risk tasks. Notably, the risk of death was considerably higher when migrants were injured aboard small vessels during night or pre-dawn operations. These findings underscore the need for structural interventions through vessel-level and national-level accident prevention approaches. Conclusion Fatal risk disparities among fishers by migration status appear to be largely attributable to structural working conditions rather than individual characteristics. This suggests that relying on migrant labor without improving hazardous working conditions undermines safety equity and fails to provide a viable solution for sustainable fisheries.

papers.title: Piece-rate Pay and Sleep Problems: A Study of 942 Midnight Delivery Platform Workers in the Republic of Korea
papers.abstract: Background Midnight delivery platform (MDP) workers engage in the entire delivery process from initial loading to final drop-off overnight, generally between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m. This study investigates the association between pay type and sleep problems among MDP workers in South Korea. Methods We conducted a nationwide survey of 942 Korean MDP workers in 2024. Pay type was categorized into three groups: ‘fixed salary’, ‘piece-rate’, and ‘mixed’. The ‘fixed salary’ workers received a fixed regular income regardless of the number of deliveries they completed, while the ‘piece-rate’ workers earned income entirely based on the number of deliveries they completed. The ‘mixed’ workers received an income combining a fixed salary with additional earnings based on delivery count. Sleep problems over the past month were assessed using three items: ‘non-restorative sleep’, ‘difficulty maintaining sleep’, and ‘difficulty initiating sleep.’ Modified Poisson regression was used to examine the association, adjusting for sex, age, education level, marital status, area, weekly workdays, and monthly individual income. Results The prevalence of non-restorative sleep, difficulty maintaining sleep, and difficulty initiating sleep were 63.6%, 38.6%, and 32.9%, respectively. Compared to ‘fixed salary’ workers, non-restorative sleep was more prevalent among the ‘piece-rate’ and ‘mixed’ workers (piece-rate: PR 1.83, 95% CI 1.28-2.63, mixed: PR 1.93, 95% CI 1.35-2.77). Difficulty maintaining sleep was more prevalent among ‘mixed’ workers compared with ‘fixed salary’ workers (PR 1.62, 95% CI 1.09-2.41). No statistically significant association was found regarding difficulty initiating sleep. Conclusions Pay including a piece-rate component may be associated with a higher prevalence of self-reported sleep-related symptoms among MDP workers.

papers.title: Workplace Violence Experienced by Clinical Students in Iran: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
papers.abstract: Background Exposure to workplace violence can adversely impact the performance and skills of clinical students as they prepare to enter the healthcare system as specialized professionals. This systematic review and meta-analysis aims to determine the prevalence of violence directed at clinical students during their clinical placements in Iran and to describe their related experiences. Methods A comprehensive search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, SID, and Magiran databases to identify all relevant studies examining workplace violence among clinical students in Iranian medical schools. Data were synthesized both descriptively and through meta-analysis. Prevalence data were extracted and pooled using random and quality effects models. Separate analyses were performed based on the type of violence, the source of violence, and the affected groups. Results Fifteen studies involving a total of 4,785 clinical students were included in the meta-analyses. The data exhibited substantial heterogeneity. Pooled prevalence rates ranged from 0.06% for sexual violence to 66.6% for verbal violence. Workplace violence was most frequently perpetrated by patients’ relatives (40%) and patients themselves (37%). Conclusion Violence against clinical students during clinical internships is common and poses significant physical and psychological risks. This study highlights the urgent need to implement multifaceted strategies to prevent workplace violence and to better prepare clinical students to manage violent incidents, respond appropriately, and report such events. Given the particularly high prevalence of verbal violence, efforts should also focus on fostering a culture of respect and improving verbal communication at the community level.

papers.title: Low Job Control Predicts Incident Insomnia: A Prospective Study Among Municipal Employees
papers.abstract: Background Psychosocial work stress may influence sleep health among workers, but prospective evidence on specific psychosocial work stressors remains limited. This study examined the association between occupational stress and incident insomnia among municipal employees in Japan. Methods A one-year prospective study was conducted among 666 municipal employees without insomnia at baseline. Incident insomnia was defined as an Athens Insomnia Scale score of ≥6 at follow-up. Occupational stress was assessed using the Brief Job Stress Questionnaire. Poisson regression models with robust variance were used to estimate relative risks (RRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs), adjusting for age, sex, job type, history of depression, and working hours. Results During follow-up, 127 participants (19.1%) developed insomnia. Reduced job control was significantly associated with an increased risk of incident insomnia (RR = 1.14, 95% CI: 1.05–1.24). Participants in the lowest quartile of job control had a significantly higher risk of insomnia than those in the highest quartile, and a significant dose–response relationship was observed across quartiles. A significant interaction between job demand and job control was also identified. Conclusions Reduced job control may contribute to the development of insomnia among workers.

papers.title: Comparison of Two-phase Decontamination Sequences After Hydrofluoric Acid Exposure: Evidence From a Viable Human Skin Model
papers.abstract: Background Exposure to hydrofluoric acid (HF) can cause systemic poisoning due to transdermal fluoride penetration (TFP). Therefore, accidents involving HF demand immediate first-aid measures. We investigated different skin-decontamination sequences and their impact on TFP in an ex-vivo human skin model. Methods Viable human skin was exposed to 30% HF for 1 min in a static diffusion-cell model, and TFP was observed for 72 h. We compared the efficiency of different decontamination sequences, consisting of a first acute decontamination phase and a second subacute decontamination phase, using various acute and subacute decontamination agents at different skin temperatures (26°C and 32°C). Results Despite quick decontamination, significant fluoride penetration was observed within the first hours of exposure across all decontamination scenarios. Acute phase: The choice of decontamination agent had minimal effect on TFP, while reducing the skin temperature from ∼32°C to ∼26°C significantly decreased fluoride absorption. Subacute phase: Decontamination with a calcium gluconate gel, with or without HEPES, significantly reduced TFP by 25% and 28%, respectively (at 32°C), compared to no additional intervention. The combination of calcium gluconate–HEPES gel and reduced skin temperature achieved a significant 52% reduction in TFP at 72 h compared to no subacute decontamination at 32°C (when primary decontamination was kept identical). Conclusion The findings from our ex-vivo experiments indicate that removal of HF by any possible means is vital in the acute phase, and that subsequent gel decontamination during the subacute phase may offer an additional benefit by reducing systemic absorption from the intradermal fluoride depot.
