papers.title: Risk Assessment Between Tritium and Radioactive Exposure Factor: Health Impact Assessment Survey in the Vicinity of Nuclear Power Plant in Wolsong
papers.abstract: Background Concerns about long term low-dose radiation exposure from living in the vicinity of Wolsong nuclear power plant (NPPs) have persisted for decades. Tritium, a mildly radioactive isotope of hydrogen released from NPPs, can contribute to internal radiation exposure through ingestion or inhalation. This study assessed internal tritium exposure and associated behavioral and environmental factors among residents living near the Wolsong NPP in Korea. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted from June to July 2022 among 1,421 residents within a 5-km radius of the Wolsong NPP. Tritium was measured by 960 participants, and biological samples and detailed questionnaires were collected to assess tritium exposure and associated factors. Results A geometric mean of 960 residents was 4.32 Bq/L (arithmetic mean: 10.16 Bq/L), with a detection rate of 77%. The detected group showed higher proportions of NPP entry (10.4% vs. 4.1%, p =0.004) and underground water use for cooking (14.5% vs. 11.4%, p =0.01), with marginal significance for local seafood consumption ( p =0. 06). Also, entering NPP (OR=3.07, 95% CI=1.50-6.31) and using purified tap water for cooking (OR=2.13, 95% CI=1.34-3.40) were significantly associated with tritium detection. Additionally, in 3 group sensitivity analysis, only entering the NPP had significant results. A spatial gradient was also observed, with higher concentrations near the NPP and lower concentrations farther away (region A to H: 6.31 to 2.72 Bq/L). Conclusions These findings highlight the importance of continued biomonitoring and evidence-based public health management to better understand internal tritium exposure among populations residing near facilities.

papers.title: Quantitative and Qualitative Evaluation of the Sweating Function of the Human Earlobe for Heat Stress Monitoring
papers.abstract: Background: This study evaluated thermoregulatory sweating at the earlobe under heat exposure as an initial step toward exploring its potential as a technically interesting candidate site for skin temperature monitoring in occupational heat stress assessment. Methods: Two experiments were conducted in healthy male participants. Sweat rates on the medial and lateral earlobe and forearm were quantitatively measured using ventilated capsule perspiration meters at 25, 30, and 35 °C ambient temperatures with 50% relative humidity. Qualitative sweating was assessed using Minor's iodine-starch test at 40°C ambient temperature and 50% relative humidity. Results: Earlobe sweat rates were consistently and significantly lower than forearm values, with minimal temperature-related variation. No iodine-starch reaction was observed on the earlobe, whereas sweating was detected on the auricle and face. Conclusion: The earlobe appeared to exhibit negligible thermoregulatory sweating under the tested conditions. Given the low likelihood of sweating-related interference, the earlobe may warrant further investigation as a technically interesting candidate site for future validation studies of skin temperature monitoring in occupational heat stress assessment.

papers.title: Redefining Worker Protection in the Algorithmic Era: From Algorithmic Justice to Insurance Systems for the Gig Economy
papers.abstract: The rapid expansion of the digital platform economy has introduced novel occupational hazards driven by algorithmic management. This short communication examines the occupational health challenges faced by gig workers in the context of algorithmic control, focusing on four key mechanisms: trade-offs between economic success and worker health, uncertainty in terms of effort and reward, unreliable assessment of job performance, and incorrect attribution of responsibility. These algorithmic hazards differ substantially from conventional occupational risks and cannot be adequately addressed by existing occupational health and safety frameworks. To address these inequities, we propose redefining occupational health and safety standards under an algorithmic justice framework. Furthermore, we suggest implementing an algorithm tax and an algorithm-dependent insurance system to establish sustainable social safety nets. These measures, along with mandatory disclosure of algorithmic management systems as 'High-Impact AI,' offer a practical regulatory pathway to enforce worker protection and fairness within the evolving legal landscape in the algorithmic era.

papers.title: Formal Caregivers' Exposure to Workplace Violence in the Swiss Home-care Setting: A Cross-sectional Study
papers.abstract: Background: Workplace violence against formal caregivers is a serious concern, affecting both their well-being and the quality of care. While workplace violence in hospitals is well studied, research on violence in home-care settings remains scarce. This study examines the prevalence, frequency, types, consequences, and risk factors of workplace violence experienced by formal caregivers from care receivers in home-care. Methods: A descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted in 2022 in a home-care organisation in French-speaking Switzerland using an electronic survey. Formal caregivers were selected using convenience sampling. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, and Pearson's chi-square and Fisher's exact tests. The Holm-Bonferroni method was applied for the post-hoc analysis. Results: Among 200 participants, 42% reported experiencing at least one form of workplace violence in the past year. Following a workplace violence event, nine affected participants took medical leave, with four being absent for more than seven days. Nursing assistants were less likely to experience workplace violence than registered nurses and health specialists. Formal caregivers with 1-4 years of experience were at higher risk of workplace violence compared to those with longer professional experience. Conclusion: This study is one of the first to examine workplace violence towards formal caregivers in the European home-care context, revealing concerning rates of workplace violence with significant consequences for caregivers, and highlighting the urgent need for greater attention to this phenomenon. Addressing workplace violence in home-care is essential to safeguarding caregiver well-being and preventing workforce shortages.

papers.title: Organizational Support for Safety and Work Ability in Healthcare Workers: A Longitudinal Study
papers.abstract: Background: Maintaining healthcare worker (HCW) work ability and continuing employment are critical issues. We examined the association of work ability with the previously unexamined work-environment factors of organizational support for safety (OSS) and surface-acting emotional labor (SaEL). Methods: A self-administered survey covering work-environment features recruited employees of five U.S. public-sector healthcare facilities in 2018-2019 and 2021. Linear regression on the outcome of work ability, both cross-sectionally and longitudinally, focused on OSS and SaEL with additional independent variables. Results: A total of 1,059 and 1,553 surveys were collected from predominantly female HCWs; 425 answered both questionnaires. Almost two thirds of the HCWs were either non-direct care or unlicensed HCWs. Work ability scores were lower in direct-care workers versus non-direct-care workers. In multivariable regression models, OSS was positively associated with work ability, and SaEL was negatively associated, cross-sectionally at baseline and follow-up. Job strain, back pain, and safety hazards were also negatively associated with work in both cross-sectional and longitudinal analyses, while social support and civility norms (combined) were positively associated. In the longitudinal analysis, only OSS positively predicted work ability, while SaEL had a borderline negative effect. Conclusion: The finding that OSS predicts work ability is novel. Despite high turnover, there has been little examination of risk factors for low work ability among HCWs. The importance of this organizational predictor justifies organization-level interventions to improve workplace safety. Such actions could simultaneously address and mitigate the additional risk factors of SaEL, job strain, and back pain in order to improve work ability for all groups of HCWs.

papers.title: Working Time Exposures and Occupational Injury Among Delivery Gig Workers in China: Indirect Pathways Through Sleep Quality
papers.abstract: Background: Delivery gig workers face elevated risks of occupational injury, yet little is known about how working time exposures contribute to injury risk and the pathways underlying this association. This study examined the associations between multiple dimensions of working time exposures and occupational injury and whether sleep quality represented an indirect pathway co-occurring with these associations. Methods: Using cross-sectional survey data from 1,537 delivery gig workers in Shanghai, China, we examined the associations between three dimensions of working time exposures (daily working hours, weekly working days, and night-shift frequency) and occupational injury. Sleep quality was examined as a potential indirect pathway based on the Effort-Recovery Model. We estimated a series of regression models and used bootstrap methods to decompose direct and indirect associations while adjusting for sociodemographic and job-related covariates. Results: Longer daily working hours and more frequent night shifts were directly associated with higher occupational injury counts. Weekly working days and night-shift frequency showed significant indirect associations with occupational injury through poorer sleep quality. Robustness checks using a binary injury indicator yielded consistent results. Conclusion: Working time exposures are associated with occupational injury risk among delivery gig workers through both direct exposure-related associations and indirect pathways involving sleep quality. Interventions and policies targeting excessive working hours, night work, and sleep quality may help reduce injury risks in this vulnerable transport workforce.

papers.title: Comparative Analysis of Respirator Fit Factors Using Korean Test Panels and Standardized Korean Headforms
papers.abstract: Background: Fit testing is essential to evaluate the effectiveness of respiratory protective equipment for ensuring occupational safety. The Republic of Korea currently lacks a standardized fit test panel that reflects domestic facial characteristics, although international guidelines emphasize its establishment. This study aimed to validate a Korean fit test panel developed according to international standards and to examine the consistency of fit test results between human participants and headforms with comparable facial dimensions. Methods: The panel was developed using facial anthropometric data from 11,429 adults in the Size Republic of Korea database based on ISO 16976-2:2022(E). Fifty participants representing the panel categories underwent quantitative fit testing with various respirator models. Fit test pass rates of human participants and headforms were evaluated against the U.S. National Personal Protective Technology Laboratory ( 2015) criterion of 64-76% to determine the panel's applicability. Results: < 0.05), with full-face types showing higher pass rates than half-face types. Human fit tests exceeded the National Personal Protective Technology Laboratory criterion (76-100%), supporting the panel's international applicability. In contrast, headform-based testing produced lower fit factors, particularly for small respirators. Intraclass correlation coefficient analysis revealed poor agreement (<16%) between human and headform results. Conclusion: The Korean fit test panel appears to represent population-specific facial dimensions and shows potential for respirator evaluation under the tested conditions. However, differences between participants and headform outcomes indicate the need for improved headform fidelity to enhance test reliability.

papers.title: Impact of the Serious Accidents Punishment Act on Occupational Injury Rates in Korea’s Manufacturing Sector: An Interrupted Time-Series Analysis
papers.abstract: Background: The Republic of Korea introduced the Serious Accidents Punishment Act (SAPA) in 2021 to improve workplace safety by holding company leaders legally accountable for serious accidents but its impact on injury trends has not been well established. This study evaluated SAPA's effect on age-sex-standardized injury incidence rates (ASRs) in the Republic of Korea's manufacturing sector, examining differences by company size (≥50 vs. <50 employees), sex, and injury type (inpatient vs. outpatient). Methods: Edition: S00-T88) were standardized using the 2015 Republic of Korea Statistical Information Service population. Generalized least squares regression analysis with an autoregressive moving average structure was performed to analyze ASR trends across subgroups. Results: Following SAPA implementation, nonsignificant decreases in both inpatient and outpatient ASR were observed among men in companies with 50 or more employees. Among women, inpatient ASR showed opposite patterns according to company size; however, after Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment for multiple comparisons, these effects did not retain significance in the full 2011-2024 dataset. A sensitivity analysis restricted to 2017-2024 suggested that the increase in <50-employee companies may represent a robust signal in the more recent period. Conclusion: SAPA implementation was not associated with statistically significant changes in injury rates in most subgroups after multiple testing adjustment, consistent with the early post-implementation experience of analogous international legislation. Exploratory subgroup analyses suggested differential responses by sex and company size, necessitating longitudinal research to evaluate the law's long-term preventive effects.

papers.title: Occupational Morbidity and Fatal Injuries in Thailand, 2007–2024: A Nationwide Time-trend Study Using Workers’ Compensation Records
papers.abstract: Background: Occupational injuries and work-related diseases remain a significant and persistent threat to the safety, health, and well-being of workers around the globe. This nationwide study aimed to examine long-term trends in occupational injuries and work-related diseases in Thailand from 2007 to 2024. Methods: Administrative data from the Thailand Social Security Office were used to assess trends and to identify factors associated with fatal outcomes among reported occupational injury cases in 2024. Annual injury rates were calculated using decided cases as the numerator and the average number of registered employees as the denominator. Risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated. Results: A total of 2,006,840 occupational injury cases were recorded. While the number of registered employees increased over time, overall injury rates declined from 24.57 to 7.29 per 1,000 workers and severe injury rates from 6.75 to 2.13 per 1,000 workers. However, fatal injury rates declined markedly but less consistently during the study period, from 9.61 to 4.94 per 100,000 workers. Musculoskeletal disorders remained the most frequently reported work-related disease. In 2024, older age (≥55 years; RR = 2.02, 95% CI: 1.56-2.62), construction-site injury (RR = 1.99, 95% CI: 1.64-2.42), vehicle-related injury (RR = 28.70, 95% CI: 24.55-33.55), and employment in establishments with ≤1,000 workers (RR = 1.75, 95% CI: 1.35-2.27) were associated with higher risk of fatal outcomes. Conclusion: While overall occupational injury rates declined substantially over time, fatal injury rates showed a less consistent decline, indicating the need for continued efforts to prevent severe occupational injuries and fatalities.

papers.title: Occupational Solar UV Exposure and Skin Cancer: A Quantitative Framework for Individual Causal Attribution in Dermatology Practice
papers.abstract: Background: Occupational solar ultraviolet radiation (UVR) exposure is a major risk factor for keratinocyte carcinomas in outdoor workers. Individual causal attribution for medico-legal purposes requires partitioning risk contributions between occupational exposure and individual susceptibility factors-a question distinct from population-level burden estimation. This study is primarily a quantitative/methodological application of FAIR to occupational UV-related skin cancer. Methods: This methodological framework study applies the FAIR approach (Filtering evidence, Association quantification, Individual partitioning, Reasoned interpretation) to occupational solar UVR and skin cancer. Meta-analyses (1995-2025) were reviewed and adjusted for phototype, sex, and immune status. Individual attribution was estimated using game-theory-based decomposition (Shapley values) and stochastic Monte Carlo simulation to propagate uncertainty. Preventive scenarios incorporated sector-specific compliance and long-term economic modeling. Results: Mean occupational causal shares were 35% for squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), 25% for basal cell carcinoma (BCC), 10% for melanoma, and 50% for actinic keratosis. The probability of exceeding the 20% medico-legal attribution threshold reached 85% for SCC and 75% for BCC. Prevention reduced expected cases by 10-15% and healthcare costs by 8-12%. Conclusions: The FAIR framework provides a transparent, reproducible approach for integrating epidemiological evidence with individual attribution. These quantitative thresholds support the clinical and medico-legal recognition of work-related skin cancers.

papers.title: Workplace HIV and TB Programmes for Laboratory Health Workers: A Rapid Review
papers.abstract: Introduction: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and tuberculosis (TB) remain global health challenges. Health workers (HWs), particularly laboratory HWs who handle infectious samples, face increased occupational risks of infection. Laboratory HWs are essential for disease diagnosis and monitoring, yet their health is endangered by workplace exposures to HIV and TB, potentially leading to workforce depletion and compromised healthcare delivery. Despite existing guidelines and policies for access and implementation of effective occupational health services (OHS), including hazard identification, medical surveillance, and postexposure preventive treatment, these are often obstructed by resource limitations. Objective: This review paper discusses the morbidity of HIV and TB among laboratory HWs, and explores the enablers and barriers to accessing HIV and TB OHS. Methods: A literature search was conducted using the EBSCOhost databases. Relevant keywords identified studies related to HWs, specifically laboratory HWs. Eligible studies were organised using a flow diagram, resulting in 13 papers. Data concerning morbidity, enabling factors, barriers, and recommendations were extracted using a modified tool. Results: Studies consistently demonstrate a high prevalence of latent TB Infection and active TB among laboratory HWs handling mycobacteria. Barriers to accessing OHS are more frequently reported than enablers, and HIV data specific to laboratory HWs were limited. Recommended interventions include enhanced surveillance, stronger OHS programmes, and integrating OHS and infection control. Conclusion: Despite growing evidence, gaps remain in implementation, and further studies are needed to assess the real-world application of recommended measures.

papers.title: Fatal Occupational Injuries in Cross-National Perspective: Panel Evidence from 46 Countries, 2008–2024
papers.abstract: Background Fatal occupational injuries account for over 2.3 million work-related deaths annually worldwide. Turkey has consistently recorded fatal injury rates among the highest in Europe, yet the structural and institutional determinants of this gap have not been examined in a longitudinal cross-national panel framework. This study examines whether economic development, sectoral structure, and informality explain this excess. Methods An unbalanced panel of 46 countries (2008–2024) was constructed using ILOSTAT fatal occupational injury statistics, Turkish Social Security Institution (SGK) records, and World Bank covariates. Three two-way fixed-effects models (country-clustered standard errors) estimated the fatal occupational injury rate as a function of GDP per capita, high-risk sector employment share, and agricultural employment share (an informality proxy). A third specification examined labour inspector density. Results Turkey's mean fatal injury rate (8.64 per 100,000) was 3.66 times the EU-25 mean (2.36). Under country-clustered standard errors, GDP per capita was negatively associated with fatal injury rates (β = −0.300, p = 0.046) and agricultural employment share was positively associated (β = 0.024, p = 0.028); high-risk sector employment share was not significant. Conclusion Turkey's excess fatality rate is not fully explained by income or sectoral structure. The findings are consistent with labour market informality contributing to the residual difference, though direct measures were not significant in sensitivity models. Coefficient signs for GDP and agricultural share held under Driscoll–Kraay standard errors robust to cross-sectional dependence, but significance did not, reflecting the short panel. Strengthening labour inspection and formalisation remains a priority for similar economies.

papers.title: Workplace Violence Against Physicians in Arab Countries: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
papers.abstract: This study aimed to estimate the prevalence of any workplace violence (WPV), physical violence, and verbal violence against physicians in Arab countries and to describe perpetrator profiles, psychological consequences, and reporting behavior. A systematic search of PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, and Cochrane Library was conducted from inception to March 2026. Cross-sectional studies reporting quantitative WPV prevalence among physicians in Arab League member states were eligible. Quality was assessed using the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale. Pooled prevalence estimates with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated using random-effects models. Prespecified subgroup analyses were performed by country and physician gender, and all analyses were conducted using R programming. Sixteen studies involving 5,861 physicians from eight Arab countries (Iraq, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Sudan, Jordan, Syria, Oman, and Kuwait) were included. The pooled prevalence of any WPV was 74.9% (95% CI: 63.7–83.5%), verbal violence 69.9% (95% CI: 59.1–78.9%), and physical violence 16.0% (95% CI: 11.0–22.5%). Among those physically attacked, 83.1% experienced recurrent incidents. Physical violence was significantly more prevalent among male than female physicians (24.2% vs. 9.4%; p = 0.034). Formal reporting occurred in only 29.8% of cases. Patients' relatives were the predominant perpetrators, and underreporting was driven by perceived futility, fear of retaliation, and shame. Workplace violence affects approximately three of four physicians in Arab countries, with verbal abuse the most common form and formal reporting remaining severely inadequate. Urgent policy responses are needed, including legal enforcement, institutional reporting systems, and structural health system improvements to address the root causes of violence in clinical settings.

papers.title: Sectoral Differences of Public Service Disruptions and Psychological Distress Among Workers After Disasters: A Cross-sectional Study
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Background The global escalation of disasters presents mental health concerns. However, disaster research primarily focuses on direct traumatic exposure, with less attention devoted to understanding how disruptions of public services after disasters are associated with psychological distress among workers from different employment sectors. Methods We analyzed one wave of the U.S. Census Bureau Household Trends and Outlook Pulse Survey (HTOPS), a cross-sectional survey of 3,971 employed respondents conducted from February 21 to March 7, 2025, to assess how disaster-related disruptions to essential services are associated with mental distress across diverse employment sectors. Mental distress was measured using the Patient Health Questionnaire-4 (range: 0–12). Results Safety service disruption showed the strongest positive association with mental distress (β = 0.071, p < 0.001), followed by social service disruption (β = 0.046, p < 0.05). Direct disaster impacts (displacement and property damage) and other service-disruption domains, including food, water, and infrastructure services, were not statistically associated with mental distress (p > 0.10). Public-sector (β = 0.116, p < 0.01) and non-profit workers (β = 0.094, p < 0.05) reported significantly higher mental distress than private-sector employees, whereas self-employed workers did not differ substantially. Public-sector employees exhibited amplified vulnerability to safety disruptions (interaction β = 0.117, p < 0.001), with no significant sectoral moderation observed for social service disruption. Conclusion Safety and social service disruptions were positively associated with post-disaster psychological distress rather than direct disaster impacts, with public-sector workers showing heightened vulnerability. Disaster preparedness should prioritize rapid service restoration and integrate sector-specific mental health interventions into planning frameworks.

papers.title: Wage Workers’ Injury Patterns by Workplace Size and Industry Across ICD-10 Categories: A Nationwide Cross-sectional Study in Korea
papers.abstract: Background Occupational injury surveillance typically depends on cases recognized as work-related, whereas health insurance claims capture treated injuries without prior attribution to work. Whether associations between claims-based injury prevalence and establishment size or industry differ across diagnostic categories and presumed mechanisms is not well established. Methods In this nationwide cross-sectional study, we analyzed National Health Insurance Service claims linked to establishment data for 11,212,512 Korean wage workers. Cases required ≥3 claims for the same three-character ICD-10 category in 2021. For all eligible categories, standardized prevalence and adjusted odds ratios were estimated by establishment size and industry; a representative subset was grouped by presumed mechanism after estimation. Results For ≥1,000 versus 5–29 workers, mechanical-group categories had lower odds (adjusted ORs, 0.33–0.72), including wrist/hand crushing injury (0.33) and external-eye foreign body (0.36). Ergonomic-group categories had slightly higher odds (1.15–1.17), but the corresponding prevalence gradients were absent when cases required ≥1 inpatient day for the category. The biomechanical comparator was null (1.00), and wrist/hand burns had the highest odds in Hotels and Restaurants versus Manufacturing (2.08). Conclusion Analysis at the category level identified patterns that diagnostic blocks obscured. Although claims cannot establish work-relatedness, they may help prioritize occupational investigation in smaller establishments and selected sectors. The ergonomic associations require confirmation. Linking claims with occupational exposure, injury-circumstance, and compensation data could identify work-related injuries absent from compensation records, complement official statistics, and inform policies addressing healthcare-access differences across worker and workplace characteristics.

papers.title: Occupational Health and Disease Prevention in Vietnam: A Mid-term Evaluation of the National Action Plan (2020 - 2030) and Policy Implications
papers.abstract: Background Vietnam is undergoing rapid industrial transition, with the occupational health burden shifting from accidents to work-related diseases. To strengthen occupational safety and health, the government enacted the National Program on Occupational Safety and Health (Decision 659/QD-TTg). This study assessed mid-term implementation using the WHO Health System Building Blocks framework. Methods We conducted a mixed-methods mid-term evaluation. Phase 1 used administrative data from all 63 provinces and centrally governed cities, including a 2020 baseline and 2021–2025 implementation data. Indicators were grouped into four WHO-adapted domains: governance, financing, service delivery, and information systems. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, trend analysis, and achievement rates against program targets. Phase 2 involved field verification in six purposively selected provinces; qualitative feedback from provincial occupational health officials was analyzed thematically. Results Provincial policy commitment increased, with approved action plans rising from 46.2% of provinces in 2020 to 88.5% in 2025. Budget allocation also expanded, although disbursement remained inconsistent. Service delivery was uneven: environmental monitoring exceeded targets, with an achievement rate of 143.4%, whereas occupational disease screening reached only 46.6% of planned targets. Information systems showed limited digitization, with completion rates below 20%, potentially contributing to under-ascertainment of occupational diseases, particularly among workers in SMEs. Conclusion Decision 659 strengthened governance and resource mobilization but has not yet translated these inputs into effective occupational health surveillance and service coverage. For 2026–2030, priorities should include digitizing the OSH registry, strengthening occupational disease detection, and shifting from punitive inspection toward technical support for SMEs.

papers.title: How Safety Audits are Superficially Trapped: An Assessment via the Hierarchy of Controls and Rasmussen's Risk Management Framework
papers.abstract: Background Safety audits are commonly used as assurance and learning mechanisms, yet little is known about what their documented corrective actions actually improve. If audit actions mainly produce local paperwork improvements, then audits may verify compliance without substantially testing the controls or organizational conditions that shape risk. Method This exploratory study assessed 448 corrective actions from 65 health and safety audit reports sourced from two large engineering and construction companies, encompassing internal audits alongside reports from 16 independent external auditing firms. Actions were coded against two complementary dimensions: the strength of the risk control implied by the hierarchy of controls, and the organizational level targeted using Rasmussen’s risk management framework. Results Corrective actions were concentrated in administrative controls and at project management, staff, and work levels. No actions were coded to company management, client, regulator, or government levels. Few actions required verification of field risk control effectiveness. Conclusion While these findings do not, by themselves, establish that audits fail as assurance mechanisms, they do suggest that documented corrective actions were concentrated at lower levels, privileging local paperwork and visible conditions over higher-order controls and upstream organizational influences.

papers.title: The Invisible Burden of Office Work: A Dose-Response Analysis of Working Hours and Upper and Lower Extremity Musculoskeletal Pain in Korea (A Cross-sectional Analysis of the 7th Korean Working Conditions Survey)
papers.abstract: Background The dose-response relationship between working hours and musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs) remains poorly understood, particularly among office workers. This study investigated the association between weekly working hours and the prevalence of upper extremity, lower extremity, and co-existing musculoskeletal pain in Korean office workers. Methods We analyzed 11,368 non-shift office workers from the 7th Korean Working Conditions Survey. Weekly working hours were categorized as: <40, 40 (reference), 41–52, and >52 h. Odds of self-reported musculoskeletal pain were estimated using weighted logistic regression models, adjusting for sociodemographic, occupational, and ergonomic factors (bad posture, repetitive movements, prolonged sitting). Effect modification by sex was tested. Results Compared with the 40-h workweek, working 41–52 h had higher odds of upper extremity (odds ratio [OR] 1.45, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.24–1.69), lower extremity (OR 1.66, 95% CI 1.34–2.05), and co-existing pain (OR 1.63, 95% CI 1.27–2.09). Working >52 h demonstrated the highest likelihood of pain, with ORs exceeding 3.1 for all outcomes. These dose-response associations remained robust independent of ergonomic hazards and consistent across sexes (P>0.05). Notably, males working <40 h exhibited higher odds of co-existing pain (OR 2.21, 95% CI 1.06–4.60), suggesting a health selection effect. Conclusion Working >40 h per week is associated with a progressively increased likelihood of musculoskeletal pain among Korean office workers, independent of physical workplace hazards. This association is consistent across sexes. Occupational health strategies should target both extreme overwork and moderate overtime (41–52 h).

papers.title: Mapping the Scientific Landscape of Boilover in Industrial Storage Tank Fires: A Combined Bibliometric and Systematic Review
papers.abstract: Boilover is a destructive phenomenon that occurs during a fire in hydrocarbon tanks with a bottom layer of water; it is characterised by an explosive eruption of burning fuel and a sudden increase in thermal radiation. Despite research conducted since the 1950s, our understanding of this phenomenon remains fragmentary, with a limited body of scientific literature (118 publications indexed in Scopus between 1959 and 2025) and a lack of validation at an industrial scale. To address these limitations, this study combines bibliometric analysis with a systematic literature review to analyse the evolution of boilover research and synthesise current knowledge of the phenomenon's mechanisms, experimental investigations, analytical and numerical modelling approaches, and the main factors influencing its development. The bibliometric analysis examines the dynamics of scientific output, collaboration networks and the thematic structure of the field, whilst the systematic review identifies the main scientific findings, the limitations of current knowledge and the key research gaps. The results highlight a high concentration of scientific impact centred on pioneering work, a division of the field into several distinct areas (combustion, process safety and risk management), and a persistent fragmentation of collaborations. The review further shows that, despite significant progress in understanding boilover mechanisms and developing analytical and numerical models, large-scale experimental validation remains limited, predictive capabilities remain insufficient, and several scientific challenges persist, particularly concerning emulsified crude oils, wall effects and scaling phenomena. This review therefore highlights the main scientific gaps and proposes several research priorities to improve understanding, prediction, and prevention of the boilover phenomenon. The review further shows that, despite significant progress in understanding boilover mechanisms and in developing analytical and numerical models, large-scale experimental validation remains limited, predictive capabilities remain insufficient, and several scientific challenges persist, particularly regarding emulsified crude oils, wall effects, and scaling phenomena. These findings highlight the main scientific gaps and establish research priorities to improve the understanding, prediction, and prevention of the boilover phenomenon.

papers.title: Interpretable Machine Learning Models for Predicting Compressive Strength of Binary Blended Geopolymer Concrete Exposed to Elevated Temperatures
papers.abstract: Predicting the strength of geopolymer concrete (GPC) after fire incidents is crucial for ensuring structural safety. From this lens, the present study investigates the prediction capabilities of machine learning (ML) algorithms to examine the residual strength of GPC after being subjected to the ISO 834 fire curve. More specifically, a comprehensive dataset from fire experiments comprising of ground granulated blast furnace slag (GGBS), fly ash (FA), sodium hydroxide (SH), sodium silicate (SS), alkaline activator to binder (AAS/B) ratio, molarity (M), extra water (EW), curing temperature (T), exposure to elevated temperature (ET) and exposure time (t) was collected and analyzed. This dataset is utilized to train and test six ML models, namely, Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Random Forest (RF), Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), Categorial Boosting (CatBoost), Adaptive Boosting (AdaBoost), and Gradient Boosting (GB). The models were trained via a cross-validation process and then examined using statistical indicators. In comparison with all the ML models, CatBoost shows the highest accuracy with an R2 of 0.997 and the lowest RMSE value. To further enhance the developed models, their interpretability was examined using SHAP, which shows that t, T, and ET were the most influential factors that govern the strength of the GPC mix. This finding highlights the potential of ML in developing light and cost-efficient prediction frameworks for post-fire assessment of binary blended GPC to help augment the specialized and expensive nature of fire testing.

papers.title: Risk Analysis of Combustible Cladding in Proximity to Vehicles
papers.abstract: Building façade fires resulting from the ignition of combustible cladding materials have been reported extensively. However, research specifically addressing the risk posed by external fire sources, such as vehicles parked near cladding, is still limited. This study applies probabilistic analysis to assess fire risks associated with car fires in proximity to combustible cladding, considering Aluminium Composite Panels (ACP) containing a polymer-based core and Expanded Polystyrene (EPS). The influence of wind conditions is incorporated into the analysis. The objective is to create a database supporting decision-making on rectification measures, reducing façade fire risks, and ensuring occupant safety. This study is developed within Cladding Safety Victoria’s framework for mitigating fire risks.

papers.title: When the Cable Insulation Burns: Experimental and 2D Modeling Study of Cables with Flame-Retardant Sheaths and Flammable Insulation
papers.abstract: The integration of flame-retardant (FR) materials into electrical cables mitigates fire hazards; however, the widespread industrial practice of pairing flame-retarded sheaths with non-flame-retarded insulations offers protection only below a critical external heat flux. Beyond this threshold, the sheath’s suppression capacity is exceeded, allowing the insulation to pyrolyze and significantly elevate the fire risk. While non-FR insulations are widely utilized for their dielectric strength, flexibility, durability, and cost-effectiveness, their contribution to fire growth remains a concern and requires further elucidation. Therefore, this study investigates the fire behavior of two industrial cables: MKEM-HF, comprising solely an FR sheath, and XMK-HF, consisting of an FR sheath over a highly flammable insulation, under a heat flux exceeding the sheath capacity to protect the inner insulation layer. Thermogravimetric (TGA) and Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC) analyses were conducted to characterize thermal degradation of the cable layers and develop pyrolysis models. Cone calorimetry at 50 $$\rm kW \cdot m^{-2}$$ assessed fire behavior under gasification and flaming, for both single- and multi-cable configurations. MKEM-HF displayed a descending MLR-HRR profile over time, whereas XMK-HF exhibited a continuously rising trend with a dominant final peak, driven by the decomposition of the insulation. A classical 1D slab model of the cone calorimetry was used for inverse estimation of thermal properties and heats of combustion. A geometrical modification on the 1D model allowed the simulation of early insulation exposure, offering a possible approach for modeling the sheath’s mechanical rupture. A more advanced 2D model, accounting for cylindrical geometry and improved boundary coupling, demonstrated superior performance in transient heat transfer and peak prediction compared to the 1D model. The study highlights the critical influence of non-flame-retarded insulation on cable fire behavior and demonstrates the necessity of advanced modeling approaches beyond simple slab approximations to capture these effects.

papers.title: Experimental study of temperature evolution and flame ejection inside a double-opening enclosure
papers.abstract: This article studied the temperature evolution and flame ejection of enclosure fires with the upper and lower openings. Experiments were conducted inside a reduced-scale enclosure with the side length of 0.4 m, which has two openings of the same size, vertically distributed and separated at a distance. Temperature inside the enclosure and flame behavior were recorded for different window sizes, heat release rates and opening separation distances. Result shows that: (1) Temperature inside enclosure rises as total HRR increases, and falls as the opening separation distance increases. This is because air flow rate entering the enclosure increases with the increase of opening separation distance. (2) Critical HRR of ejection rises as the window size increases, and decreases as the increase of opening separation distance. This is because that when the upper opening position is higher, flames are more likely to eject out from the opening after reaching the enclosure top. (3) A normalized separation distance was proposed, which well characterized the effect of separation distance on inside temperature and flame ejection, and the temperature and critical flame ejection were correlated well by the normalized distance. This study for the first time revealed the temperature evolution and flame ejection inside a double-opening enclosure, analyzed the effect of opening separation distance, and proposed the models to quantify the inside temperature and critical HRR for flame ejection, which would make a significant contribution in the theory of building fire dynamics.

papers.title: Data-Driven Selection of Parametric and Travelling Fire Models for Performance-based Fire Design
papers.abstract: Selecting appropriate design fire models remains a key unresolved challenge in performance-based structural fire engineering, where the applicability of the Eurocode EN 1991-1-2 parametric fire curve and travelling fire (TF) models is not clearly defined. This study proposes a quantitative threshold for selecting between the EN and TF models based on full-scale experimental results. A total of 222 available full-scale natural fire experiments are summarised and used as benchmark data. For each experiment, average compartment fire temperature–time curves are predicted using the EN and TF models, respectively, and their predictive accuracy is quantitatively assessed to determine the best-performing model for each fire test. A logistic regression (LR) model is then derived from the available dataset to predict the best-performing model for a given set of fire inputs. As the required TF model inputs, namely the peak fire temperature, heat release rate per unit area, and fire spread rate, were not reported in the experimental data, a sensitivity study is conducted to evaluate their influence on the derived LR model. The results show that the LR model is most sensitive to the assumed fire spread rate. Therefore, three applicability segments are introduced into the LR model to cover a wider range of fire scenarios. The proposed LR model achieves an average training accuracy of 0.736 and an ROC–AUC of 0.808. A probabilistic risk assessment case study using Monte Carlo simulation demonstrates that the proposed LR model reduces both over- and under-design compared with EN-only or TF-only methods, providing a more balanced and reliable framework for current performance-based structural fire design.

papers.title: Effects of State of Charge on Fire Characteristics and Smoke Spread in 18,650 Lithium-Ion Batteries in a Tunnel
papers.abstract: In this work, the combustion dynamics and smoke spread behavior of 18,650 lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) with varying states of charge (SOC: 25%–100%) were experimentally investigated in a model-scale tunnel. The results show that the fire evolution of LIBs can be divided into three stages: initial ignition, intermittent combustion characterized by repeated burst combustion and jet-fire events, and combustion decay. SOC strongly influenced the thermal hazard intensity; the peak flame temperature increased with SOC and reached 1081.4 °C at 100% SOC. The smoke movement during LIB fires exhibited several typical stages, including initial plume formation, ceiling impingement and radial diffusion, smoke stratification with longitudinal propagation, and repeated jet-induced smoke accumulation. The intermittent jet-fire behavior generated multiple high-momentum pulses that transferred kinetic energy to the smoke layer and locally re-accelerated the longitudinal spread. A local velocity increase of 14.6%–40.4% was observed between adjacent measuring points, and this short-term re-acceleration was more pronounced at higher SOCs and near the fire source. These results reveal the coupling between SOC, intermittent jet-fire behavior, and smoke spread dynamics, providing useful insights for smoke control and safety management in tunnel fires involving lithium-ion batteries.

papers.title: High-Temporal-Resolution Long-Term Prediction Model for Fire Temperature Field of Timber Arch Lounge Bridges Based on Spatiotemporal Attention
papers.abstract: Fires inflict substantial losses of life and property annually, posing a severe threat to global cultural heritage, particularly wooden structures such as timber arch lounge bridges. Timber arch lounge bridges, also known as Chinese covered timber bridges or covered bridges, feature complex fire spread dynamics, which poses a challenge to the accuracy and real-time capability of fire prediction technology. However, existing computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulation methods, when applied to timber arch lounge bridges, are computationally expensive and impractical for real-time applications. To address these challenges, this study proposed a fire prediction fusion framework with high temporal resolution and long-term forecasting capability based on spatiotemporal attention mechanisms. First, the sparsity prediction module generates a sparse sequence through recurrent iterative operations. Subsequently, the interpolation module interpolates the missing values to form a complete prediction sequence. The fusion framework demonstrated enhanced long-term prediction performance across both timber arch lounge bridge and closed-building layouts compared to the baselines. Moreover, the fusion framework achieves a 36-fold speed increase over conventional CFD methods in timber arch lounge bridge layouts, indicating its performance advantage. While the current model is trained and validated under a specific fire scenario, these results suggest that the proposed framework has the potential to provide a high-accuracy real-time fire prediction method for emergency management and fire-fighting rescue.

papers.title: Flammability and Feasibility Analysis of Mixture Refrigerants Consisting of R1243zf, RE170, and Flame Retardants (R13I1, R134a, or R125)
papers.abstract: Burning velocity is one of the fundamental flammability parameters, and the maximum burning velocity is a crucial criterion of flammability classification of refrigerants. In this study, an experimental system for measuring the burning velocity of low-carbon flammable gases was established based on ISO standard 817. The combustion reactions of mixture refrigerants consisting of R1243zf, RE170 and flame retardants (R13I1, R134a, or R125) were experimentally investigated. In addition, a combustion reaction kinetic model applicable to R1243zf and its mixtures was established, consisting of 178 species and 1442 elementary reactions. The modified kinetic mechanism reproduced the ISO 817 vertical-tube-derived burning-velocity dataset for R1243zf and its mixtures with a mean deviation of 14.5%. This comparison is regarded as a method-specific benchmark rather than a complete validation of the unstretched adiabatic laminar burning velocity. From the perspective of the thermodynamic properties, flammability and global warming potential (GWP), R1243zf/R13I1/R134a and R1243zf/R13I1/R125 revealed the better flexible in composition proportions optimization since which own sizable zones of Class A1 (as per ASHRAE standard 34) and GWP100< 150 concurrently. Further, based on theoretical calculations, the performance and coefficient of performance (COP) of 20 representative mixtures were evaluated, and the candidate blend compositions identified through preliminary thermodynamic, environmental, and flammability screening were proposed accordingly to meet the application requirements in an air conditioning system.

papers.title: Meet the Two Organizations that Helped Create Fire Protection Engineering and Why it Still Matters Today
papers.abstract: For over 130 years, Underwriters Laboratories', 1 legacy has shaped daily life through groundbreaking research on new and emergency hazards, rigorous safety testing, and lifesaving standards.Now known as UL Research Institutes (ULRI), one of its most remarkable achievements remains largely unknown.In 1903, through a visionary partnership with the Armor Institute of Technology (today known as the Illinois Institute of Technology: Illinois Tech), Underwriters Laboratories established more than a new engineering degree program-they created the field of fire protection engineering as we know it.At ULRI, fire protection engineering remains as core to realizing its mission as it was in 1903. Born From TragedyThe timing was no accident.America was burning.The period between the 1860s and 1940s-dubbed by disaster historian Scott Gabriel Knowles as the "Conflagration Era" 2witnessed 18 of the 20 deadliest fires in American history.Urban conflagrations like the Great Chicago Fire (1871) and subsequent major fires in Boston (1872), Seattle (1889), Baltimore (1904), and the San Francisco earthquake and fire (1906) weren't just disasters; they were wake-up calls that traditional approaches to fire safety could fail catastrophically.The Conflagration Era overlapped the Progressive Era (1890s-1920s) -a time of great criticism and public mistrust in industrial and business practices and growing monopolies 1 In 2022 the organization known as Underwriters Laboratories became three independent safety science organizations: UL Research Institutes, UL Standards & Engagement, and UL Solutions.Each continue to share the mission of working for a safer world.In this article, Underwriters Laboratories is used throughout to refer to the historic organization prior to its transformation into three organizations in 2022.UL Research Institutes (or ULRI) is used throughout to refer to the contemporary organization which continues fire protection and prevention research among other areas of specialization.2 Knowles, Scott Gabriel.The Disaster Experts: Mastering Risk in Modern America.

papers.title: Study on the Fire Resistance and Scaling Laws of Geometrically Similar CFST Column Under Eccentric Compression
papers.abstract: Due to the high cost of full-scale fire tests, researchers often use scaled tests to evaluate the fire resistance of full-scale components. Traditional fire similarity theory requires proportional scaling of the heating curve. Small-scale models need higher heating rates, which are often beyond furnace limits, making scaled tests difficult in practice. To address this challenge, a thermo-mechanical sequential coupling method was developed and validated. A series of geometrically similar concrete-filled steel tubular (CFST) columns were designed. The study investigates the relationship between the fire resistance similarity ratio and the size ratio under the ISO-834 standard fire curve. The effects of eccentricity and load ratio on the fire resistance of geometrically similar CFST columns were also examined. The results show that: (i) The failure mode is independent of size. Axially loaded columns exhibit bulging failure, while in eccentrically loaded columns, the compression zone decreases and the tension zone expands as eccentricity increases; (ii) The fire resistance decreases significantly with increasing eccentricity and load ratio, with stronger effects observed in larger columns; (iii) At small eccentricity or load ratio, the fire resistance is governed by the interaction between the concrete core and steel tube, whereas at large eccentricity or load ratio, it is mainly determined by the steel tube; (iv) An empirical formula considering eccentricity and load ratio is proposed, providing guidance for scaled fire tests of CFST columns.

papers.title: Improvement Forecasts for Asynchronous Observations in Data-Driven Wildfire Spread Prediction
papers.abstract: Data assimilation (DA) methods enhance the accuracy of prediction models by integrating observational data. Due to the large scale of wildfires, the observed fire perimeter may consist of fire front segments from multiple time points, which are referred to as asynchronous observations. Asynchronous observations contain lag errors that are not accounted for by traditional DA algorithms. This paper proposes an Ensemble Transform Kalman filter incorporating a centralized extrapolation strategy (ETKF-centralized) to reduce the lag error associated with asynchronous fire fronts. To evaluate the performance of ETKF-centralized, a landscape wildfire is simulated using PROMETHEUS to generate asynchronous observations. Since the actual mechanism of wildfire spread cannot be fully captured during prediction, we selected a different model, FARSITE, as a basic prediction model. The results show that the similarity index of ETKF-centralized forecast fire exceeds 0.85 with a lead time of 4 h, and the root mean square error is reduced by 29% compared with standard ETKF. Furthermore, ETKF-centralized is successfully applied to a 900 m2 field experiment, demonstrating its strong potential for application in wildfire forecasting.

papers.title: Advancing Automated Fire Safety Code Compliance: Automatic Annotation of BIM Door Elements
papers.abstract: Automated code compliance checking often faces challenges due to insufficient semantic information in Building Information Modeling (BIM) models, particularly during the early design stages, when only basic geometrical and alphanumerical information may be available. This study extends previous research on machine-learning-based annotation of ‘Exit’ doors by investigating whether additional BIM-derived features and adapted feature-engineering strategies can support the identification of both ‘Exit’ and ‘Apartment Exit’ doors in early-design residential architectural BIM models. A data-driven workflow was developed using features extracted from BIM models containing basic representations of doors, walls, stairs, and rooms, defined by their approximate geometry, dimensions, locations, and element types. For ‘Exit’ door classification, the model achieved an F1-score of 0.97 and produced correct predictions for the three test buildings used in the evaluation. For ‘Apartment Exit’ door classification, the integration of probability-encoded features improved the F1-score from 0.93 to 0.99 and increased the building-level test scores from [0.18, 0.47, 0.89, 1.00] to [0.82, 0.77, 0.95, 1.00] for the four test buildings, respectively. The results indicate that structured geometrical and alphanumerical information available in early-design BIM models can provide useful input for ML-based semantic enrichment of door elements. The main contributions of this study are: (1) the definition of eight BIM-derived spatial and topological features that can be extracted from basic building-element representations; (2) the adaptation of probability-encoded feature engineering to bounded integer-valued features using neighbor-based mean estimation for unseen values; and (3) the extension of the door-annotation workflow from ‘Exit’ to ‘Apartment Exit’ classification in Belgian high-rise buildings. The proposed approach is intended to support early-stage compliance checking by reducing the need for manual semantic annotation, while further validation on more diverse building datasets is required to assess broader generalizability.

papers.title: Parametric Analysis and Predictive Modeling for Post-fire Ventilation Following CO2 Fire Extinguishment
papers.abstract: Low-pressure carbon dioxide fire suppression systems, while effectively extinguishing fires in enclosed spaces, create a high-concentration CO2 environment that poses a significant safety risk to personnel. Designing an efficient post-fire ventilation system to reduce the CO2 volume fraction to a safe level is therefore of critical importance. This study integrates full-scale fire suppression experiments with PyroSim numerical simulations to investigate the post-fire ventilation process following CO2 extinguishment. A CFD model was developed, calibrated (turbulent Schmidt number Sct = 0.7), and validated against three experimental cases (mean R2 = 0.97, RMSE = 0.62). Parametric analysis revealed that the air change rate (ACH) is the dominant parameter governing ventilation efficiency, with 12 h− 1 recommended as the optimal value. The airflow organization — specifically, a centralized top-supply, bottom-exhaust configuration with vents on the same side — significantly influences the dilution rate by working synergistically with the natural buoyancy-driven stratification of CO2. Based on the optimized configuration, 27 simulation scenarios spanning nine initial CO2 volume fractions (14%-54%) and three ACH values (8, 12, 20 h− 1) were simulated. A predictive model for the safety ventilation duration was derived through log-linear regression (R2 = 0.99), providing a quantitative tool for post-fire ventilation system design and risk assessment.

papers.title: Using Multimodal Large Language Models for False Alarm Reduction in Image-Based Fire Detection
papers.abstract: Existing vision-based methods suffer from high false alarm rates in urban flame detection. Applying Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) for secondary filtering shows great potential for reducing false alarms, yet they have high inference latency and are prone to reasoning collapse on negative samples without explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) guidance. To overcome these challenges, this study proposes Flash-Cascade, the first sub-second MLLM-based firewall that leverages CoT for efficiently filtering false alarms. We deconstructed the flame detection process into four logical stages (planning, observation, analysis, and judgment), which informed the design of three switchable reasoning modes (Detailed, Quick, and Rapid) to achieve inference acceleration via CoT compression. We fine-tuned Qwen2-VL-7B-Instruct on a multi-granularity instruction dataset via Low-Rank Adaptation. This process decoupled the model’s discriminative capability from long-form text generation, thereby enabling robust performance even without explicit CoT guidance. On our newly constructed benchmark incorporating real-world hard negatives, Flash-Cascade achieves an accuracy of 97.79% and an F1-score of 0.977 in Rapid mode, outperforming the zero-shot baseline by 61.63 percentage points (pp) and 0.515, respectively. Furthermore, it outperforms the state-of-the-art object detector DEIMv2 by 14.64 pp in accuracy. The method exhibits exceptional sample efficiency, converging with only 600 samples and 2 epochs, and improves inference speed by 810% over standard CoT. This study opens new avenues for robust and efficient flame detection in high-interference scenarios.

papers.title: Study on Axial Bearing Performance of Reactive Powder Concrete-Filled Square Steel Tube Columns After High Temperature
papers.abstract: This study investigated the axial compressive behavior of reactive powder concrete-filled steel tube (RPC-FST) columns after high temperatures. To evaluate the effects of heating duration, spiral stirrup spacing, and steel tube thickness on the post-fire performance of RPC-FST columns, ten specimens were first subjected to high-temperature tests and then subjected to axial compression load tests. The experimental results indicate that all specimens exhibited local buckling failure. The severity of local buckling decreased with increasing steel tube thickness and heating duration, as well as with decreasing spiral stirrup spacing. Compared with the unheated specimens, the specimens with heating times ranging from 140 to 260 min showed a reduction of 2.18–37.46% in the ultimate load and 11.00–38.51% in the elastic stiffness. Under identical heating conditions, the ultimate load increased with increasing steel tube thickness and decreasing spiral stirrup spacing. Specifically, when the steel tube thickness increased from 4 to 10 mm, the ultimate load capacity and elastic stiffness increased by 21.98 and 19.35%, respectively. Moreover, reducing the spiral stirrup spacing from 80 to 40 mm resulted in a 23.30% increase in ultimate load capacity. Based on the experimental results, a calculation method for predicting the axial bearing capacity of RPC-FST columns after high temperature was proposed. The proposed method was evaluated against the experimental results, existing design specifications, and previously reported prediction models, demonstrating its applicability and providing useful references for future research.

papers.title: Effect of Fabric Stretch on the Thermal Protective Performance of Firefighter Clothing: An Experimental and 3D Numerical Analysis
papers.abstract: During firefighting operations, movements such as bending elbows and knees induce deformation of the outer shell material, affecting the thermal protective performance (TPP) of firefighter clothing. However, the effects of fabric stretching under different thermal environments and the associated microstructural mechanisms remain unclear. To investigate this, experiments were conducted at four stretch levels (0%, 3%, 6%, 12%) under three thermal conditions (8.5 kW/m2 radiant heat, 30 kW/m2 flame, 84 kW/m2 hybrid heat), measuring fabric structural properties and TPP. Results indicated that stretching reduced fabric porosity and slightly increased thickness, with TPP decreasing more noticeably under low-radiation heat. To elucidate the heat transfer mechanisms, a three-dimensional finite element model incorporating yarn geometry and air pores was developed. Simulations revealed that stretch-induced structural changes enhanced the intrinsic thermal insulation performance (TIP) of the fabric. Parametric analyses further showed that increasing surface convection produced only minor changes in thermal resistance, whereas increasing fiber thermal conductivity resulted in a more noticeable reduction. Combined experimental and simulation results demonstrated that changes in TPP were governed by the competing effects of (i) improved thermal insulation due to increased fabric thickness and (ii) enhanced conductive heat transfer due to increased fiber–sensor contact area. Although stretching increased TIP, the latter effect dominated, resulting in lower TPP values. These findings elucidate the heat transfer mechanisms of stretched fabrics and support TPP evaluation considering fabric deformation. They also provide practical guidance for the design of firefighting suits with adequate ease allowances in body regions undergoing substantial movement, thereby improving firefighter thermal protection and safety.

papers.title: Synergistic Suppression of Coal Dust Explosions by a Novel Phosphorus-Grafted Fly Ash Composite: Preparation, Performance, and Mechanism
papers.abstract: Coal dust explosions pose a severe threat to industrial safety, while the large-scale disposal of fly ash (FA) presents a significant environmental challenge. To utilize this industrial solid waste for safety applications, a novel phosphorus-modified fly ash composite explosion suppressant (FA@H3PO4) was developed. The suppressant was synthesized via alkali activation pretreatment followed by phosphoric acid grafting. Characterization using SEM, EDS, and FTIR confirmed that the modification effectively increased the surface roughness of FA and successfully introduced phosphorus-containing flame-retardant groups. Explosion suppression performance was evaluated in a visual vertical combustion tube, where FA@H3PO4 demonstrated significantly superior performance compared to raw FA. At a concentration of 60 wt%, the modified agent reduced the flame propagation velocity to 2.6 m/s, resulting in a discontinuous “ghost flame” structure; the peak flame temperature was drastically suppressed to approximately 241 °C, compared to 1285 °C for pure coal dust. Furthermore, the addition of 60 wt% FA@H3PO4 led to an 80% decrease in maximum explosion pressure (Pmax) and a 100% extension of the time to peak pressure. Thermal analysis (TG) reveals that the suppression mechanism relies on a synergistic effect: the physical cooling and barrier function of the fly ash skeleton, combined with the chemical scavenging of free radicals by the grafted phosphorus groups. This study provides a cost-effective and efficient technical pathway for coal dust explosion control.

papers.title: Numerical Study on Fire Resistance of Square UHPC Filled Steel Tubular Slender Columns Under Axial Compression
papers.abstract: The mechanical response mechanisms of square ultra high performance concrete filled steel tubular (UHPCFST) columns under elevated temperatures differ significantly from those of conventional concrete filled steel tubular (CFST) columns; however, related investigations remain scarce. In this study, a validated thermo-mechanically coupled finite element model was developed to systematically evaluate the effects of section size, slenderness ratio, steel ratio, and load level on the fire resistance of square UHPCFST columns, and to elucidate the distinct load-bearing mechanisms of UHPCFST and CFST columns under fire conditions. The results demonstrate that section size, slenderness ratio, steel ratio, and load level significantly affect fire resistance. Specifically, increasing the section size from 200 to 1000 mm improves fire resistance by approximately 123.5%, whereas increasing the slenderness ratio from 30 to 70 decreases it by 57.4%. Conversely, the effect of material strength is relatively insignificant. At the same load level, UHPCFST columns exhibit 15%–45% lower fire resistance than CFST columns, but demonstrate enhanced load-sharing efficiency between the steel tube and core concrete. Based on the parametric study, a calculation method for predicting the fire resistance of rectangular UHPCFST columns is proposed.

papers.title: Assessing the Relative Contribution of Pre‐Deployment Abroad Versus In‐Mission Dirofilaria immitis Infections in French Military Working Dogs Screened Post‐Mission: A Quantitative Risk Assessment
papers.abstract: Dirofilaria immitis (D. immitis) is a mosquito-borne nematode responsible for canine cardiopulmonary dirofilariasis, a parasitic infection widely distributed worldwide and established in mainland France, particularly in southern regions. Military working dogs (MWDs) may be at increased risk of exposure to vector-borne pathogens because of their predominantly outdoor lifestyle and frequent missions abroad. Nevertheless, D. immitis infection remains sporadic in this population, likely due to well-implemented medical prophylaxis. The aim of this study was to investigate the likely origin of D. immitis infections detected in MWD during post-mission screening using a quantitative risk analysis approach. Scenario trees were developed to describe the sequences of events leading to the return of an infected dog from a mission abroad, accounting for parasite biology, prophylactic measures, and compliance. The model estimated a mean annual number of 4.25 infected MWD returning from missions out of an average annual population of 466 returning dogs, of which 79% were detected through post-mission screening. Most infections were likely acquired before deployment, either during previous missions, at the breeding facility before purchase, or within mainland France. Only 7.9% of infections acquired during missions were expected to be detected by testing performed at the end of the post-mission quarantine period. Alternative scenarios highlighted the effectiveness of chemoprophylaxis, as its absence was associated with a 3.2-fold increase in the number of infected dogs. Simulations also showed that extending the interval between return and testing would substantially improve the detection of mission-acquired infections. These findings support the continued use of preventive measures while questioning the adequacy of current post-mission screening alone for identifying D. immitis infections acquired during deployment.

papers.title: Natural Is Not Necessarily Safer: A Probabilistic Assessment of Risk–Risk Trade‐Offs Between Cardiovascular and Genotoxic Effects of Food Preservatives
papers.abstract: To extend product shelf life, it is especially important to prevent foods from deteriorating. Apart from the traditional methods of adding salt or sugar in large amounts, other additives, such as food preservatives, can also be applied to achieve the aim of food preservation. This study employs probabilistic risk assessment (PRA) to quantify human health impacts associated with exposure to sodium chloride, sucrose, benzoic acid (BA), and sorbic acid (SA), utilizing cardiovascular disease (CVD) prevalence and micronuclei (MN) induction frequency as dual epidemiological and toxicological endpoints. We evaluated the risks of natural and artificial preservatives in products, such as pickled vegetables, fermented vegetables, candied fruits, and preserved fruits, with the same antibacterial efficiency and under controlled pH and water activity conditions. The results revealed a significant risk trade-off: Although the CVD prevalence associated with natural preservatives reached 16.2%–18.2% across different food categories, the MN frequency induced by artificial preservatives remained comparatively lower at 7.4%–11.6%. The results suggest that combining natural and artificial preservatives may reduce sodium chloride or sucrose intake and the associated cardiovascular health risks compared with using natural preservatives alone. These findings indicate that although limiting high-sodium and high-sugar foods is crucial for cardiovascular health, dietary exposure to artificial preservatives, such as BA and SA, was associated with relatively low estimated genotoxic risks, though potential hepatic or renal impacts warrant further investigation.

papers.title: Anticipating Surprises by Expanding a Risk Assessment's Possibility Space Into the Unknown With C–K Theory
papers.abstract: What should a risk assessor do if she suspects the possibilities derivable from presently available knowledge are incomplete? Risk analysts often encounter this problem when assessing risk in open systems that produce novel outcomes leading to surprises. The solution is to expand the possibility space into the unknown. Yet the novel possibilities then included cannot be mere figments of the imagination; they must be tethered to presently available knowledge to be credible. This may seem paradoxical: to go beyond presently available knowledge by assessing novel possibilities, which, to be credible, must be grounded in presently available knowledge. Yet it is not quite as contradictory as it may first seem. C–K Theory (CKT) was developed to explain how innovators overcome a similar problem when designing a new product. An innovation involves creating something that has novel features. Some of its components may, therefore, not yet exist, and there may even be uncertainty about whether they are technically feasible. This lack of knowledge makes it difficult to determine the innovation's possibility space—a difficulty similar to that faced when assessing risks in open systems. CKT describes how innovators overcome this problem by iteratively moving between a knowledge space comprising established facts and decidable propositions and a conceptual space representing novel, as-yet-undecidable propositions. As illustrated herein using the cases of the credit crunch and the 9/11 terrorist attack, CKT can help anticipate surprises by generating, expanding, and integrating the possibility space within the extended (C, U) risk-assessment framework.

papers.title: Forecasting LLM‐Enabled Biorisk and the Efficacy of Safeguards
papers.abstract: Capabilities of large language models (LLMs) on several biological benchmarks have prompted not only excitement about their usefulness for research but also concern about biosecurity risks. We recruited 46 subject-matter experts in biology and biosecurity, and 22 generalist forecasters to estimate the risks of growing LLM capabilities. Most respondents expected some hypothetical LLM capabilities to increase their estimates of risk and dramatically underestimated the rate of LLM progress in those capabilities. When these capabilities arose, the median forecast did update as anticipated. The median expert initially predicted a 0.3% annual risk of a human-caused epidemic that causes 100,000 deaths. This estimate then rose to 1.5% conditional on several hypothetical LLM capabilities, including matching the performance of a top-performing team of virologists on a virology troubleshooting test, which the median expert did not expect to occur until 2030. Given this finding, we conducted a baselining study and found that LLMs already crossed this performance threshold in April 2025. A follow-up survey conducted after these results were available found that forecasters significantly updated their median unconditional risk estimates upward, with the new median expert forecast of annual risk rising to 1.5% (as anticipated by the earlier conditional forecasts). More encouragingly, most experts thought that the adoption of LLM safeguards and mandatory nucleic acid screening would negate the risk associated with some hypothetical LLM capabilities.

papers.title: Assessment of Risks, Efficiency, Costs, and Gain of Natural Hazard (Catastrophe) Consequences Prevention Based on Geophysical Monitoring
papers.abstract: The purpose of this paper is to quantitatively estimate the efficiency of forecasting hazards and catastrophic processes induced by high-energy terrestrial sources, based on an integrated monitoring of the state of geophysical processes. Using methods of mathematical statistics and detection theory, relations have been obtained that can be used to calculate the coefficients of the efficiency of warning of catastrophes and the costs associated with a predicted event. The hazard (catastrophe) prevention efficiency coefficient has been shown to be dependent only on the conditional probability of missing a hazard. The relative cost parameter is a function of five parameters: a priori probability of the unwanted event, a conditional false alarm probability, a conditional missed detect probability, relative costs in the case of false alarm probability, and costs to minimize consequences of the hazardous event in case it has been accurately forecast. The gain from organizing geophysical monitoring has been estimated for a few dangers and catastrophes of terrestrial nature. The gain has been shown to be significant in many cases. An energy-based classification of the most important natural sources of hazards and catastrophes, as well as their consequences, is proposed or improved.

papers.title: An Agent‐Based Model for Post‐Disaster Resource Allocation Considering Dynamic Demand
papers.abstract: In the response phase of a disaster, effective and equitable resource allocation is critical for meeting the needs of affected populations and maintaining the social order in disaster-stricken areas. However, dynamic demand driven by the mobility of disaster-affected populations can substantially impact resource allocation outcomes. To consider this mobility in the resource allocation problem, in this paper, we employ an agent-based model to simulate cross-shelter movements and assess the performance of resource allocation strategies considering a gradual increase of total available resources over time. A novel resource allocation strategy is proposed, which leverages demand estimation through a machine learning (ML) method-XGBoost. We then compare this approach against two conventional strategies: uniform distribution and historical data averaging. Through case studies using real-world data of Typhoon Ragasa from Shenzhen in China and Lal-lo in the Philippines, we demonstrate that our proposed strategy comprehensively outperforms the other two in terms of effectiveness, equity and stability. In conclusion, this ML-based prediction approach offers valuable insights to support decision-makers in the formulation of resource allocation plans.

papers.title: Systemic Risk Revisited: A Working Definition and Diagnostic Framework for Risk Analysis
papers.abstract: Systemic risk has gained increasing attention across disaster risk reduction, climate governance, finance, infrastructure, and other domains, yet its meaning and application remain inconsistent. Existing definitions emphasize interdependence, contagion, complexity, uncertainty, cascading effects, and system-wide disruption, but differ in analytical focus and operational use. This paper reviews major definitional traditions and argues that a working definition and diagnostic framework can clarify the analytical basis of systemic risk. We define systemic risk as potential damage, loss, and impact that propagate through interdependencies, feedbacks, and nonlinear processes within or across interconnected systems. Building on this definition, the paper develops a diagnostic framework based on system structure, propagation pathways, dynamic mechanisms, and cascading consequences. These dimensions help distinguish systemic risks from risks that are severe, complex, or large scale but remain relatively contained, and provide a structured basis for examining how adverse consequences propagate within and across interconnected systems in different domains.
